items.videoDescription:
What if you could turn a random Instagram Reel into an entire ambient music track in just 12 minutes?
Here's the experiment.

I found a video of a musician creating strange, atmospheric sounds using everyday electrical devices.
No traditional instruments. Just electricity, electronics, and some wonderfully unconventional sound design.
Then I gave that video to GPT-6 + OpenAI Codex with a simple request: "Create four minutes of relaxing ambient music inspired by this."
12 minutes later, I had a complete 4-minute ambient track. No hours spent tweaking synthesizers. No complicated music production workflow.
Just a visual and sonic reference, a creative prompt, and AI doing its thing.

In this video, you'll see the original experimental sound performance, followed by the AI-created result.
And the fascinating part isn't just the speed.
It's how AI can take an unusual creative reference and turn it into something entirely different while preserving the original atmosphere.

One Instagram Reel. One AI-powered workflow. Four minutes of ambient music. Twelve minutes to create it.
The line between inspiration and production is getting remarkably thin.

Would you listen to an entire album made this way?

#GPT6 #OpenAICodex #AIMusic #AmbientMusic #GenerativeAI #CreativeCoding #Shorts

items.title: Claude Code Can Recreate Any Website Animation Frame by Frame | /reanimate
items.excerpt: Ever found an amazing animation on a website and wished you could recreate it in your own project? Not just something similar. The actual movement, timing, transitions, and visual effects. Meet /reanimate, a new open-sou
items.videoDescription:
Ever found an amazing animation on a website and wished you could recreate it in your own project?

Not just something similar. The actual movement, timing, transitions, and visual effects.

Meet /reanimate, a new open-source Claude Code skill that reverse-engineers animations frame by frame and rebuilds them directly in your code.

And the results are pretty impressive.

Here's how it works:

Capture: Give Claude a website URL, screen recording, MP4, or GIF containing the animation you want.

Analyze: The skill extracts movement, timing, easing curves, element positions, and visual properties frame by frame.

Rebuild: Claude recreates the animation using your existing technology stack, including CSS, Framer Motion, GSAP, or Three.js.

Compare: It records the recreated animation and compares it against the original.

Refine: The agent identifies differences and automatically iterates until the result meets its target or reports remaining issues.

And here's where things get really interesting.

This isn't limited to simple CSS transitions.

Reanimate can inspect complex graphics built with:

Three.js: Interactive 3D scenes and animations

WebGL and WebGPU: GPU-powered visual effects

Canvas: Procedural graphics and particle systems

GSAP and Framer Motion: Complex timelines, transitions, and interactive effects

The skill can even trace shaders, GPU rendering calls, and animated properties to understand how sophisticated visual effects work.

But how accurate is it?

According to the project's own demonstrations:

A complex 3D cube animation recreated with 0.11% pixel difference

Interactive feature cards with less than 0.6% difference

A particle-based star animation with just 0.014% difference during a click effect

These are developer-reported examples, not guaranteed results for every animation.

The skill's pixel-perfect mode targets a mean pixel mismatch of 2% or less.

And unlike simply generating a video that looks similar, the result is actual editable code you can integrate into your project.

Install /reanimate:

npx skills add NiazMorshed2007/reanimate -g

Then open Claude Code and try something like:

/reanimate the hero animation from https://example.com into components/Hero.tsx

You'll need Bun 1.1+ on macOS or Linux. The first run also downloads Chromium and FFmpeg.

The project is free and open source under the MIT license. Remember to respect the original creators' rights when reusing visual assets.

And here's why I find this particularly exciting.

Until recently, recreating a sophisticated website animation meant spending hours studying the original, guessing how it worked, and manually tweaking countless tiny details.

Now an AI coding agent can record, analyze, reconstruct, and visually verify the entire process.

We're moving from AI that copies what a website looks like to AI that can reconstruct how it moves.

That's a pretty significant step for creative coding and frontend development.

And a potentially dangerous development for anyone hoping their beautiful website animation will remain unique for long.

/reanimate on GitHub:
https://github.com/NiazMorshed2007/reanimate

Live demonstrations:
https://reanimate.niazmorshed.dev/

#ClaudeCode #Reanimate #CreativeCoding #WebAnimation #MotionDesign #VibeCoding

items.title: MetaWrap: Turn Any AI-Generated 3D Character Into a MetaHuman | Blender + Unreal Engine 5
items.excerpt: AI can generate impressive 3D characters in seconds. But there's always been one annoying problem. Beautiful geometry doesn't automatically mean a production-ready character. Messy topology. Unpredictable edge loops. Dif
items.videoDescription:
AI can generate impressive 3D characters in seconds.

But there's always been one annoying problem.

Beautiful geometry doesn't automatically mean a production-ready character.

Messy topology. Unpredictable edge loops. Difficult rigging. Broken facial expressions.

And quite a lot of cleanup before you can actually use the character in a game or animation.

Meet MetaWrap, a Blender add-on that converts AI-generated characters, 3D scans, and custom sculpts into standardized MetaHuman topology.

And it's a pretty interesting solution to one of the biggest problems in AI-assisted 3D production.

Here's how it works.

1. Start with almost any 3D character.

Import a model generated with Tripo, Meshy, Rodin, Hunyuan3D, or another 3D generator.

You can also use a traditional sculpt or a scanned character.

2. Automatically wrap the geometry.

MetaWrap places anatomical landmarks and adapts the MetaHuman template mesh to match your character's head and body.

If the automatic result isn't quite right, you can manually adjust the landmarks.

3. Transfer textures and details.

The add-on transfers the original character's colors onto MetaHuman UV coordinates.

You can also project high-resolution sculpted details and bake normal, cavity, and wrinkle maps.

4. Check facial expressions.

Inspect how the new geometry behaves with MetaHuman expressions, refine facial features, and correct problematic areas before export.

5. Send everything to Unreal Engine.

MetaWrap transfers the geometry and textures into Unreal Engine, where the character can be further developed using MetaHuman Creator and the MetaHuman animation pipeline.

And here's the really important part.

The resulting character uses standardized MetaHuman topology, regardless of the topology produced by the original AI generator.

Instead of fighting a completely different mesh every time, you get a consistent starting point for your character production workflow.

The package also includes MetaSculpt for detail refinement and MetaGroom for working with character hair.

Compatibility:

Blender 5.0–5.2

Unreal Engine 5.6–5.8

Windows 64-bit

Minimum 16 GB RAM

NVIDIA RTX GPU with at least 8 GB VRAM

Price: $158 for the Founder Edition, a one-time purchase covering MetaWrap, MetaSculpt, and MetaGroom.

Of course, this isn't a magic button that turns every messy AI-generated character into a flawless production asset.

Complex geometry, facial details, skin deformations, and textures may still require manual refinement.

And MetaWrap doesn't replace the actual MetaHuman rigging system inside Unreal Engine.

But here's what I particularly like about this approach.

Instead of building yet another isolated AI character generator, MetaWrap connects generative 3D tools to an established professional production pipeline.

Generate the character with AI.

Standardize its topology.

Refine it in Blender.

Finish it in Unreal Engine.

That's the kind of integration that could make AI-generated 3D genuinely useful in real production.

Because generating a beautiful character is only the beginning.

Making that character actually work is where things get interesting.

Explore MetaWrap:
https://www.metawrap.ai/

items.videoDescription:
Well, I guess it's time to uninstall Hermes Desktop and move back into the terminal.

Hermes Agent v0.23.0 just added native inline image rendering.

And honestly, this is exactly the kind of small improvement that makes terminal-based AI agents much more enjoyable to use.

Here's what's new:

Inline images: Pictures appear directly inside the terminal conversation instead of showing file paths.

AI-generated visuals: See images produced by your agent without opening another application.

Computer Use screenshots: Inspect screenshots captured by your AI tools right in the conversation.

Image attachments: Paste or attach images and see them alongside your messages.

Full-color rendering: Supported terminals display actual images rather than ASCII approximations.

Terminal support includes:

Ghostty and Kitty: Native image rendering in CLI and TUI.

iTerm2, WezTerm, and Konsole: Inline images in the classic CLI.

VS Code terminal: Full-resolution images when terminal image support is enabled.

Other terminals: Colorful Unicode block rendering as a fallback.

And there's more in the Hermes Agent 0.23.0 Hearth Release, including /rewind, shared conversation gateways, browser access, and improved multi-agent workflows.

But for me, the inline images are a particularly welcome addition.

Because sometimes I don't want another desktop application.

I just want my terminal to do everything.

Code? Terminal.

AI agents? Terminal.

Screenshots? Terminal.

At this rate, the only remaining reason to leave the terminal will be remembering what sunlight looks like.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon Built a 3D Renderer From Scratch (No Blender)
items.excerpt: Gemini 4 Carbon just built its own 3D rendering pipeline using C++ and NVIDIA CUDA, then created a 60-second physics-based animation without Blender or traditional keyframe animation. This isn't AI-generated video. It's
items.videoDescription:
Gemini 4 Carbon just built its own 3D rendering pipeline using C++ and NVIDIA CUDA, then created a 60-second physics-based animation without Blender or traditional keyframe animation.

This isn't AI-generated video. It's AI-generated software creating a physically simulated 3D scene.

In this experiment by @fofrAI, Google's Gemini 4 Carbon took on an entire technical 3D production workflow.

Here's what Carbon reportedly built:

• Custom CUDA/C++ renderer: a GPU-accelerated path tracer written from scratch to calculate realistic lighting, reflections, and shadows.

• MuJoCo physics integration: rigid-body simulation handling gravity, collisions, friction, and physical interactions.

• Rube Goldberg machine: a complex chain-reaction mechanism with balls, levers, and interconnected moving objects.

• 120,000 physics steps: 60 seconds of simulated motion at 2,000 steps per second, without manually animated keyframes.

• Procedural 3D environment: a complete studio scene with a continuous cinematic camera movement.

• AI-generated soundtrack: original music created with Google's Lyria 3.5, synchronized with the camera animation.

The important distinction: Gemini didn't simply generate frames from a text prompt. It wrote rendering software, integrated an existing physics engine, constructed a scene, and produced the resulting animation.

Tools like Blender, Houdini, and NVIDIA Omniverse aren't disappearing. But AI agents that can build specialized 3D pipelines on demand could change how digital content is produced.

Is this the future of procedural 3D animation, or just an impressive technical experiment?

items.videoDescription:
What if an AI agent could handle an entire 3D production pipeline?

Meet Tripo Agentic Canvas, a new AI-powered workspace inside Tripo Studio. And this is a pretty interesting step toward autonomous 3D production.

Here's the problem.

AI can already generate impressive 3D models.

But getting those models ready for actual production is another story.

Retopology. UV mapping. Texturing. Rigging. Mesh repair. Export settings.

An endless collection of technical steps between "Look what AI generated!" and "I can actually use this."

Tripo Agentic Canvas tries to automate that entire process.

Instead of manually switching between different tools, you describe what you want to create.

The built-in AI agent plans the workflow, organizes the operations into connected nodes, and executes the steps in sequence.

And you can see everything happening on one visual canvas.

Here's what Agentic Canvas can do:

AI workflow planning: Describe your goal and let the agent organize the necessary production steps.

Node-based pipelines: Connect 3D generation, retopology, UV mapping, texturing, rigging, and export.

Interactive editing: Modify individual nodes without rebuilding the entire project.

AI 3D Lab: Inspect, repair, and modify assets using natural-language instructions.

Reusable workflows: Save pipelines and apply them to new models or entire batches of assets.

Human supervision: Review intermediate results or let the agent execute an approved plan automatically.

And here's where things get really interesting.

Tripo demonstrated two complete production workflows.

1. From Concept Art to a Rigged Unreal Engine Character

Start with a reference image.

The agent plans the process, generates individual character components, assembles them, refines the geometry, and creates a skeletal rig.

The final asset can then be exported for further work in Unreal Engine.

Instead of manually moving files between disconnected tools, the entire process stays organized inside one workflow.

2. From a Sketch to a 3D-Printable Model

This one is particularly useful.

Start with a rough drawing or reference image.

The agent generates a 3D model and prepares it for physical production.

But creating something that looks like a printable object isn't enough.

The mesh actually needs to be suitable for printing.

So the workflow can inspect the model for:

Holes and non-manifold geometry

Problems with watertight surfaces

Insufficient wall thickness

Mesh defects that could cause printing failures

Then AI 3D Lab attempts to repair the geometry before exporting the model for slicing.

And here's an important distinction.

Mesh repair isn't the same as retopology.

Retopology changes the structure or density of the mesh.

Mesh repair addresses problems that could prevent the object from being manufactured correctly.

Both may be necessary, but they solve different problems.

And there's another feature I particularly like.

You can save the entire workflow as a reusable template.

Imagine building a pipeline for preparing game characters.

You generate the first character, refine the steps, and get everything working.

Then you reuse the same process for the next ten characters.

Or fifty.

That's considerably more interesting than manually repeating the same operations every time.

But does this mean AI can now produce flawless, production-ready 3D assets?

Not quite.

Automatic rigging still needs deformation checks.

Game assets still need appropriate optimization and engine testing.

And 3D-printing workflows still require validation before sending a model to a physical printer.

There's also a practical limitation.

Agentic Canvas is currently in beta, available to Tripo MAX and Team users, with access gradually expanding to other accounts.

Generation and processing operations consume Tripo credits.

Still, here's what I find fascinating.

We're moving from AI models that generate individual assets to AI agents that manage the entire production process.

And that's a much more significant change than simply generating prettier 3D objects.

For years, building 3D content meant carefully coordinating specialized tools and repetitive production stages.

Now those stages are becoming something an AI agent can plan, connect, and execute.

The future of AI-assisted 3D might not be another spectacular text-to-3D model.

It might be an agent that knows what to do with the model after generating it.

And honestly, that's the part of 3D production that could use some serious automation.

items.excerpt: Someone just gave the 3ds Max viewport a serious visual upgrade. And it costs just $15. Meet xCavity, a new plugin that brings Blender-style cavity shading, MatCaps, and screen-space lighting effects directly into the na
items.videoDescription:
Someone just gave the 3ds Max viewport a serious visual upgrade.

And it costs just $15.

Meet xCavity, a new plugin that brings Blender-style cavity shading, MatCaps, and screen-space lighting effects directly into the native 3ds Max viewport.

No complicated material setups.

No OSL shader tricks.

No switching to an external renderer just to get a better look at your geometry.

Just install the plugin, select a viewport shading mode, and start modeling.

And honestly, this is one of those small tools that makes you wonder why the functionality wasn't already built into 3ds Max.

Here's what xCavity offers.

1. Blender-Style Cavity Shading

If you've ever used Blender's Solid viewport with Cavity enabled, you probably know how useful it can be.

Small surface details become easier to read.

Edges and creases stand out.

Complex hard-surface geometry suddenly becomes much more understandable.

xCavity brings a similar approach to 3ds Max.

2. MatCap Shading

Want to inspect your model with a clean, studio-style material?

MatCaps provide convenient lighting and material appearances without requiring a complete scene setup.

They're particularly useful for checking forms, surface transitions, and proportions while modeling.

3. Screen-Space Global Illumination (SSGI)

Here's where things get especially interesting.

xCavity includes screen-space global illumination, adding an approximation of indirect lighting to the viewport.

This can help objects feel more grounded and give models additional depth without performing an offline render.

There's also support for screen-space reflections (SSR) and diagnostic visualization modes.

4. Native Nitrous Viewport Integration

And this is arguably the most important technical detail.

xCavity works directly with the 3ds Max Nitrous viewport through DirectX.

It doesn't require assigning special materials to your objects or replacing your existing shaders.

Instead, the new shading options integrate into the regular viewport shading menu alongside familiar modes such as Clay.

The developer designed them to behave like native viewport styles.

No OSL. No material overrides. No additional rendering engine.

And because the processing happens through the viewport graphics pipeline, the result is designed to remain responsive during modeling.

5. Customizable Appearance

You're not locked into a single preset.

The plugin provides adjustable shading and post-processing options so you can tune the look to your modeling workflow.

Whether you're working on mechanical parts, product designs, detailed hard-surface assets, or architectural geometry, having better visual feedback can make a surprising difference.

But there's an important distinction.

SSGI and SSR are screen-space effects.

They use information available to the viewport rather than calculating complete physically accurate global illumination.

That means off-screen geometry, hidden surfaces, and complex lighting situations can produce limitations or artifacts.

This is a modeling and viewport visualization tool, not a replacement for V-Ray, Corona, Arnold, or Redshift.

And that's perfectly fine.

Because sometimes you don't need a physically accurate render.

You just need to see what you're modeling.

And that's exactly why I like this idea.

A good modeling viewport should make geometry readable, provide useful visual feedback, and stay out of your way.

Blender has offered some excellent viewport visualization tools for years.

And bringing similar capabilities into 3ds Max through a lightweight plugin makes a lot of sense.

Especially for artists who spend most of their time modeling rather than rendering.

The price? $15.

Not a bad proposition for something you might use throughout every modeling session.

Just check compatibility with your particular version of 3ds Max before purchasing.

items.title: NVIDIA VFlash: 5× Faster AI Robot Planning with Better Accuracy | Physical AI
items.excerpt: What if robots could think and react five times faster without upgrading their hardware? And what if they became more accurate at the same time? Meet NVIDIA VFlash, a new visual planning framework designed to make AI-pow
items.videoDescription:
What if robots could think and react five times faster without upgrading their hardware?

And what if they became more accurate at the same time?

Meet NVIDIA VFlash, a new visual planning framework designed to make AI-powered robots and autonomous vehicles dramatically faster at deciding what to do next.

And the technical results are pretty impressive.

Here's the problem.

Modern vision-language models can understand images, describe environments, and generate plans for robots.

But there's a catch.

When a robot needs to calculate a movement trajectory, traditional autoregressive models often generate coordinates one token at a time.

One coordinate. Then another. Then another.

For robots operating in the physical world, that can be painfully slow.

VFlash takes a different approach.

Instead of predicting every coordinate sequentially, it generates complete visual planning structures in parallel.

An entire bounding box.

A complete 2D or 3D trajectory.

A sequence of movement points.

All in one parallel drafting step.

And here's where things get really interesting.

VFlash uses a lightweight, five-layer transformer to predict these structured outputs.

The larger vision-language model provides context and processes the resulting plan, rather than generating every coordinate individually.

The result? A massive reduction in decoding time.

According to NVIDIA's benchmarks on Jetson Thor:

Traditional autoregressive planning: 3,552.7 milliseconds

VFlash planning: 703.3 milliseconds

Overall model pipeline: Approximately 5.1× faster

Decoding alone: 3,107.6 ms reduced to just 258.2 ms

Decoding acceleration: Approximately 12× faster

On NVIDIA DGX Spark, the complete planning step dropped from 3,356.5 ms to 649.9 ms.

That's another roughly fivefold improvement.

But speed isn't the only improvement.

NVIDIA also reports better geometric accuracy.

42.6% lower average 3D displacement error

28–61% lower waypoint errors across selected evaluations

70.2% success rate on MolmoSpaces robot manipulation tasks

62.6% success rate for the original baseline

61.0% success rate with traditional autoregressive visual plans

So VFlash didn't just generate robot movements faster.

In these experiments, it also produced more accurate plans.

And that matters enormously for physical AI.

Imagine a robot arm manipulating fragile objects, a humanoid navigating a crowded room, or an autonomous vehicle continuously planning its next movement.

Every unnecessary delay in planning can make the system less responsive.

But there's an important technical distinction.

VFlash isn't a completely new robot foundation model.

It's a decoding framework that accelerates how existing vision-language models generate structured visual plans.

And the reported speedups refer to measured AI model pipelines, not necessarily the complete physical reaction time of a robot.

Real-world performance still depends on sensors, motor controllers, actuation, and the surrounding system.

Still, the implications are fascinating.

We've spent years making AI models larger and more capable.

Now researchers are discovering that changing how models generate their outputs can deliver enormous performance improvements without replacing the underlying hardware.

And there's another interesting aspect.

Robots don't necessarily need to think entirely in words.

A language model might describe an action as:

"Move the robotic arm toward the object, grasp it, and place it on the table."

But a physical machine ultimately needs coordinates, trajectories, spatial relationships, and control signals.

VFlash is designed to make that transition from perception to action considerably more efficient.

From predicting words to predicting movement.

And that's a pretty important step toward making AI useful in the physical world.

Because the next generation of AI isn't just going to answer questions on our screens.

It's going to move things.

Build things.

And interact with the world around us.

And when robots start acting in the real world, milliseconds suddenly matter a lot more than tokens per second.

items.excerpt: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on some tasks but remains behind it on several others. But here's the experiment that really caught my attention. Inkling 2 Small autonomously trained another AI model. Thinking Machines gave it a cha
items.videoDescription:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on some tasks but remains behind it on several others.

But here's the experiment that really caught my attention.

Inkling 2 Small autonomously trained another AI model.

Thinking Machines gave it a challenge:

Take Qwen3.5-4B and improve its ability to forecast time series.

Things like weather patterns, electricity demand, and Wikipedia page views.

And then they let the agent work.

Here's what happened:

Inkling analyzed the forecasting problem.

It wrote its own evaluation code.

It discovered and corrected a bug in that evaluator.

It prepared training datasets.

It experimented with supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

It tried reinforcement learning (RL).

It compared checkpoints and selected the best-performing model.

The final result?

4 hours and 17 minutes of autonomous work

$426 spent through Tinker

Qwen3.5-4B successfully fine-tuned

More than 2× improvement in the internal forecasting score

Approximately 15% lower prediction error on previously unseen data

And that's a much more interesting result than simply winning another chatbot benchmark.

An AI agent researched, trained, evaluated, debugged, and improved another AI model.

Not perfectly. Not without limitations.

But with relatively little human intervention during the experiment.

And there's more.

Thinking Machines also tested Inkling 2 Small on GPU kernel optimization.

On PMPP-Hard, a benchmark involving 69 GPU programming challenges, the model solved an average of 54.25 tasks across four independent attempts.

That's close to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 55.25.

The model was also trained to handle extended coding tasks across different agent frameworks, with more emphasis on verifying its work rather than simply producing code that passes tests.

Now for availability.

Inkling 2 Small is currently available through Tinker Playground, including model sampling and fine-tuning.

The weights are still closed.

However, Thinking Machines plans to release the full weights under Apache 2.0, following external safety testing.

The company has indicated that this could happen within a week of the November 5 announcement, although the exact timing depends on those reviews.

And here's why I find this release particularly interesting.

For years, most AI benchmarks measured whether a model could answer difficult questions.

Now we're increasingly evaluating whether models can complete complex work.

Build a website.

Develop an application.

Optimize GPU code.

Run scientific experiments.

Or fine-tune another neural network.

The next major step for AI agents might not be generating better answers.

It might be independently improving the systems and tools we already use.

And watching a supposedly "small" model train another model in four hours is a pretty compelling demonstration of where things are heading.

594 billion parameters. Seventeen billion active. And apparently, Small is the new Large.

items.excerpt: What if you could generate entire interactive worlds using AI, control them with text prompts, and explore them by moving the camera? And what if you could run the whole thing on a single consumer GPU? Meet Hy-Nomas, a n
items.videoDescription:
What if you could generate entire interactive worlds using AI, control them with text prompts, and explore them by moving the camera?

And what if you could run the whole thing on a single consumer GPU?

Meet Hy-Nomas, a new open-source interactive world model released by Tencent Hunyuan.

And this is a pretty interesting development in the rapidly evolving world of generative AI.

We've already seen Google Genie and Odyssey creating explorable AI-generated environments.

But Tencent is taking a different approach.

It's releasing the model weights, training code, and inference tools for everyone to experiment with.

Here's what Hy-Nomas can do:

Generate interactive worlds: Create evolving environments from text prompts.

Control the camera: Change viewpoints, movement, and camera trajectories.

Modify the world as you go: Introduce new objects, change the scenery, switch visual styles, or describe new actions.

Remember previous scenes: Maintain context between generated video segments using a persistent KV cache.

Generate vertical video: Produce 720 × 1280 output at 24 FPS.

Use reference images: Start a world from an uploaded image in the updated online demo.

LoRA fine-tuning: Adapt the model for specialized applications, including robotics.

But here's the really interesting part.

Hy-Nomas can run on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090.

Normally, a world generation model of this kind would require a much more expensive multi-GPU setup.

And Tencent's standard inference configuration does indeed use eight GPUs.

However, the developers created a special low-memory mode that makes single-GPU inference possible.

How does it work?

INT8 quantization reduces memory requirements for model weights.

An INT8 KV cache stores previously generated context more efficiently.

An FP8 video decoder further reduces memory consumption.

CPU offloading moves components between system RAM and GPU memory when needed.

A sliding context window helps prevent GPU memory usage from growing indefinitely.

There's a catch, of course.

Running on an RTX 4090 doesn't mean generating worlds in real time.

The advertised 24 FPS describes the output video's playback frame rate, not the speed at which the model generates it.

And CPU offloading introduces additional overhead.

Still, getting a model like this running on consumer hardware is a significant step toward making interactive world generation more accessible.

And the project is genuinely open source.

Tencent released it under the Apache 2.0 license, including:

Model weights on Hugging Face

Training and inference code

An interactive web demo

LoRA fine-tuning tools

Integration options for ComfyUI, SGLang, and other community projects

The developers have also published a technical report and Hy-Nomas-Bench, a collection of 280 test cases covering interaction, camera control, and spatial memory.

But independent comparisons of real-world generation speed and quality are still needed.

Why does this matter?

Because world models could become much more than another way to generate videos.

Imagine AI agents learning to navigate virtual environments, robots practicing tasks in simulated worlds, or game developers building interactive prototypes from simple descriptions.

And now imagine researchers and independent developers being able to experiment with the underlying technology themselves.

We're moving from AI-generated videos to AI-generated worlds.

And increasingly, those worlds won't need a giant cloud computing cluster to exist.

One RTX 4090. An open-source world model. And an almost unlimited number of strange places to explore.

Not bad.

items.title: 12 Claude Code Agents Turned 64 Scientific Papers Into an Interactive Physics Lab
items.excerpt: What if you could turn dozens of scientific research papers into an interactive laboratory you can actually experiment with? Not just summaries. Not another chatbot explaining complicated equations. Actual working simula
items.videoDescription:
What if you could turn dozens of scientific research papers into an interactive laboratory you can actually experiment with?

Not just summaries. Not another chatbot explaining complicated equations.

Actual working simulations built directly from published research.

A fascinating Claude Code experiment attributed to Boris Cherny, the creator of Claude Code, shows what happens when you give 12 AI agents 64 scientific papers about fluid dynamics and ask them to build a browser-based laboratory.

And the result is beautiful.

Here's what the agents reportedly created:

Interactive fluid simulations: Choose different experiments and watch physical phenomena unfold.

Adjustable parameters: Change conditions using sliders and immediately see how the results respond.

Multiple simulation methods: Compare different approaches using the same experimental settings.

Scientific references: Explore equations, source code, and measurements alongside each animation.

Research verification: Compare simulation outputs with the results reported in the original papers.

But here's the really interesting part.

The agents didn't all work on the same problem.

They had specialized responsibilities.

Research agents extracted equations, assumptions, and experimental parameters from the papers.

Development agents translated those methods into working simulation code.

Interface agents built the interactive controls and visualizations.

Review agents checked the implementations against the original research, looking for numerical errors, instability, and discrepancies.

According to the circulated demonstration, the project covered 11 simulation methods across 28 reference scenarios, with seven meeting the selected validation tolerances and four requiring further review.

Those figures are reported rather than independently verified.

And that distinction matters.

A beautiful simulation isn't necessarily a scientifically accurate simulation.

But imagine applying this workflow to your own research.

A collection of scientific papers becomes an interactive environment where you can test assumptions, compare methods, adjust variables, and inspect the underlying code.

Want to try something similar?

Here's a prompt you can adapt for Claude Code:

"Turn these research papers into an interactive browser-based laboratory.

Extract the methods, equations, assumptions, and experimental parameters from each paper, including page references.

Assign different methods to specialized agents, using shared inputs and measurement tools so the results can be compared.

Have independent review agents verify each implementation against the original paper. Document discrepancies and clearly mark unverified results.

Build an interactive interface with parameter sliders, visual simulations, method comparisons, and access to the source code behind each experiment.

Make the experiments reproducible, including their dependencies, reference data, and validation procedures."

Start with one paper and one experiment, verify the results, and expand from there.

And here's what I find genuinely exciting.

We're moving beyond AI that simply reads research papers and tells us what they say.

We're approaching a world where AI agents can help turn scientific knowledge into working, explorable software.

From reading science to experimenting with it.

That's a much more interesting use of AI than generating another thousand summaries nobody will ever read.

items.videoDescription:
Remember when drones needed human pilots, GPS, and a reliable connection to navigate?

Well, apparently, those days are numbered.

Researchers at Purdue University have demonstrated an autonomous drone that can follow a person through a dense forest without GPS or cloud connectivity.

And the footage is genuinely unsettling.

Here's what the drone can reportedly do:

Autonomous tracking: Identify and follow a moving person without continuous manual steering.

No GPS required: Navigate without relying on satellite positioning.

No internet connection: Process navigation and tracking information onboard.

Real-time obstacle avoidance: Navigate around trees and other obstacles while maintaining its route.

Movement prediction: Estimate where a person is heading when they temporarily disappear behind obstacles.

Environmental mapping: Build a representation of the surrounding environment using onboard sensors.

Viral posts have also credited Claude Opus 5.5 with helping develop this kind of autonomous tracking system, although its involvement in the Purdue demonstration hasn't been independently confirmed.

And here's the slightly terrifying part.

The same technology that could help rescue teams locate missing people in forests could also enable increasingly sophisticated autonomous surveillance.

Or something considerably worse.

We're entering an era where AI-powered machines can perceive their surroundings, make navigation decisions, and physically pursue moving targets.

Without waiting for instructions from a remote server.

Of course, this is still an experimental research demonstration, not proof that autonomous drones can reliably track anyone under all conditions.

But watching that little machine weave between trees while following a human is enough to make you wonder where all this is heading.

The future of robotics is looking impressive.

Unfortunately, it also looks like the opening scene of a science-fiction horror movie.

And as software developers love to say:

It's not a bug. It's a feature.

It's real-time generative art driven by environmental data.

Created in 2017, Gust belongs to Canogar's Echo series, which explores a fascinating idea: screens are no longer just windows into digital worlds.

They're becoming something closer to skin.

Flexible surfaces that wrap around objects, buildings, and architecture, responding to the world around them.

Instead of simply showing us images, these screens begin to sense their environment.

The result is something between a digital organism, a living painting, and a piece of architecture.

And personally, I find that far more interesting than another enormous advertising billboard.

items.videoDescription:
Google just made Antigravity a little more useful for developers, researchers, and anyone working with AI-generated code and data.

Google Antigravity now supports Jupyter Notebooks natively.

And yes, that means you can finally open .ipynb files directly inside your AI development workspace.

No switching to another application just to inspect your agent's results.

Here's what's new.

With Antigravity's built-in Jupyter Notebook viewer, you can explore:

Python code cells: View source code with syntax highlighting.

Markdown documentation: Read explanations, formulas, and experiment notes.

Data tables: Inspect structured results without leaving the workspace.

Charts and visualizations: View graphs and plots saved in the notebook.

Images: Examine visual outputs produced during experiments.

Cell outputs: Review text, calculations, and results from previous executions.

And here's why this matters for AI coding agents.

Imagine asking your agent to analyze a dataset, investigate a machine learning model, or prepare a scientific experiment.

The agent produces a Jupyter Notebook containing code, explanations, charts, and results.

Previously, reviewing everything could mean switching between different tools.

Now you can inspect the entire notebook directly inside Antigravity.

Code, data, explanations, and visualizations in one place.

And that makes it easier to understand what your AI agent actually produced.

There's one important limitation.

This is currently a native notebook viewer, not a complete Jupyter execution environment.

You can inspect existing code and saved outputs, but running cells still requires a Jupyter runtime or another execution workflow.

So don't confuse notebook visualization with full interactive notebook execution.

The feature arrived with Antigravity v2.29.0, released on November 3, 2026, and was highlighted by Google on November 5.

It's a relatively small update compared with autonomous coding agents and cloud execution.

But sometimes the most useful improvements are the ones that remove unnecessary friction.

Because AI agents generating code is impressive. Being able to inspect and understand what they actually did is even more important.

And native Jupyter support is another step toward making agentic development environments useful beyond traditional software engineering.

items.title: ComfyUI-PhotoDeblur: Fix Camera Shake & Motion Blur with HI-Diff and MISCFilter
items.excerpt: That night photo was almost perfect. Except your hands decided to shake at exactly the wrong moment. Meet ComfyUI-PhotoDeblur, a free, open-source node pack by porfeng that helps restore photos affected by camera shake a
items.videoDescription:
That night photo was almost perfect. Except your hands decided to shake at exactly the wrong moment.

Meet ComfyUI-PhotoDeblur, a free, open-source node pack by porfeng that helps restore photos affected by camera shake and motion blur.

And here's the interesting part: it works at your photo's original resolution. No mandatory downscaling just to fit the image into VRAM.

Instead of reaching for another generative upscaler, you get two specialized image-restoration models inside ComfyUI:

HI-Diff: A diffusion-based deblurring model that gradually reconstructs sharper details.

MISCFilter: A direct, single-pass restoration model. No diffusion sampling steps required.

Think handheld night photos, smeared neon signs, soft storefront edges, blurry architectural details, and motion trails around lights.

What makes the nodes useful?

Tiled processing: Split large photos into manageable regions and blend them back together. The suggested starting point is 768-pixel tiles with 96 pixels of overlap.

Flexible blending: Linear, cosine, Gaussian, and average options help reduce visible seams.

8-way TTA: Average rotated and mirrored predictions to improve stability, at roughly eight times the model computation.

Match Input Tone: Reduce broad color shifts so the restored photo stays closer to the original.

Official checkpoints: Download and verify RealBlur_J, RealBlur_R, or GoPro weights directly through a ComfyUI node.

Want to try it?

Install comfyui-photodeblur through ComfyUI Manager or clone the repository into custom_nodes. Load one of the included example workflows.

Start with RealBlur_J, tile 768, overlap 96, TTA off. Run the same photo through both models and compare the results at 100% zoom.

The developer even reports using an 8 GB GPU for the tiled examples. MISCFilter does require NVIDIA CUDA and CuPy, so check the installation notes.

One important reality check: deblurring isn't time travel.

No model can guarantee recovery of details that were never captured. Severe defocus, blown highlights, and tiny heavily blurred faces remain difficult. And because HI-Diff is a learned restoration model, you should still inspect fine details for artifacts.

But if you've ever lost an otherwise beautiful photo to shaky hands, this is exactly the kind of practical ComfyUI tool worth bookmarking.

GitHub, installation and sample workflows:
https://github.com/porfeng/ComfyUI-PhotoDeblur

#ComfyUI #PhotoDeblur #HIDiff #MISCFilter #PhotoRestoration #MotionBlur #OpenSourceAI

items.videoDescription:
What if you could explore more than 1,500 beautifully designed logos from the golden age of graphic design?

No generic AI-generated symbols. No random logo templates.

Real trademarks created by professional designers more than 50 years ago.

Meet symbools, a remarkable digital archive of Trademarks & Symbols, Volume 2: Symbolical Designs, compiled by Japanese design researcher Yasaburo Kuwayama and originally published in 1973.

And honestly, this is a little treasure chest for anyone interested in typography, branding, visual identity, and design history.

Here's what's inside:

1,504 original trademarks and symbols

725 credited designers

1,142 companies and organizations

30 countries represented

SVG and PNG files available individually

Searchable metadata identifying designers, companies, and industries

And here's what makes the collection particularly interesting.

The symbols are organized by visual form and subject.

Explore human figures, animals, birds, flowers, trees, geometric shapes, arrows, circles, typography, and Japanese characters.

You can browse by category, search for a designer or company, and inspect individual designs.

Find a symbol you like?

Open it, examine the details, and copy or download the vector artwork.

The archive was digitized by Kelvin Adithya, who carefully traced the original designs from a scanned copy of Kuwayama's book.

And the project is still being refined, with individual symbols corrected and polished over time.

But here's what I find fascinating.

Look at these designs.

Minimal geometry. Clever negative space. Strong proportions. Simple forms that communicate entire ideas.

Many of them still look remarkably contemporary.

And they were created in an era when designers didn't have Figma, Illustrator, or an AI agent capable of generating 200 logo variations before lunch.

Just research, geometry, experimentation, and an extraordinary amount of visual judgment.

This is why I love historical design archives.

They remind us that great visual ideas don't suddenly become obsolete because the tools change.

You can study how designers simplified complex ideas, balanced shapes, and created memorable symbols using very little visual information.

One important licensing detail.

The archive is free for noncommercial use, including research, teaching, mood boards, and design inspiration.

The original trademarks remain the property of their respective owners.

So you can study the designs and learn from them, but you can't simply download one and use it as your company's new logo.

And that's probably for the best.

Because the real value here isn't copying a 1973 trademark.

It's understanding what made those designs work in the first place.

More than 1,500 symbols. Fifty-three years of design history. And a lifetime of visual inspiration.

Definitely worth bookmarking.

items.title: Autopilot: An AI Game Tester That Plays, Finds Bugs & Learns | Unreal, Unity & Godot
items.excerpt: What if you could give an AI agent your unfinished game and tell it: "Play this. Find everything that's broken. And don't stop until you've tested it properly." Well, someone built exactly that. Meet Aura Autopilot, a ne
items.videoDescription:
What if you could give an AI agent your unfinished game and tell it:

"Play this. Find everything that's broken. And don't stop until you've tested it properly."

Well, someone built exactly that.

Meet Aura Autopilot, a new open-source AI game testing agent that actually plays your game, investigates the code, discovers bugs, and gets better with every session.

And this is a pretty fascinating development for game creators.

Here's how it works.

Instead of simply analyzing your source code and guessing what might go wrong, Autopilot launches the game and starts playing.

It reads your project's code, learns the mechanics, interacts with the environment, and tests how everything behaves.

And yes, it actually controls the game.

It can navigate levels, fight enemies, interact with objects, explore systems, and attempt complex objectives.

Here's what Autopilot can do:

Autonomous gameplay: Play your game through simulated keyboard and mouse input.

Bug detection: Explore levels and identify broken mechanics, unexpected behavior, and gameplay issues.

Feature verification: Test specific functionality and check whether it behaves as intended.

Goal-based testing: Complete objectives such as defeating a boss or finishing a level.

Code analysis: Study the project to understand how game systems work.

Persistent memory: Remember previous attempts and improve its strategies over time.

Testing reports: Document findings and report issues after each session.

And here's the really interesting part.

Autopilot doesn't approach every test as a completely new problem.

It learns from previous gameplay attempts.

The first time it encounters a game, it might struggle with navigation, combat, or unfamiliar mechanics.

But as it explores, it builds knowledge about the game and improves its decision-making.

The developers describe it as a continually learning playtesting system.

And the benchmark results are promising.

According to the developers' tests:

Autopilot: Completed 7 out of 7 game-testing tasks.

Claude Code: Completed 5 out of 7.

Another game-testing agent: Completed 4 out of 7.

That's a 100% success rate versus 71.4% for Claude Code in this small evaluation.

Autopilot was also approximately 1.7× faster than Claude Code, averaging 262 seconds per task instead of 437.

The team separately reports a threefold speed improvement over its previous Aura Verification Agent.

Of course, these are developer-reported benchmarks involving seven tasks in one Unreal Engine project, not proof of universal superiority.

Four ways to test your games:

1. Exploration

"Explore the crafting system and report anything unusual."

2. Testing

"Play through this level and identify all visible gameplay issues."

3. Verification

"Check whether the tree shakes when the player hits it with an axe."

4. Goal

"Defeat the boss without letting your health drop below 20%."

Autopilot launches the game, attempts the task, and generates a report.

And it works with the major game engines:

Unreal Engine 5

Unity 6

Godot 4

Windows and macOS

Want to use it with Claude Code or Codex?

After installing Autopilot and completing its setup, connect your preferred coding agent.

For Claude Code:

autopilot connect claude

For OpenAI Codex:

autopilot connect codex

Then simply ask: "Use Autopilot to explore my current game level, test its mechanics, and report any bugs you find."

The plugin is open source under Apache 2.0. It can use your existing Claude Code or Codex subscription for the coding-agent component, although the decision-model service has its own usage requirements. It's not an entirely offline local AI system. But here's what I find particularly exciting.
We've spent the last few years teaching AI agents to write games. They can generate characters, create environments, implement mechanics, and build entire playable prototypes.

Now they're starting to test those games themselves. Imagine asking an agent to implement a new combat mechanic. 
Discovers that the player gets stuck during an attack animation. Then reports exactly what happened so the problem can be fixed. That's a much more interesting development workflow than simply asking AI to write code and hoping everything works.

Of course, automated testing won't replace experienced QA teams, human playtesters, or actual game design judgment. But it could make testing faster, more frequent, and much more accessible to independent developers. And there's something wonderfully absurd about the idea.

AI builds your game. AI plays your game. AI finds the bugs.
At some point, we might need to remind the agents that humans would occasionally like to play too.

Autopilot on GitHub: https://github.com/ramenvr/autopilot
Download and installation: https://www.tryaura.dev/autopilot/
Official documentation: https://www.tryaura.dev/documentation/autopilot

45 million tokens. Seven hours. One flying superhero.

And we're only getting started with agentic coding.

items.excerpt: Apparently, pulling your phone out of your pocket to approve an AI agent's actions is now considered too much work. So someone built a ring that lets you do it with your thumb. Meet Aina Ring, a new AI-powered smart ring
items.videoDescription:
Apparently, pulling your phone out of your pocket to approve an AI agent's actions is now considered too much work.

So someone built a ring that lets you do it with your thumb.

Meet Aina Ring, a new AI-powered smart ring featuring a tiny OLED display, gesture controls, voice input, and integration with AI agents.

And honestly, it's a pretty interesting idea.

Here's the concept.

As AI agents become increasingly autonomous, humans might spend less time performing tasks and more time approving decisions.

Send that email?

Approve.

Join the meeting?

Approve.

Book a ride?

Approve.

And Aina wants to put those approvals directly on your finger.

Here's what the ring can do:

AI Agent Approvals: Get a notification when your agent needs permission to continue. Flick your thumb to approve or reject.

Smart Cues: Receive contextual suggestions based on your calendar, location, habits, and connected devices.

Voice Commands: Hold the button to talk to an AI agent, dictate notes, or create reminders.

Mac Controls: Manage meetings, mute your microphone, and control applications through gestures.

Phone Calls: See who's calling, answer, or decline without reaching for your phone.

Media Controls: Play, pause, skip tracks, and adjust volume.

But here's the really interesting part.

Aina doesn't want to become another miniature smartphone.

Its interface is designed around something called Cues.

Instead of showing dozens of notifications, the system learns your routines and suggests one relevant action at a time.

For example:

You're about to join a meeting.

Your ring displays:

"Open meeting on Mac?"

One flick of your thumb.

Done.

Or your AI agent wants to send a presentation to a client.

The request appears on your finger.

Approve or reject.

No need to open another chat window.

And yes, there's actual hardware behind the idea.

Small OLED display protected by glass

Seven thumb-controlled gestures

Titanium construction

Up to 18 hours of battery life

IP65 dust and water resistance

Seven available ring sizes

Four color finishes

The ring connects to an iPhone and works with a companion Mac application.

Android and Windows aren't supported yet.

Now for the price.

Aina has opened preorders starting at $399, with a regular list price of $499.

The first devices are expected to ship in early 2027.

And unlike some crowdfunding reservations, the preorder currently requires full payment.

Of course, this is still a new product, and most of its capabilities are based on the manufacturer's demonstrations and claims.

We'll need real-world testing to see how reliably it predicts useful actions, integrates with agents, and performs throughout the day.

But here's why I find the concept fascinating.

We're watching AI interfaces move beyond traditional screens.

First, we had keyboards.

Then touchscreens.

Then voice assistants.

Now we're getting devices designed primarily for approving actions performed by autonomous agents.

And that's a genuinely different way of thinking about human-computer interaction.

Instead of opening applications to do something, you increasingly tell an agent what needs to happen.

And when the agent requires your permission, you simply approve it.

Although I can already imagine the downside.

My AI agents will probably interrupt me every 30 seconds asking permission to do something ridiculous.

And now, instead of ignoring their messages, I'll have to explain why I'm constantly flicking my finger at strangers.

Welcome to the future of wearable AI.

items.title: Sand3D: 106,000+ Parametric 3D Models for AI | 3.8× Fewer Tokens Than Blender Python
items.excerpt: What if AI could generate an entire 3D model by writing a few hundred tokens of Python? Not just a beautiful image. Not an uneditable collection of polygons. An actual parametric 3D object with named components, adjustab
items.videoDescription:
What if AI could generate an entire 3D model by writing a few hundred tokens of Python?

Not just a beautiful image. Not an uneditable collection of polygons.

An actual parametric 3D object with named components, adjustable dimensions, and reproducible geometry.

Meet sand3d by Sandflow AI, a new open-source Python library accompanied by an enormous dataset of 3D models designed specifically for training large language models.

And this is exactly the kind of development I find exciting about the future of AI-powered 3D.

The numbers are impressive:

106,094 3D objects converted into a unified code representation

10,456 articulated models with moving parts

Five source datasets, including Objaverse, CAD, Articraft, NVIDIA SimReady, and AutoMate

3.8× fewer tokens than conventional Blender Python in the team's CAD comparison

Fully reproducible geometry generated from short Python programs

Open-source library released under Apache 2.0

But here's the really interesting part.

These aren't ordinary 3D meshes. They're programs that describe how objects are built.

Traditionally, many publicly available 3D datasets contain enormous collections of polygons.

Thousands of triangles. Inconsistent topology. Objects that look convincing but are difficult to edit, animate, or understand structurally.

For AI models, learning from that kind of data can be challenging.

Sandflow took a different approach.

They reconstructed more than 100,000 existing 3D objects as compact Python programs.

And each program describes the object in meaningful parts.

Imagine a mechanical assembly.

Instead of receiving an anonymous mesh containing thousands of triangles, an AI model can work with:

Named components and their relationships

Adjustable dimensions and proportions

Geometric operations such as extrusion, cutting, and filleting

Materials and object placement

Mechanical joints, movement axes, and limits

Complete assemblies built from smaller parts

Want to change the width of a bracket?

Change a parameter.

Need a larger opening in a mechanical component?

Adjust the corresponding dimension.

Want to modify a moving mechanism?

Edit the joint definitions and regenerate the geometry.

That's the beauty of parametric 3D.

And Sandflow designed its language to be particularly efficient for LLMs.

In a comparison involving 30 CAD parts, the team reports that sand3d required 3.8 times fewer tokens than equivalent Blender Python scripts.

That's approximately 74% less code for the model to process.

The library also supports exporting geometry into formats including GLB, STL, OBJ, URDF, and OpenUSD.

And here's why this matters.

We've spent years teaching AI models to generate images, videos, textures, and 3D meshes.

But creating a visually convincing model isn't the same as creating something that can be reliably modified or used in a professional production pipeline.

Parametric code gives AI a much more structured way to understand and create geometry.

And with more than 100,000 examples now available for research and training, developers have a substantial dataset to experiment with.

Imagine asking Claude Code, Codex, or another LLM:

"Create a mechanical assembly with adjustable dimensions, movable joints, and separate components suitable for exporting to a CAD workflow."

Instead of producing an enormous Blender script filled with hard-coded coordinates, the agent could use compact, reusable geometric instructions.

Of course, this doesn't mean every LLM can suddenly generate flawless engineering-grade CAD models.

The converted objects still need quality checks, and the dataset's usefulness for training future models will need to be demonstrated experimentally.

But the direction is fascinating.

We're moving from AI that generates the appearance of objects toward AI that can describe how those objects are actually constructed.

And personally, I've been expecting this transition for quite a while.

Maybe the future of AI-generated 3D won't be another giant model producing increasingly beautiful triangle soup.

Maybe it'll be a language model that understands geometry well enough to build an editable object directly through code.

And with sand3d, we're getting another important piece of that puzzle.

What if you could type using a font inspired by Michelangelo's own handwriting?

Meet Michelangelus, a beautiful new serif typeface created by Italian design studio Studiogusto, inspired by the handwriting of Renaissance master Michelangelo Buonarroti.

And the story behind it is just as fascinating as the design itself.

The designers studied more than 300 original manuscripts, examining Michelangelo's letters, signatures, proportions, and distinctive writing style.

But they didn't simply copy his handwriting.

They transformed it into an entirely new, carefully constructed digital typeface.

Here's where the inspiration came from:

Lowercase letters: Based on Michelangelo's handwritten manuscripts and personal correspondence.

Capital letters: Inspired by his signature on the Pietà and the monumental inscription on St. Peter's Basilica.

Four styles: Regular, Italic, Bold, and Bold Italic.

500+ glyphs: Latin characters, ligatures, stylistic alternates, numbers, fractions, and symbols.

Special characters: Currency symbols, religious marks, historical symbols, and decorative letterforms.

And here's another interesting detail.

Michelangelus was commissioned by the Vatican's Fabbrica di San Pietro and developed in collaboration with Microsoft.

The typeface was designed to bring Renaissance craftsmanship into modern digital communication, including Microsoft 365.

And the best part?

You can download it for free.

It's a beautiful example of how historical research, typography, and modern technology can work together.

Five centuries after Michelangelo, his handwriting is finding a new life on our screens.

From Renaissance manuscripts to digital typography.

Not bad for a font inspired by someone who never used a keyboard.

Explore and download Michelangelus:
https://michelangelus.studiogusto.com/

Studiogusto design project:
https://www.studiogusto.com/project/michelangelus

#Michelangelus #Michelangelo #Typography #FontDesign #GraphicDesign #RenaissanceArt #DigitalArt

items.excerpt: Anthropic just entered the race for the ultimate personal AI assistant. Meet Claude Duet, a new proactive AI agent powered by Claude Opus 5.5. And unlike regular Claude, this one doesn't just sit around waiting for your
items.videoDescription:
Anthropic just entered the race for the ultimate personal AI assistant.

Meet Claude Duet, a new proactive AI agent powered by Claude Opus 5.5.

And unlike regular Claude, this one doesn't just sit around waiting for your prompts.

It actually comes to you first.

Claude Duet monitors your connected apps, identifies things that need attention, sends morning briefings, and works on tasks in the background, even when your computer is turned off.

Here's what makes it interesting:

Claude Opus 5.5: Anthropic's powerful reasoning model handles the work.

One ongoing conversation: Your tasks, questions, and projects live in a single continuous chat.

Proactive monitoring: Duet checks connected apps every few hours and alerts you when something matters.

Background execution: Its own virtual computer and browser let it work independently of your devices.

6,000+ connectors and plugins: Access tools through Claude Marketplace, including Gmail, Slack, Notion, Stripe, Shopify, and more.

AI-powered shopping: Duet can purchase products using Stripe Link or Shopify Shop Pay, with your approval.

You can ask it to manage emails, prepare financial reports, build dashboards, schedule meetings, develop web apps, or simply figure out what deserves your attention today.

But there's something I find a little strange.

Anthropic chose a single-agent experience built around one never-ending conversation.

Personally, I'm not entirely convinced this is better than having multiple specialized agents working on different projects.

We've already seen similar debates around OpenAI's Dots.

And then there's the security.

In true Anthropic fashion, Claude Duet comes with an impressive collection of safeguards:

The agent never directly sees your passwords or authentication tokens.

A dedicated safety classifier protects sensitive information.

Sending messages, making payments, signing documents, and deleting data require your approval.

Trading stocks and transferring money between accounts are prohibited, even with permission.

So yes, your AI assistant can help run your business.

It just can't become your personal hedge fund manager.

There's another catch.

Claude Duet shares usage limits with your regular Claude subscription, including the tokens consumed by background tasks.

And while the 6,000+ integrations sound impressive, that's the broader Marketplace catalog, not a guarantee that every integration works perfectly in Duet today.

Availability:

Claude Duet is launching as a research preview on iOS, Android, and the web.

For now, access is limited to US subscribers on Claude Pro and Max plans, through a waitlist.

Still, I'm genuinely curious about this one.

Opus 5.5 is a powerful foundation for an autonomous agent, and Anthropic's approach to combining reasoning, persistent context, and background execution could make Duet a serious competitor to OpenAI Dots, Meta Muse, and other proactive assistants.

The AI assistant wars are getting interesting.

And apparently, the next big feature isn't answering your questions.

It's knowing what you need before you even ask.

Claude Duet announcement and waitlist:
https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-duet

#ClaudeDuet #Anthropic #ClaudeAI #Opus55 #AIAgents #AIAutomation #ProactiveAI

items.videoDescription:
What if you could create an entire song without ever leaving your conversation with ChatGPT or Claude?

No switching tabs. No copying prompts between applications. No complicated API setup.

Meet Suno MCP Beta, the new official integration that brings Suno's AI music generation directly into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Claude Code, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible assistants.

And this could make AI-powered music production considerably more interesting.

Here's what you can do:

Create songs through conversation: Describe the mood, genre, instruments, and lyrics. Your AI assistant helps develop the concept, and Suno generates the music.

Turn voice memos into songs: Upload a recording, melody, or musical loop and build an entire track around it.

Create covers and remixes: Reinterpret existing songs from your Suno library.

Extend compositions: Continue a track, experiment with new sections, or create different versions.

Make mashups: Combine musical ideas and tracks from your library.

Use Suno Voices: Bring your saved voices into new creations.

Manage your music: Save generated songs to your Suno library and organize them into playlists.

And here's the best part.

You don't need a Suno API key.

Just connect your existing Suno account, authorize access, and start creating music from your favorite AI assistant.

The integration uses the credits from your current Suno subscription.

And yes, it supports Suno Free accounts too.

Although some AI assistants may require a paid plan to connect custom MCP servers.

Want to try it with Claude Code?

Run this command:

claude mcp add --transport http suno https://api.suno.com/mcp

Then open Claude Code, run /mcp, and authorize your Suno account.

For ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Cursor, or other compatible tools, use the same MCP server URL:

https://api.suno.com/mcp

And here's why I find this particularly interesting.

We've already seen AI coding agents generate animations, build 3D environments, edit videos, and create entire games.

Now music generation can become another component of the same creative workflow.

Imagine developing a video with Claude Code and asking:

"Create a cinematic ambient soundtrack for this scene. Start with soft synthesizers, gradually introduce orchestral textures, and build toward a dramatic ending."

Suno generates the track.

Don't like the result?

Just continue the conversation.

"Make it darker. Remove the vocals. Try a slower version."

Your AI assistant becomes the creative director. Suno becomes the music production engine.

Of course, this is still a beta release, and access is currently being rolled out through an early-access waitlist.

But the direction is clear.

We're moving from AI tools that work separately to entire creative workflows coordinated through a single conversation.

And personally, I find that far more exciting than another standalone AI generation interface.

One conversation. Multiple creative tools. An entire production pipeline.

Now all we need is an AI agent with decent musical taste.

https://suno.com/mcp

items.videoDescription:

And the result is surprisingly beautiful.

Instead of simply reading about the Little Prince's adventures, you can step into his universe, explore tiny planets floating above the clouds, and experience familiar moments from the story in 3D.

- Claude Opus 5.5: AI-assisted coding, game logic, and development

- Blender: Processing models, assembling scenes, and creating visuals
- Unity: Bringing everything together into a playable browser game
- 16 days: From concept to a publicly playable experience
Even the promotional trailer was reportedly created using Claude Opus 5.5 and Blender from a single prompt.
And here's another interesting detail.

The developer plans to open-source the entire project and publish a detailed breakdown of the development process.
This isn't just another AI-generated 3D demo.
It's an example of how AI coding agents, generative 3D tools, and traditional game engines can work together to dramatically accelerate independent game development.
Of course, AI doesn't replace the need for creative direction, good taste, or game design.
But it certainly changes how much one person can build.
Sixteen days. One developer. A universe inspired by The Little Prince.
And you can play it right now.

items.videoDescription:
Meet Emma, a real-time AI video avatar powered by Nuplex 1.0, the new full-duplex audiovisual foundation model from Nuance Labs.

Unlike traditional AI avatars that wait for you to finish speaking, Emma can listen, react, and respond while you're still talking.

And you can try her directly in your browser without creating an account.

Developed by former Apple researchers, Nuplex takes a different approach to human-AI interaction.

Instead of relying on a traditional speech-to-text, LLM, text-to-speech, and facial animation pipeline, Nuplex combines audiovisual perception and generation into a real-time full-duplex system.

What makes Emma different?

• Simultaneous listening and speaking: Emma can respond naturally without waiting for rigid conversational turns.

• Real-time facial expressions: nodding, smiling, blinking, and reacting while you speak.

• Natural conversational timing: Nuance Labs reports that Nuplex matched human reply timing in 89% of 1,785 recorded conversational questions.

• Multimodal perception: the system processes vocal tone, timing, and visual signals to understand conversational context.

• Expressive digital human: Emma's face and voice are licensed from a real actress, with distinctive expressions and mannerisms.

• Browser-based demo: talk face-to-face with Emma without installing software or creating an account.

• Nuplex Beta API: developers can build real-time conversational AI personas and integrate them into their own applications.

The bigger shift isn't just more realistic AI-generated faces.

It's moving from turn-based AI assistants toward digital humans that can actually participate in a conversation.

The 89% timing result comes from Nuance Labs' own research and has not been independently validated.

items.videoDescription:
Blender 5.3 is officially here, bringing native 3D Gaussian Splatting, NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction, and major upgrades to Cycles, EEVEE, and Geometry Nodes.

This is more than a routine Blender update. It's a significant step toward integrating photorealistic 3D captures into professional VFX workflows.

What's new in Blender 5.3:

• Native 3D Gaussian Splatting: import PLY, SPZ, and glTF files, manipulate splats with Geometry Nodes, and render in Cycles, EEVEE, or Workbench.

• DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction: faster, cleaner interactive Cycles viewport rendering on compatible NVIDIA GPUs, with dramatically reduced animation flickering.

• Physically based dispersion: realistic rainbow effects in glass and gemstones, plus anisotropic roughness for transmissive materials.

• EEVEE upgrades: Material Lighting Nodes for advanced per-light shading control and panoramic fisheye camera support.

• Blender Projects: a new optional project system for managing assets, pipeline settings, and color configurations.

• Compositor improvements: effect stacks, 17 additional nodes, and up to 10x faster Anisotropic Kuwahara filtering on Apple GPUs.

• Better animation workflows: Grease Pencil Carver, ripple editing, and OpenTimelineIO support.

Blender is becoming an increasingly powerful tool for combining 3D reconstruction, procedural workflows, and physically based rendering.
