items.videoDescription:
Someone built a Claude Code skill that turns real-world roads into retro pixel-art adventures.

And I have absolutely no idea why I love this so much.

Meet Pixel Path, an open-source Claude Code skill that transforms any road trip into an interactive, first-person pixel-art experience.

Just give Claude two locations.

For example:

"Make me a pixel path from Paris to Versailles."

And watch what happens.

Here's how it works:

Real roads: Uses OpenStreetMap to calculate the actual route.

Real buildings: Recreates buildings and landmarks based on their geographic locations.

Real landscapes: Uses elevation data to generate hills, forests, water, and the surrounding terrain.

AI-generated pixel art: RetroDiffusion creates the visual assets.

Interactive driving: Travel along the route, adjust your speed, pause, or reverse.

Browser-based experience: The finished world runs as a lightweight web page.

The result feels like someone combined Google Maps with an old-school arcade driving game.

Except the streets are real.

And here's another interesting detail.

You can choose different levels of visual detail, from free placeholder graphics to more elaborate AI-generated scenery.

The skill itself is free and open source. Generating custom pixel-art assets through RetroDiffusion requires paid API credits.

Install Pixel Path in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add jonwheatley/pixel-path
/plugin install pixel-path@pixel-path

Then ask Claude to create a pixel-art journey between any two places.

Is this going to revolutionize transportation?

Probably not.

Do we desperately need an AI agent turning our daily commute into a 1990s driving game?

Also probably not.

But apparently, if someone vibe-coded it, someone somewhere must have needed it.

And sometimes that's all the justification a creative project needs.

Pixel Path on GitHub:
https://github.com/jonwheatley/pixel-path

#ClaudeCode #PixelArt #VibeCoding #OpenStreetMap #CreativeCoding #RetroGaming #Shorts

items.title: Cinecode: Claude Code Can Now Make Entire Movies with JavaScript | Free AI Filmmaking Skill
items.excerpt: What if you could create an entire animated film without using a traditional AI video generator? Meet Cinecode, a new free, open-source filmmaking skill that lets Claude Code and Cursor turn simple prompts into complete
items.videoDescription:
What if you could create an entire animated film without using a traditional AI video generator?

Meet Cinecode, a new free, open-source filmmaking skill that lets Claude Code and Cursor turn simple prompts into complete videos.
And we're not just talking about short animations.

Cinecode can produce films longer than 10 minutes, complete with visuals, narration, music, sound effects, and editing.

Here's what you can create:

Short films: Animated stories with characters, environments, and cinematic camera movements.

2D and 3D animations: Procedural visuals built using JavaScript, Canvas, Three.js, and WebGL.

Product commercials: Animated advertisements with branding, typography, and visual effects.

Explainer videos: Educational content with diagrams, kinetic typography, and animated illustrations.

Music videos: Visuals synchronized with beats, rhythm, and lyrics.

YouTube documentaries: Longer videos with chapters, narration, research, and visual storytelling.

Social media content: Vertical videos designed for Shorts, Reels, and TikTok.

But here's what makes Cinecode particularly interesting.

Every generated frame is rendered from code.

Instead of asking an AI video model to predict pixels, Cinecode gives an AI coding agent a complete filmmaking workflow.

Here's how it works.

Step 1: Describe your idea

Tell Claude what you want to create.

For example:

"Create a 60-second cinematic animation about a lonely robot discovering an abandoned city."

Step 2: Develop the creative direction

Cinecode helps plan the story, visual style, camera movements, timing, transitions, and sound design.

You can choose between different aesthetics, including cinematic realism, anime, pixel art, claymation, paper cutouts, and experimental motion graphics.

Step 3: Generate the animation

Claude writes JavaScript that builds and animates the scenes.

The system renders individual frames through headless Chrome, using Canvas or Three.js.

Step 4: Create the soundtrack

Cinecode can generate procedural audio, mix sound effects, synchronize music, and add optional AI narration using Gemini TTS, ElevenLabs, or supported local voices.

Step 5: Review and export

The workflow produces a draft, checks visual and audio quality, allows revisions, and renders the final video as an MP4.

And here's another useful detail.

Cinecode has two production modes.

Quick Mode

Designed for shorter animations, commercials, explainers, and social media videos.

It can handle projects up to approximately three minutes, with a relatively lightweight review process.

Film Mode

Designed for longer productions, including short films, documentaries, and YouTube videos exceeding ten minutes.

It divides production into stages, with checkpoints for the script, visual direction, animatic, sound, and final render.

And the entire project runs on your own computer.

You don't need a separate paid video generation service.

The main requirements are:

Claude Code or Cursor

Node.js 22+

Python 3.9+

FFmpeg

Chrome, Chromium, or Edge

AI agent usage and optional voice-generation services may still incur costs. Longer productions also require more rendering time and disk space.

Want to try Cinecode?

For Claude Code, install it with:

git clone https://github.com/sarpstar/cinecode.git ~/.claude/skills/cinecode

For Cursor:

git clone https://github.com/sarpstar/cinecode.git ~/.cursor/skills/cinecode

Then open a new project and tell your agent:

"Let's make a short film with Cinecode. I want a 60-second animated science-fiction story with procedural 3D visuals, cinematic lighting, original sound design, and a finished MP4."

And here's why I find this fascinating.

We're seeing two very different approaches to AI filmmaking.

One generates video directly with enormous neural networks.

The other uses powerful coding agents to build the systems that create the animation.

And code-generated films have an important advantage.

You can change the timing, adjust the camera, modify the geometry, update the typography, or render the same scene again with predictable results.

Of course, creating a polished 10-minute film is considerably more demanding than generating a short animation.

But the possibility of turning a creative idea into a complete, reproducible, code-driven production is genuinely exciting.

We're moving from AI that generates video clips to AI agents that understand an entire filmmaking workflow.

And perhaps the next independent animation studio won't need a traditional rendering pipeline.

Just a computer, a good idea, and an AI agent that knows a little about cinema.

Cinecode on GitHub:
https://github.com/sarpstar/cinecode

English documentation and examples:
https://github.com/sarpstar/cinecode/blob/main/README.en.md

Free and open source under the MIT license.

items.title: Spaghetti Splatting: 3D Gaussian Splatting Meets Physics Simulation
items.excerpt: Meet Spaghetti Splatting, a new 3D reconstruction and differentiable rendering technique that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting from individual points to continuous curves. And it could be particularly useful for rendering a
items.videoDescription:
Meet Spaghetti Splatting, a new 3D reconstruction and differentiable rendering technique that extends 3D Gaussian Splatting from individual points to continuous curves.

And it could be particularly useful for rendering and simulating hair, wires, vegetation, and other complex strand-like geometry.

Traditional 3D Gaussian Splatting represents scenes using collections of individual 3D Gaussians. It delivers impressive photorealistic rendering, but reconstructing long, connected structures remains challenging.

Spaghetti Splatting takes a fundamentally different approach.

Instead of isolated point primitives, it uses connected, learnable curve segments that can reconstruct thin geometry while maintaining structural continuity.

Here's what makes the research interesting:

• Beyond 3DGS: mathematically generalizes Gaussian Splatting from point-based Dirac masses to continuous curvilinear representations.

• Connected 3D geometry: reconstructs hair strands, cables, wires, meshes, and vegetation as continuous structures rather than scattered points.

• Differentiable rendering: supports optimization of curved geometry directly from images.

• Gaussian and Beta kernels: supports different convolution kernels for flexible geometric representation.

• Efficient rasterization: linearizes camera projection per segment to accelerate training and rendering.

• Native anti-aliasing: improves visual stability across different viewing distances.

• Competitive reconstruction quality: the authors report improvements over specialized line-based reconstruction methods.

• Physics-ready structures: connected strands can be used in simulations involving deformable curves, including hair dynamics.

The important distinction is that Spaghetti Splatting doesn't merely make thin objects look better.

It reconstructs connected geometry that can potentially become part of a physical simulation pipeline.

That could help bridge the gap between neural rendering, 3D reconstruction, and traditional computer graphics workflows.

Physics compatibility doesn't mean the method includes a complete cloth or hair simulation engine. Its contribution is producing connected geometry suitable for downstream simulation.

Research paper:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12716

Project page and interactive examples:
https://spaghetti-splatting.github.io/

Research by George Shramko and collaborators from Simon Fraser University, Wayve Labs, the University of British Columbia, and the University of Toronto.

Could connected neural primitives become the next major step beyond point-based 3D Gaussian Splatting?

#SpaghettiSplatting #GaussianSplatting #ComputerGraphics

items.title: AI-Commander: A Retro 90s Terminal UI for OpenCode, Hermes & AI Coding Agents | Built in Rust
items.excerpt: Someone just brought the golden age of DOS file managers back to life. Except this time, they're running AI agents. Meet AI-Commander, a new open-source terminal interface built by developer Mikhail Malyshev. And I have
items.videoDescription:
Someone just brought the golden age of DOS file managers back to life. Except this time, they're running AI agents.

Meet AI-Commander, a new open-source terminal interface built by developer Mikhail Malyshev.

And I have to admit, this thing gives me an unreasonable amount of childhood joy.

Remember Norton Commander?

The blue screens. The silver dialog boxes. The function keys. The beautiful feeling that you were operating a serious computer just by pressing F2.

Well, imagine that aesthetic combined with modern AI coding agents.

That's AI-Commander.

It's a multi-harness TUI designed to bring different AI agent runtimes into one familiar, old-school interface.

Here's what it can do.

1. Multiple AI agent backends

Instead of creating another AI model or agent framework, AI-Commander acts as a frontend for existing agent harnesses.

The current public implementation includes:

OpenCode: Connects through its server API, streams responses, and retrieves available models.

Hermes Agent: Runs through the Hermes CLI, streams output, and manages conversations.

More harnesses planned: The architecture is designed for additional integrations, including DeepSeek's agent harness.

The idea is to make different agent runtimes accessible through a consistent interface.

2. A proper old-school terminal UI

And this is where the nostalgia really kicks in.

You get:

Conversation history in a sidebar

A central chat window

A message composer

Classic Norton Commander-inspired dialogs

Function-key controls

A built-in file browser

Full mouse and keyboard navigation

Russian and English interface languages

It looks like 1995. But the things running inside it belong to 2026.

3. Live agent activity

AI-Commander doesn't just display the final answer.

It supports streaming text, reasoning output, tool calls, Markdown, and code blocks.

You can switch between available models and configure defaults for different harnesses.

There's also support for file and image attachments.

And yes, you can browse files using an interface inspired by Norton Commander.

Which might be the most emotionally satisfying way to attach a screenshot to an AI agent ever invented.

4. Built entirely in Rust

The project uses:

Rust for the application

Ratatui for the terminal interface

Crossterm for terminal interaction

Tokio for asynchronous operations

No browser window pretending to be a desktop application.

No giant web frontend just to display a chat conversation.

A native terminal application with a lightweight architecture.

And it feels refreshingly fast.

5. Designed to support more agents

The architecture uses a pluggable backend interface.

Each new harness gets its own adapter while the rest of the UI stays consistent.

That's particularly interesting because the AI agent ecosystem is becoming increasingly fragmented.

Claude Code.

Codex.

OpenCode.

Hermes.

DeepSeek's experimental agent harnesses.

Everyone has their own runtime, configuration, interface, and way of handling sessions.

But what if you could use your favorite agents without constantly switching interfaces?

That's the idea behind AI-Commander.

Of course, it's still an early-stage project.

The publicly available code currently implements OpenCode and Hermes. Broader support, including DSH, remains part of the development direction rather than a finished integration.

But that's also what makes it interesting.

It's a small, open-source project with a clear idea and plenty of room to grow.

And honestly, I love that someone decided the future of AI agents should look like a DOS application from the 1990s.

We've spent years making developer tools look increasingly polished and complicated.

Rounded corners.

Glass effects.

Animated sidebars.

Entire Chromium instances just to display some text.

And then someone says: What if we simply brought Norton Commander back?

Perfect.

No notes.

Well, maybe a few GitHub issues.

AI-Commander is available on GitHub.

If you like the project, give it a star, open an issue, suggest your favorite agent harness, or contribute.

And if you're old enough to remember Norton Commander, consider this a perfectly valid excuse to feel twelve years old again.

GitHub repository:
https://github.com/mb-mal/ai-commander

Created by: Mikhail Malyshev (@tsingular)

#AICommander #RustLang #OpenCode #HermesAgent #AIAgents #TerminalUI #OpenSource #VibeCoding

items.videoDescription:
Smart TVs have become ridiculous.

You buy a television, turn it on, and somehow end up staring at advertisements, sponsored recommendations, and apps you never asked for.

One developer finally decided he'd had enough.

So he used Claude Code to reverse-engineer his TV and rebuild the entire home screen.

Meet Free My TV, an open-source project that gives smart TVs a clean, Apple TV-inspired interface without the usual advertising clutter.

And the results are pretty impressive.

Here's what he achieved:

Replaced the stock interface with a minimalist, Apple TV-style home screen

Removed sponsored content, banners, and autoplaying promotions

Disabled unnecessary preinstalled apps and background services

Reported approximately 70% lower RAM usage

Claimed a 3× faster interface

Added customizable apps, recommendations, weather, and automatic light/dark themes

The public repository also documents a 60% memory reduction for the home screen on a tested TCL Google TV.

And here's the best part.

He made the whole thing open source.

Free My TV can be installed on compatible smart TVs, customized using Claude Code, and reversed if you want your original interface back.

No root access required. No permanent deletion of the original system apps.

It's a fascinating example of AI-assisted reverse engineering and software customization.

Instead of accepting whatever interface the manufacturer decided to ship, you can increasingly build something that actually works for you.

Imagine buying a $1,000 TV and needing an AI coding agent to remove the advertisements.

items.excerpt: What if you could give Claude Code an entire Mac of its own? Not just terminal access. Not a browser sandbox. An actual macOS desktop, running inside your terminal. Meet terminal-mac, a free, open-source project that let
items.videoDescription:
What if you could give Claude Code an entire Mac of its own?

Not just terminal access. Not a browser sandbox.

An actual macOS desktop, running inside your terminal.

Meet terminal-mac, a free, open-source project that lets AI agents control a separate virtual Mac while you continue using your own computer.

And the implementation is pretty fascinating.

In this video, you'll see Claude using terminal-mac to interact with a virtual macOS desktop.

Here's what makes it interesting:

Real macOS: Runs a complete macOS virtual machine using Apple's Virtualization framework.

Desktop inside your terminal: Watch the virtual Mac through Ghostty, Kitty, or iTerm2.

AI Computer Use: Agents can take screenshots, click, type, scroll, drag, and interact with applications.

MCP integration: Connect Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other compatible AI agents.

Dedicated agent environment: The virtual Mac has its own applications, files, accounts, and permissions.

Independent mouse and clipboard: Your AI agent doesn't need to hijack your physical cursor or clipboard.

Multiple virtual Macs: Create separate environments for different agents or tasks.

And here's the best part.

You can actually watch your AI agent working inside a complete desktop environment without surrendering control of your own computer.

Imagine giving Claude a task that requires navigating applications, configuring software, testing interfaces, or performing complex desktop workflows.

Instead of clicking around your personal Mac, it does everything in its own virtual machine.

Your computer. Your work. Claude's computer. Claude's work.

Everyone gets a desktop.

How to install terminal-mac:

On an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS 14 or later:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/govijr/terminal-mac/releases/latest/download/get.sh | bash

Start your virtual Mac:

terminal-mac up

Then connect Claude Code using the included plugin:

/plugin install terminal-mac --marketplace govijr/terminal-mac

The plugin provides MCP tools and a skill that teaches Claude how to interact with the virtual desktop.

A few things worth knowing:

The first setup requires downloading and installing macOS, creating a user account, and granting permissions inside the virtual machine.

You'll also need sufficient RAM and storage. The default virtual disk has a logical size of 64 GiB, although actual disk usage grows as needed.

And since the project is still an early release candidate, expect occasional rough edges.

But here's what I find genuinely exciting.

We've spent years teaching AI agents to use our computers.

Now we're starting to give them computers of their own.

And that changes the possibilities for testing, automation, software development, and running multiple agents without interfering with your everyday work.

The future might not be an AI controlling your desktop.

It might be an entire office full of virtual computers, each operated by its own AI agent.

Except the office lives inside your Mac.

And nobody needs to book a meeting room.

terminal-mac on GitHub:
https://github.com/govijr/terminal-mac

Free and open source under the MIT license.

#TerminalMac #ClaudeCode #ComputerUse #AIAgents #MacOS #OpenSource #VibeCoding

items.title: ZBrush 2027 Is Here! New UV Editor, Selection Sets & 3D Layers on iPad
items.excerpt: Maxon just released ZBrush 2027.0 for desktop and iPad, and this update brings some genuinely useful improvements to digital sculpting. Here's what's new. 1. A Proper UV Editor in ZBrush Desktop This is probably the bigg
items.videoDescription:
Maxon just released ZBrush 2027.0 for desktop and iPad, and this update brings some genuinely useful improvements to digital sculpting.

Here's what's new.
1. A Proper UV Editor in ZBrush Desktop This is probably the biggest addition.
ZBrush now has a dedicated UV editing environment built using technology from Cinema 4D. Instead of constantly exporting your sculpt to another application, you can create, unwrap, edit, and pack UVs directly within the ZBrush workflow.

The new UV Editor supports:
UDIM workflows: Organize textures across multiple UV tiles.
Texel density controls: Maintain consistent texture resolution across different parts of a model.
Trim sheets: Reuse texture details efficiently across complex assets.
Automatic unwrapping: Generate UV layouts with different unwrapping methods.
UV packing: Arrange islands efficiently within the available texture space.
PolyGroup-based unwrapping: Use existing PolyGroups to help organize UVs.
Customizable interface: Adjust the workspace to your needs.
For character artists, creature designers, and anyone preparing high-resolution sculpts for texturing, this is a significant workflow improvement.

2. Selection Sets
Here's another feature that's less spectacular in a trailer but potentially extremely useful in everyday production.
ZBrush can now save and recall multiple states of your sculpt.
Selection Sets can store:
PolyGroups Mask PolyPaint UV configurations Morph Targets And you aren't limited to a fixed number of saved sets.

3. ZBrush for iPad Gets 3D Layers
Now for the tablet version. ZBrush for iPad finally gets proper non-destructive 3D Layers. This brings an important part of the desktop sculpting workflow to Apple's tablet.

For example:
Create a layer for facial wrinkles.
Add another for skin details.
Store PolyPaint changes separately.
Save and manipulate masks.
Blend different sculpting states.
Show, hide, or bake individual layers.

4. Spotlight Comes to iPad
Another major desktop feature has arrived on the tablet.
Spotlight lets you use reference images directly inside the sculpting viewport.

This makes it possible to:
Sculpt using photographic references.
Paint textures through images.
Create details using reference imagery.
Generate 3D geometry from images.
Keep visual references visible while sculpting.
And because it's running on an iPad, you can combine those tools with Apple Pencil.
That's a particularly interesting workflow for creature artists, portrait sculptors, and concept designers.

5. Better Cross-Platform Workflows
Maxon has also been improving the surrounding ZBrush ecosystem.
Recent updates introduced native Windows on ARM support, expanded GoZ compatibility with Autodesk Maya and 3ds Max, and customizable hotkeys that can be shared between desktop and iPad.

These features arrived in earlier 2026 updates rather than being entirely new to 2027.0, but they remain important parts of the current workflow.
You can move projects between supported applications while preserving compatible geometry and asset information. And custom keyboard shortcuts make it easier to maintain familiar controls when moving between desktop and tablet.

One important detail: The new advanced UV Editor is a desktop feature. The iPad version has UV Master, but not the same dedicated UV editing environment.

So what's the bigger picture?

For years, ZBrush has been one of the most powerful sculpting tools available.

But certain production tasks still required switching to other applications.

UV editing was an obvious example.

And while ZBrush for iPad was impressive from the beginning, the missing desktop features limited some professional workflows.

ZBrush 2027.0 addresses both problems.

The desktop version becomes more self-contained.

The iPad version becomes more capable.

And the gap between sculpting, texturing, and preparing assets for production gets a little smaller.

Personally, I think that's more useful than adding another experimental AI button.

Not every update needs to generate something automatically.

Sometimes, artists just want better tools for making things themselves.

And a proper UV Editor inside ZBrush has been a long time coming.

ZBrush 2027.0 was released on October 14, 2026.

items.title: Claude Code May Have Discovered a New Planet. NASA Is Checking.
items.excerpt: What if an AI coding agent helped discover a planet that astronomers had missed for seven years? And what if NASA actually agreed to investigate? That's exactly what's happening. Independent researcher Pavel Rabtsevich u
items.videoDescription:
What if an AI coding agent helped discover a planet that astronomers had missed for seven years?
And what if NASA actually agreed to investigate?
That's exactly what's happening.
Independent researcher Pavel Rabtsevich used Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to analyze archived data from NASA's TESS space telescope.
The result? A possible new exoplanet orbiting a star approximately 116 light-years from Earth.

Here's what the AI-assisted investigation uncovered:
- A star called TIC 4206066
- A mysterious 0.05% drop in brightness every 3.18 days
- Each dip lasts approximately two hours
- The signal is consistent with a planet roughly 1.4 times Earth's radius
- Similar signals appear in telescope data collected years apart

Claude Code handled much of the technical work: processing telescope data, writing transit-detection algorithms, analyzing light curves, checking neighboring stars, and testing alternative explanations.

The human researcher directed the investigation, challenged the results, and established the criteria for success or failure.
And here's where it gets really interesting.

NASA's TESS mission has approved follow-up observations under Director's Discretionary Target Program 100. The observations are scheduled for October 31 to November 26, 2026. tess.mit.edu

The planet isn't confirmed yet. The signal could have another explanation, and that's precisely what the new observations will investigate.
But the implications are fascinating.

We're watching AI coding agents move beyond generating software and into actual scientific research.

One researcher. Public NASA data. A few AI agents. And possibly an entirely new world.
The video shows an interactive 3D visualization of the candidate planetary system, created by the researcher.

items.excerpt: Apparently, someone decided that smartphones weren't enough. We now need screens in our sweaters. Researchers at the National University of Singapore have developed a fully functional color touchscreen woven directly int
items.videoDescription:
Apparently, someone decided that smartphones weren't enough.

We now need screens in our sweaters.

Researchers at the National University of Singapore have developed a fully functional color touchscreen woven directly into clothing.

And no, they didn't just glue a tiny display onto a sleeve.

The electronics are literally inside the threads.

Here's what they've managed to create:

54 electronic fibers, containing thousands of microscopic LEDs

96 × 54 pixel resolution, because apparently we're bringing 1990s graphics back

30 FPS video playback, directly on your sleeve

Full-color touchscreen, supporting multiple simultaneous touches

Working apps, including a calculator, compass, and photo gallery

Bluetooth connectivity, voice commands, and temperature monitoring

50 machine washes, with little loss of display or touch functionality

And somehow, the fabric remains flexible and breathable.

The really impressive part is the engineering.

Each fiber contains tiny electronic components that work together to create a display and detect touch.

So instead of wearing a device, the clothing itself becomes the interface.

Of course, it's still a laboratory prototype.

The resolution is terrible, the electronics need external power and controllers, and nobody has explained why watching a video on your forearm is better than simply taking your phone out of your pocket.

But who cares?

You can now watch gloriously pixelated memes on your sweater.

Humanity has spent decades making screens smaller. Now we're weaving them into knitwear.

And here's the inevitable next step.

We've already got phones, watches, headphones, and glasses that need charging.

Soon your sweater will ask you to plug it in before going to bed.

Welcome to the future of wearable technology.

items.excerpt: Apparently, everyone wants to be a film director now. And AI startups are making absolutely sure we have enough software for that. Meet OpenDirector v0.1.0, a new open-source AI filmmaking platform from ThinkFlowLab, pow
items.videoDescription:
Apparently, everyone wants to be a film director now.

And AI startups are making absolutely sure we have enough software for that.

Meet OpenDirector v0.1.0, a new open-source AI filmmaking platform from ThinkFlowLab, powered by vLLM-Omni and compatible with MiniMax H3 video generation.

And unlike another standalone AI video generator, this one attempts to bring the entire production process into a single workspace.

From an idea to a finished short film.

Scripts. Storyboards. Visual references. AI-generated footage. Editing. Audio. Final export.

All inside a locally running application.

Here's what OpenDirector can do:

1. AI-Assisted Creative Direction

Start with an idea and discuss it with the built-in AI assistant.

Develop your concept, generate visual references, create assets, and organize everything into a structured production workflow.

2. Infinite Canvas for Visual Production

Instead of throwing every generated image and video into one enormous history panel, OpenDirector gives you a visual canvas.

Organize images, videos, audio, and text.

Connect related assets and references.

Generate variations and refine individual elements.

Review generation history.

Keep your projects organized on your own computer.

A revolutionary concept, apparently: knowing which render belongs to which project.

3. Specialized Storyboard Presets

OpenDirector includes several useful presets for keeping visual elements consistent:

Character Three-View: Generate multiple views of a character.

Face Three-View: Explore facial features from different angles.

Product Three-View: Create consistent product references.

Storyboard: Generate four separate storyboard frames.

Multi-Camera: Explore a scene from four different camera perspectives.

These workflows help establish characters, environments, and composition before generating the final footage.

4. AI Video Generation with MiniMax H3

OpenDirector supports self-hosted models through configurable inference services.

The developers demonstrated the platform using FastH3 served through vLLM-Omni.

Their example is a 60-second animated short film called We Can Still Win, about a middle-aged Dota 2 player.

The video was generated using an AI-assisted workflow, then assembled inside OpenDirector.

5. Actual Video Editing

And yes, there's a timeline.

Not just another collection of generated clips.

You can:

Arrange video and audio tracks.

Trim clips and adjust their timing.

Change playback speed.

Control audio volume.

Preview your sequence.

Render the final video to MP4.

6. Export to Professional Editing Software

This might be one of my favorite features.

OpenDirector doesn't force you to finish everything inside its own editor.

It supports:

MP4: Render the finished video.

FCPXML: Export an editing timeline for compatible professional NLE workflows.

JSON: Export structured project data.

Asset bundles: Package your media for further editing.

So you can use AI to assemble the first version and continue refining it in another application.

And here's the important part.

OpenDirector is local-first, not necessarily 100% offline.

The application runs on your computer, and projects are stored locally.

But generation can use either self-hosted models or external API providers.

If you connect cloud models, your generation requests are processed by those services.

Running powerful models such as MiniMax H3 locally also requires suitable GPU hardware.


The developers provide a skill that lets your AI coding agent handle installation.

Give Claude Code or Codex this prompt:
"Install and start OpenDirector by following the official installation skill:

https://github.com/ThinkFlowLab/OpenDirector/blob/main/.agents/skills/install-opendirector/SKILL.md

Check the system requirements first, explain what needs to be installed, and ask before changing my existing environment."

The project requires Python 3.11+, Node.js, Git, and FFmpeg.
And it's free and open source under Apache 2.0.

One important caveat: this is version 0.1.0, the first public release. The team hasn't yet verified every workflow end to end, and MP4 rendering currently requires keeping the editor open in Chrome or Edge.

OpenDirector is at least taking a useful approach by combining AI generation with project management, visual references, editing, and exports that can continue into professional workflows.

It's turning hundreds of disconnected generations into one coherent film.
And that's where tools like this could become genuinely valuable.

Now, if the next AI director could also organize my existing render folders, that would be an even bigger breakthrough.

items.title: How to Make AI Videos That Don't Look Like AI | Malevich, Photoshop & Seedance 2.0
items.excerpt: What if the secret to making beautiful AI videos was to stop letting AI do all the creative work? No glossy anime aesthetics. No plastic-looking characters. No generic cinematic lighting. Just old-school avant-garde art,
items.videoDescription:
What if the secret to making beautiful AI videos was to stop letting AI do all the creative work?

No glossy anime aesthetics. No plastic-looking characters. No generic cinematic lighting.

Just old-school avant-garde art, hand-drawn frames, and AI animation.

I came across a fascinating creative workflow inspired by the work of Kazimir Malevich and the Russian avant-garde.

And the results are genuinely beautiful.

The idea is simple: instead of asking AI to generate an entire video from scratch, you create a distinctive visual style yourself and let AI bring it to life.

Here's how the process works.

1. Start with historical artwork

The visual inspiration comes from A Game in Hell (1914), an experimental illustrated book associated with Kazimir Malevich and Olga Rozanova, now represented in MoMA's collection.

A century-old avant-garde aesthetic becomes the foundation for contemporary AI animation.

2. Draw the frames manually in Photoshop

Instead of using AI-generated images, create your own artwork using:

Kyle's Ultimate Pastel Palooza brushes

Vintage paper textures

Rough charcoal-style lines

High-contrast monochrome silhouettes

Deliberately imperfect, hand-drawn shapes

3. Animate with Seedance 2.0

Use an image-to-video generator to bring your illustrations to life.

The trick is preserving the original handmade aesthetic instead of letting the model turn everything into polished, generic AI imagery.

4. Avoid the uncanny valley

Simplified puppet-like characters, deliberately stylized faces, and imperfect frame-to-frame movement can make the animation feel more expressive.

Sometimes less realism produces better results.

5. Use a precise visual prompt

Here's the core style prompt:

"Avant-garde auteur animation, 2D hand-drawn aesthetic with line-boil effect. Charcoal pencil texture on vintage parchment paper, high-contrast monochrome silhouettes. Only black lines."

Then add your scene description and the movement you want.

And here's what I find particularly interesting.

We're so obsessed with making AI video look photorealistic that we sometimes forget how much character traditional animation can have.

Imperfect lines. Strange proportions. Rough textures.

Things that most AI generators try desperately to smooth out.

But those imperfections are exactly what make the visuals interesting.

And this is a great reminder that AI doesn't have to replace artistic direction.

It can support it.

The best AI video isn't necessarily the one that looks the most realistic.

Sometimes it's the one that looks the least like AI.

https://www.instagram.com/sa1ntdenis/

items.videoDescription:
OpenAI just put a $200 retro handheld in its merch store. And this one actually does something.

Meet the ModRetro Chromatic: Codex Edition, a collaboration between OpenAI and ModRetro, the hardware company founded by Oculus creator Palmer Luckey.

The original transparent DevDay edition was a limited giveaway. Collectors quickly started listing units on eBay for thousands of dollars.

Now the new Codex Edition is available through OpenAI Supply Co. for $200, including a programmable game cartridge.

But the interesting part isn't the collector's item. It's the workflow.

Prompt → Game → ROM → Real Cartridge.

1. Describe a Game Boy game to Codex.

Install the ModRetro Chromatic plugin in Codex, then describe your idea.

An 8-bit platformer? A tiny top-down adventure? An unusually ambitious crime simulator for a screen with 160 × 144 pixels?

2. Build and test it.

Codex can work with GB Studio, GBDK-2020, and other Game Boy development tools.

It helps create sprites, tilemaps, game logic, and a playable .gb or .gbc ROM.

You can test the result in a browser emulator, point out bugs, and ask the agent to revise it.

3. Put it on an actual cartridge.

Connect the Chromatic over USB-C, enable Developer Mode, and flash a compatible rewritable cartridge.

The Codex Edition includes one.

Then unplug your computer and play your own game on the handheld.

And the hardware is properly retro.

The Chromatic uses an FPGA-based architecture designed for Game Boy and Game Boy Color compatibility, rather than simply running a software emulator.

It has a pixel-accurate 160 × 144 display, physical buttons, and cartridge support.

One correction worth making: this $200 Supply Co. version has a transparent ABS shell and Gorilla Glass. It's not identical to the earlier DevDay giveaway or premium magnesium-and-sapphire Chromatic configurations.

Want to try the idea without buying a console?

OpenAI has published 13 Codex-built Game Boy Color games, including FlapGPT, Codex Land, and Ash & Oath.

You can play them free in your browser or download their ROM files.

And yes, I love this ridiculous combination of modern agentic coding and technology that feels like it belongs in a school backpack from 1998.

We've spent years making AI build increasingly complicated web apps.

Now it can make a game you can physically click into a cartridge.

The future is apparently running on AA batteries.

items.excerpt: What if you could take a viral video, give it to an AI, and turn it into an actual video game? Not just a visual recreation. A fully explorable 3D world. And what if the entire process took just 40 minutes? About a year
items.videoDescription:
What if you could take a viral video, give it to an AI, and turn it into an actual video game?
Not just a visual recreation. A fully explorable 3D world.
And what if the entire process took just 40 minutes?

About a year ago, a video featuring an enormous, seemingly endless fortress went viral on Twitter.
Yesterday, I gave that video to Claude Opus 5.5, connected it to an AI image generator for creating assets, provided specialized Three.js development skills, and asked for one thing:
"Build me a game like this. But make it possible to actually reach the roof of the fortress."
And Claude took the assignment rather seriously.
First, it analyzed the original video and calculated what exploring this massive structure would actually involve.

The results were ridiculous:
- 2.2 kilometers of walking to reach the roof
- 46 minutes at normal walking speed
- Two movement modes: walking and sprinting with Shift
- A fully explorable fortress with interconnected interior spaces
Then it built the game.

What Claude created in approximately 40 minutes:
- A playable 3D fortress inspired by the original video
- Procedurally assembled architecture and explorable interiors
- AI-generated visual assets
- A physics and movement system
- Original background music
- Walking and sprinting mechanics
- A guided navigation system that automatically leads you to the roof

All running directly in your browser.
No traditional game development pipeline. No manually building hundreds of rooms. Just Claude Opus 5.5, Three.js, AI-generated assets, and a prompt.
And here's what I find most interesting.

We're getting dangerously close to the era of personal video games.
See something interesting on the internet? Turn it into a game.
Want to explore a fictional world? Generate it.
Wish your favorite game had different mechanics, environments, or an entirely new storyline? Just ask.
Of course, this experiment still has bugs. I could spend another few hours adding gameplay mechanics, improving the environments, and polishing everything.
But I think I'll stop here.
Because the interesting part isn't whether the game is perfect.
It's that a single person can now turn a random internet video into an explorable world in less than an hour.
And that's a pretty remarkable change.

Play the game yourself:
https://claude.ai/artifact/78NPvbJMLcQikzukVq7BqW

Tip: Click the Guide button to automatically navigate through the fortress and reach the roof. Or explore it yourself, if you've got 46 minutes to spare.

items.title: Hermes Marketplace Is Here! 1,000+ AI Plugins, Claude Pro/Max, Blender & MCP Tools
items.excerpt: While the AI industry keeps reinventing plugins, connectors, apps, and marketplaces, Nous Research has decided to put everything in one place. Meet Hermes Marketplace, the official plugin and skill directory for Hermes A
items.videoDescription:
While the AI industry keeps reinventing plugins, connectors, apps, and marketplaces, Nous Research has decided to put everything in one place.

Meet Hermes Marketplace, the official plugin and skill directory for Hermes Agent.

And this is becoming a seriously interesting ecosystem.

The marketplace already lists more than 1,000 plugins, bringing together AI agent skills, MCP servers, model integrations, creative tools, automation systems, and community extensions.

Here's what makes Hermes Marketplace interesting.

The ecosystem supports a portable plugin format called Portable Agent Plugins v1.

A package can combine:

MCP servers: Give Hermes access to external applications and tools.

Agent skills: Teach Hermes how to use those tools effectively.

Configuration: Define the tools, dependencies, and settings required for the workflow.

In other words, you're not just installing a collection of API endpoints.

You're giving your agent new capabilities and instructions for using them.

And some of the new integrations are genuinely exciting.

1. Claude Subscription DirectSDK

This might be one of the most interesting additions.

It lets Hermes Agent use your existing Claude Pro or Max subscription through the official Claude Code CLI.

No separate Anthropic API key. No separate per-token API bill.

Hermes keeps its own agent loop, tools, memory, approvals, and session management while Claude handles model inference.

Install:

hermes plugins install claude-subscription-directsdk

Then select the provider through hermes model.

There's a catch, of course.

This is an experimental integration, and requests consume your existing Claude subscription allowance. It isn't unlimited free inference.

2. Blender Lab MCP

Now we're getting to the creative stuff.

Hermes can connect directly to Blender through the official Blender Lab MCP integration.

The plugin provides tools for inspecting and modifying 3D scenes, executing Blender operations, and automating production workflows.

It also includes a specialized Blender skill.

And if the required software isn't installed, the workflow can help set it up.

The installer downloads Blender 5.1 or newer, verifies the downloaded files using SHA-256 checksums, and installs it into your user directory after approval.

Install:

hermes plugins install blender

One security consideration: the Blender integration can execute Python inside Blender, so review the workflow and permissions before enabling it.

3. TouchDesigner MCP

This one is particularly interesting for generative art, interactive installations, and real-time graphics.

Hermes can control a running TouchDesigner session through an MCP server.

That opens up possibilities for working with:

Procedural visuals

Interactive animations

Audio-reactive graphics

GLSL shaders

Real-time creative environments

Install:

hermes plugins install touchdesigner

The integration connects to a local TouchDesigner MCP endpoint on port 40404.

4. Memory Wiki

Ever wondered what your autonomous agent actually remembers about you and your projects?

Memory Wiki introduces a visual dashboard for exploring Hermes' persistent memory.

You can browse subject pages, daily activity logs, and information derived from your previous sessions.

It also provides a read-only inspection panel for MEMORY.md and USER.md.

Finally, a way to see what your AI thinks it knows about you.

Install:

hermes plugins install hermes-memory-wiki

5. Telegram Business Mode

And here's something useful for people running businesses.

Hermes can act as a Telegram Business assistant.

It reads incoming customer messages, prepares suggested replies, and sends the drafts to you for approval.

You can:
Send the suggested response
Edit it
Discard it
Nothing gets sent to the customer until you explicitly approve it.

Install:
hermes plugins install hermes-telegram-business

This is currently an experimental Hermes Labs plugin, rather than a fully supported official integration. But here's what I find most interesting about the entire marketplace.

Want Claude reasoning inside Hermes? Connect your subscription.
Want an agent that works in Blender? Install the MCP integration.
Want automated business communications? Add Telegram.
Want real-time generative visuals? Connect TouchDesigner.

items.title: Google Genie 4 Is INSANE! AI Generates Interactive Worlds With Sound | 10+ Demos
items.excerpt: What if AI could generate an entire world while you're exploring it? Not a video. Not a traditional game. An interactive reality that reacts to everything you do. And now it has sound. And people who actually talk back.
items.videoDescription:
What if AI could generate an entire world while you're exploring it?

Not a video. Not a traditional game. An interactive reality that reacts to everything you do.

And now it has sound. And people who actually talk back.

Meet Google DeepMind's Genie 4, the next generation of AI world models.

And this is getting dangerously close to science fiction.

In this video, I've brought together Google's official presentation and more than 10 demonstrations of AI-generated worlds.

From photorealistic environments to surreal landscapes, talking characters, and interactive simulations.

And the results are genuinely fascinating.

Here's what's new in Genie 4:

Real-time world generation: Explore environments that continuously evolve as you move.

Native AI audio: Hear footsteps, wind, water, environmental sounds, and music generated alongside the visuals.

Interactive dialogue: AI-generated characters can speak and respond to what's happening around them.

Live scene editing: Change the weather, introduce characters, or transform the environment using text prompts.

More realistic physics: Improved simulations of movement, collisions, and physical interactions.

More believable humans: Characters can move, react, and interact with their surroundings more naturally.

But here's where things get really interesting.

Genie 4 doesn't work alone.

Google connected it to Gemini 3.8 Flash, which acts as a reasoning agent inside the simulation.

Gemini observes the generated world, breaks complex tasks into smaller steps, checks the results, and adjusts its plans when something changes.

In one demonstration, Google even shows a simulated Apollo humanoid robot playing checkers, using Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 together.

And this reveals something important.

Google isn't building these worlds just so we can play games.

World models are part of its long-term research toward artificial general intelligence.

Robots and autonomous AI agents need environments where they can learn, experiment, make mistakes, and understand consequences.

And simulated worlds could be considerably cheaper and safer than testing every new behavior with physical robots.

Imagine training thousands of robots without smashing thousands of actual robots into actual walls.

But the creative possibilities are just as exciting.

Game developers could prototype entire interactive worlds.

Filmmakers could experiment with scenes before filming.

Designers could build explorable environments from simple prompts.

AI agents could practice complex tasks in simulated spaces.

And the rest of us could finally explore those bizarre places we remember from our dreams.

Of course, we're not living in The Matrix just yet.

Genie 4 still struggles with long-term consistency, complex physics, spatial accuracy, and details that gradually change during extended interactions.

And you can't just sign up and start exploring today.

As of October 31, 2026, Genie 4 is available only to selected research testers.

Google plans to expand access to Google AI Ultra subscribers through Project Genie, followed by early-access developers using Gemini API and Google AI Studio.

No public release date or pricing has been announced.

But watching these demonstrations, one thing becomes increasingly obvious.

We're moving from AI that generates content to AI that generates experiences.

First, we generated images.

Then videos.

Now we're generating worlds that respond to us.

And eventually, those worlds might become places where both humans and AI agents learn, create, and interact.

The Matrix used to be a movie. Now it's starting to look suspiciously like a product roadmap.

This video is an edited compilation featuring Google's official Genie 4 presentation and more than 10 demonstration clips. The showcased worlds are research demonstrations, not footage of a publicly available product.

items.excerpt: What if you could take apart a V8 engine, explore an aircraft's landing gear, or see exactly how a walking robot works? Without touching a real machine. Meet Teardown, a free, open-source Claude Code skill that transform
items.videoDescription:
What if you could take apart a V8 engine, explore an aircraft's landing gear, or see exactly how a walking robot works?

Without touching a real machine.

Meet Teardown, a free, open-source Claude Code skill that transforms mechanical systems into interactive 3D simulations.

And the results look seriously impressive.

Instead of creating another static 3D model, Claude builds an entire interactive laboratory where you can disassemble machines, control individual mechanisms, and watch the physics unfold.

Here's what Teardown can do:

Interactive 3D models: Rotate, zoom, and explore machines from different angles.

Exploded views: Take mechanisms apart and examine individual components.

Working animations: Watch gears, pistons, actuators, and mechanical linkages move.

Live measurements: Monitor joint torque, mechanical loads, movement, and other parameters.

Independent controls: Isolate subsystems and experiment with their behavior.

Automated demonstrations: Generate guided tours and animated videos of the mechanisms.

And the fascinating part?

The 3D geometry is generated programmatically using Three.js.

No prebuilt CAD model required.

The project includes three complete examples:

V8 engine: Explore pistons, cylinders, and the four-stroke combustion cycle.

Cessna 337 landing gear: Watch the hydraulic mechanism retract the wheels.

Strandbeest: Explore the remarkable walking mechanism inspired by Theo Jansen's kinetic sculptures.

But here's what makes Teardown technically interesting.

Instead of animating dozens of components independently, Claude builds a mathematical model that controls the entire mechanism.

Take the aircraft landing gear.

One actuator moves a rack by 201 mm.

That rack drives a 32-tooth gear with a module of 4 mm, producing a pitch diameter of 128 mm.

Half the gear's pitch circumference is approximately 201 mm.

So the rack's movement corresponds to a 180-degree rotation.

And the gear, landing gear legs, animations, charts, and instrument readings all follow the same underlying calculation.

One mathematical model. An entire machine moving in sync.

That's the difference between making a convincing animation and attempting to simulate how a mechanism actually works.

Of course, there's a catch.

The quality depends heavily on your reference material.

The creator experimented with generating a pangolin, an armadillo, and a scorpion without providing proper anatomical references.

The results? Three rather primitive models.

But give Claude technical drawings, dimensions, and real mechanical specifications, and things get considerably more interesting.

Want to try it?

Install the skill:

npx skills add elvarofficial/teardown -g -a claude-code

Then install the required dependencies:

cd ~/.claude/skills/teardown
npm install
npx playwright install chromium

Open Claude Code and run:

/teardown

You'll need Node.js 20 or newer. Video rendering also requires FFmpeg, with Python 3 used for sound generation.

The skill is free and MIT licensed. Claude Code usage may still consume your subscription allowance.

And here's why I find this project exciting.

We're moving from AI that explains how machines work to AI that can build interactive environments where you can actually explore those explanations.

For engineering education, robotics, product design, and technical visualization, that's a fascinating direction.

Imagine turning an engineering textbook into an interactive mechanical laboratory.

Instead of just reading about how something works, you could take it apart and see for yourself.

Try the interactive demos:
https://visual-learning.app/

Teardown on GitHub:
https://github.com/elvarofficial/teardown

Created by: Elvar (@elvar_official)

items.excerpt: What if your entire AI-powered content business operated from a tiny virtual city? With a newsroom, a video studio, a post office, a café, and even a bank? Meet Grok City, a fascinating experiment in multi-agent automati
items.videoDescription:
What if your entire AI-powered content business operated from a tiny virtual city?

With a newsroom, a video studio, a post office, a café, and even a bank?

Meet Grok City, a fascinating experiment in multi-agent automation built around Grok Bots.

And yes, every AI agent has its own little office.

We've all seen automated content factories before.

AI finds trending topics, writes scripts, generates videos, adds captions, and publishes everything to social media.

But this one takes the concept a little further.

Six AI agents. Six different jobs. One connected workflow.

Here's who lives in the city:

Scout (Newsroom): Searches for emerging AI stories before they go viral.

Hook (Writers' Room): Creates three opening hooks, tests them with Grok, and lets the human choose the winner.

Reply (Café): Handles comments, community interactions, and sponsorship messages.

Reel (Studio): Creates and renders videos, then delivers them to the Post Office.

Post (Post Office): Publishes threads and videos to X. A tiny paper airplane even flies out when something gets posted.

Ledger (Bank): Tracks revenue and helps identify which content actually makes money.

And here's the interesting part.

Everything is connected through a single content pipeline.

From discovering a story to tracking the revenue it generates.

There's a live activity log showing what every agent is doing, where tasks are moving, and what has already been completed.

And when something requires human judgment?

It appears in a separate "Needs You" inbox.

Approve. Reject. Make a decision. Let the agents continue.

Now, do AI agents actually work faster because they live in an adorable virtual city?

Absolutely not.

The little buildings, walking characters, and animated handoffs are mostly visual decoration.

But they do something surprisingly useful.

They make a complicated multi-agent system understandable at a glance.

You can actually see how the content factory is organized, which agent owns each task, and how work moves through the pipeline.

That's valuable when your automation grows beyond a couple of scripts.

And I have to admit something.

I spent several months building something remarkably similar.

Not the city, obviously.

A multi-agent system for research, content opportunities, automation, performance tracking, and continuous improvement.

Unfortunately, I got a little too ambitious with the underlying architecture and the self-improvement mechanisms.

And never quite finished the whole thing.

Watching Grok City makes me think I should probably get back to it.

Although I'm definitely not adding a virtual city.

The agents have enough work already. They don't need office real estate.

items.videoDescription:
What if AI agents could handle an entire motion design project, from the first storyboard to the final After Effects render?

Not just generate a few video clips.

Actually work with professional creative software, build compositions, animate layers, and produce a finished promotional video.

Well, Krea AI just shared a fascinating look at how its own team is experimenting with exactly that.

And this is the kind of AI filmmaking workflow I find genuinely exciting.

Meet Krea's agent-powered creative pipeline, combining Claude, Krea MCP, Figma, and Adobe After Effects.

Here's how the process works.

Step 1: Claude creates the storyboard in Figma

The workflow starts with a creative brief.

Claude uses Krea MCP to generate visual assets, explore creative directions, and help assemble the storyboard in Figma.

Instead of jumping straight into video generation, the team establishes the visual language, composition, and sequence of shots.

Step 2: AI prepares the animation in After Effects

Once the storyboard is approved, a specialized Krea Agent works with Adobe After Effects.

The demonstrated workflow uses agents to help:

Build and organize compositions

Arrange visual elements and layers

Create animation keyframes

Coordinate timing across the timeline

Develop transitions and motion effects

Prepare the project for rendering

Step 3: Agents coordinate the production

This is where things get particularly interesting.

Rather than treating each creative step as an isolated AI generation, the workflow connects them into a coordinated production process.

Visual assets move from concept development into animation, while agents handle increasingly technical parts of the process.

And the final result is created inside professional production software.

Not just another AI-generated MP4 with no editable project behind it.

But here's why I think this matters.

For the past few years, most AI video tools have followed the same basic formula:

Write a prompt. Generate a clip. Download it. Repeat until something looks acceptable.

That's useful for exploration, but it isn't a complete production workflow.

Professional motion design involves composition, layers, timing, typography, animation curves, revisions, and countless small decisions.

Krea is exploring how AI agents can participate in that actual production process.

And the distinction is important.

The goal isn't simply to generate better video.

It's to automate more of the work between having an idea and delivering a finished project.

Now, an important limitation.

Krea's publicly documented After Effects plugin primarily focuses on generating imagery, backgrounds, plates, and motion-design concepts inside Adobe.

The more autonomous workflow described in this demonstration should be viewed as an example of Krea's internal production approach, not proof that every user can already reproduce the entire pipeline with one click.

And creative supervision still matters.

But the direction is fascinating.

We've already taught AI agents to write code. Now we're teaching them to operate the tools creative professionals actually use.

Figma for visual planning.

Krea for generating assets.

After Effects for animation and compositing.

Claude for reasoning and coordinating the workflow.

Personally, I'd much rather see more integrations like this than another startup trying to reinvent a miniature version of After Effects in a browser.

The future of AI filmmaking might not be a single magical video model.

It might be an entire production team of agents working inside the software we already know.

And that's a considerably more interesting future for creative AI.

items.title: Google Ran Gemma 4 in Space. Its First Response Was a Poem! | Project Suncatcher
items.excerpt: Remember when "cloud computing" was just a metaphor? Well, Google is taking it rather literally. On October 30, 2026, Google announced that its AI model Gemma 4 had successfully generated a response from orbit and transm
items.videoDescription:
Remember when "cloud computing" was just a metaphor?

Well, Google is taking it rather literally.

On October 30, 2026, Google announced that its AI model Gemma 4 had successfully generated a response from orbit and transmitted it back to Earth.

And the first response?

A haiku.

Yes. We've reached the point where artificial intelligence is writing poetry in space.

Meet Project Suncatcher, Google's ambitious experiment to explore whether future AI data centers could operate in orbit, powered by solar energy.

Here's what happened:

October 1, 2026: Google launched its prototype satellite aboard a SpaceX rocket.

Onboard AI hardware: The satellite carries Google's data-center-class Tensor Processing Unit (TPU).

Onboard model: Google's open-weight Gemma 4.

First successful response: Engineers sent a prompt from Earth asking the model to write a haiku about being in space.

The result: Gemma processed the request in orbit and transmitted its poem back as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway.

The poem:

Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai called it a "Hello World" moment for Project Suncatcher.

But Google isn't alone in this race.

In November 2025, Starcloud launched an NVIDIA H100 GPU into orbit, later demonstrating AI training and inference in space.

Now Google has achieved its own milestone using a TPU rather than an NVIDIA GPU.

And here's where things get really interesting.

Google is exploring a future in which networks of solar-powered satellites could provide large-scale AI computing infrastructure.

Imagine orbital data centers connected by laser links, operating above Earth's atmosphere.

Of course, there are enormous engineering challenges:

Cooling powerful processors in a vacuum

Protecting chips from radiation

Maintaining high-bandwidth satellite connections

Launching, maintaining, and eventually replacing orbital hardware

Making the entire system economically viable

So no, Google hasn't built a fully operational space data center yet.

But it has demonstrated that an advanced AI model can respond to a prompt using data-center-class hardware in orbit.

Next milestone: two interconnected experimental satellites in 2027.

And if Starship eventually makes launching large quantities of computing hardware economically practical, things could get very interesting.

I suppose one day I'll tell my grandchildren:

"You know, we called it cloud computing long before the cloud was actually above our heads."

And they'll probably think I'm making it up.

items.videoDescription:
What if you could create hundreds of beautiful pixel art animations without drawing a single sprite?

No Photoshop. No Aseprite. No pre-made image assets.

Just Claude Code, JavaScript, and a surprisingly effective creative workflow.

Meet PixelFX, an open-source collection of 244 code-generated pixel art effects, complete with a Claude Code skill that helps you create your own.

And some of these animations look genuinely fantastic.

Here's what you'll find:

Fire and explosions: Flames, smoke, sparks, and magical fireballs

Magic and combat: Lightning, ice spells, energy beams, and sword attacks

Weather effects: Rain, snow, clouds, and atmospheric particles

Character animations: Movement, impacts, status effects, and attack sequences

UI animations: Achievements, notifications, transitions, and collectibles

Sci-fi effects: Force fields, holograms, energy cores, and glitches

And here's the interesting part.

Every animation is generated programmatically.

Instead of using existing sprites, the code calculates how pixels should appear and move over time.

That means you can change colors, adjust timing, modify particle behavior, and generate entirely new variations.

You can use the effects directly in JavaScript games or export them as sprite sheets for engines like Godot, Unity, and GameMaker.

But the real secret isn't the code. It's the process.

The project builds on a creative methodology shared by Hugo Duprez, the developer behind Sprite Fusion.

And his advice is surprisingly practical.

1. Treat code like clay.

Don't expect a perfect result from one prompt. Ask Claude to generate 5–10 variations, render them, and choose the most promising direction.

2. Trust your eyes.

AI can write the animation code, but you're still responsible for the creative direction. Refine the timing, movement, colors, and tiny details until the result actually feels right.

3. Feed your creativity.

Study great pixel art, games, films, and visual effects. Better references lead to better creative decisions.

PixelFX packages this approach into a reusable Claude Code skill.

Install it in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add patch-gg/pixelfx
/plugin install pixelfx@pixelfx

Then ask Claude to create something like:

"Create five variations of a magical ice explosion, render previews, and help me choose the best one for my pixel art game."

The skill can generate the effects, render previews, and help you refine them through multiple iterations.

And the whole project is free and open source under the MIT license.

What I particularly like about this approach is that AI isn't simply generating finished images.

It's generating the underlying systems that create the visuals.

And those systems can be edited, reused, and improved.

That's a much more interesting direction for AI-assisted game development.

244 effects. No image assets. Just code, iteration, and good taste.

items.title: Adobe Premiere Pro Gets Generative Remove! Erase Objects From Video With AI
items.excerpt: Remember when removing an unwanted object from a video meant opening After Effects, tracking masks, rebuilding backgrounds, and spending hours cleaning up individual frames? Well, Adobe just made that considerably easier
items.videoDescription:
Remember when removing an unwanted object from a video meant opening After Effects, tracking masks, rebuilding backgrounds, and spending hours cleaning up individual frames?

Well, Adobe just made that considerably easier.

Meet Generative Remove, a new AI-powered object removal tool built directly into Adobe Premiere Pro.

And the best part?

You don't even need to leave your timeline.

A boom microphone in the shot?

Gone.

A light stand someone forgot to move?

Gone.

An annoying tourist walking through your perfect cinematic composition?

Well, Adobe would very much like to make them disappear too.

Here's how Generative Remove works.

Step 1: Select the object

Open your footage in Premiere Pro Beta and use Object Mask or a vector shape to select whatever you want to remove.

It can be a person, microphone, lighting stand, unwanted logo, or another distracting object.

Step 2: Track the movement

Premiere's built-in tracking system follows the object throughout the clip.

You can adjust the mask to include shadows, reflections, and other visual details that should disappear with it.

Step 3: Click Remove

And here's where the magic happens.

Adobe's cloud-based generative AI reconstructs the missing background while attempting to preserve the original footage outside the selected area.

Step 4: Keep editing

The generation happens in the background.

You can continue working on your timeline while Premiere processes the removal.

Step 5: Review or regenerate

The finished clip appears on your timeline with a special AI badge.

Not happy with the result?

Adjust the mask and try again.

Or restore the original footage with a single click.

And yes, the workflow is non-destructive.

Your original footage remains available.

There's another useful detail.

You can remove multiple objects from the same shot.

Create separate masks, track them independently, and select them together for a single generation.

No need to process every unwanted object separately.

But here's the catch.

Generative Remove is still in beta, and the technical limitations are fairly restrictive.

Current beta limitations:

Maximum clip duration: 10 seconds

Supported resolution: 480p to 1080p

Maximum frame rate: 30 FPS

SDR footage only

No HDR or 10-bit support yet

Internet connection required

Cloud processing rather than local GPU inference

And then there's the inevitable Adobe detail.

Generative credits.

Because apparently, removing something from your video also removes something from your credit balance.

Adobe currently charges 40 Firefly generative credits per second.

That means:

5-second clip: 200 credits

10-second clip: 400 credits

Three attempts at a 10-second removal: 1,200 credits

Premiere shows the credit cost before processing, so at least there won't be any surprises.

Well, apart from the occasional mysterious object appearing where your microphone used to be.

But here's what I find particularly interesting.

For years, removing objects from video has been one of those tasks that required specialized compositing tools.

After Effects, Nuke, dedicated cleanup software, or increasingly complicated AI workflows.

Now that capability is moving directly into the editor.

Select. Track. Remove. Continue editing.

That's a much more practical application of generative AI than simply generating another cinematic clip from a prompt.

Because professional filmmaking isn't just about creating new footage.

It's also about fixing the footage you've already shot.

Of course, generative removal still struggles with difficult backgrounds, complex motion, reflections, and occlusion.

And ten seconds at 1080p isn't exactly a feature-film cleanup pipeline.

But the direction is clear.

AI video tools are gradually becoming part of the professional editing workflow instead of existing as separate applications.

And honestly, that's exactly where I'd rather see them.

Less switching between software. More actual editing.

Now, Adobe, about those generative credits...

What if you could create an entire interactive 3D world just by describing it?

No manual modeling. No complicated scene setup. No hours spent writing Three.js code.

Just type a prompt and let AI build a world you can actually explore.

Meet Kimi 3D Worlds, a new interactive demo on Hugging Face Spaces powered by Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro.

And the results are pretty impressive.

Here's how it works:

Describe your world: A futuristic cyberpunk city, a medieval castle, an alien planet, or anything else you can imagine.

Add a visual reference: Upload a sketch or choose a visual style to guide the generation.

Let Kimi write the code: The model generates an executable 3D scene using Three.js and WebGL.

Explore the result: Open the generated environment in your browser and move the camera around freely.

And here's what makes it interesting.

These aren't just AI-generated images pretending to be 3D.

Kimi actually writes the code that creates the environment.

That means the resulting scenes can include:

Procedural 3D geometry: Buildings, landscapes, objects, and environmental details.

Dynamic lighting: Atmospheric illumination, shadows, and visual effects.

Custom shaders: Materials, textures, and stylized rendering.

Object animations: Moving elements and animated environments.

Interactive cameras: Explore the generated world from different perspectives.

Browser-based rendering: Experience the scene directly through Three.js and WebGL.

And the model behind it is enormous.

Kimi K3.1 Pro uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with:

2.8 trillion total parameters

104 billion activated parameters

1-million-token context window

Native text and image understanding

Moonshot AI has specifically improved the model's coding and 3D creation capabilities.

But here's an important distinction.

Kimi 3D Worlds isn't a traditional generative world model like Google Genie or Odyssey.

Instead of generating new video frames as you move, Kimi generates the actual code for an interactive environment.

Once the code is ready, your browser renders the 3D scene.

And that's a very different, potentially more editable approach.

Why do I find this exciting?

Because the distance between imagining a world and building a playable version of it is getting remarkably small.

Want a futuristic city for your game?

Describe it.

Need a stylized environment for an interactive website?

Generate one.

Want to recreate a strange location from a dream?

Well, now you have a pretty interesting place to start.

Of course, generated scenes may still need optimization, debugging, and considerable artistic refinement.

But for rapid prototyping, creative coding, interactive storytelling, and experimental game development, this is a fascinating tool.

We're moving from asking AI to draw imaginary worlds to asking it to build worlds we can actually enter.

And the best part?

You can try the demo yourself.

items.videoDescription:
Remember when rigging a 3D character meant manually placing bones, painting skin weights, and spending hours fixing broken deformations?

Well, apparently, now you can just tell AI:

"Add tail bones."

And it actually builds them.

Meet HYPER3D Rigging by Deemos, a new AI-powered rigging and animation system that lets you create and modify character skeletons using natural-language prompts.

And this is a pretty fascinating development for 3D artists, animators, and game developers.

Here's what Hyper3D Rigging can do:

Automatic rigging: Generate skeletons for existing 3D characters.

Humanoid characters: Create full-body rigs with individual finger bones.

Animals and fantasy creatures: Rig quadrupeds, birds, dragons, and other unusual characters.

Prompt-based skeleton editing: Add or remove bones using ordinary language.

Custom bone hierarchies: Adapt the skeleton to unusual anatomy.

Automatic skinning: Generate weights connecting the character mesh to its skeleton.

250+ motion presets: Quickly animate characters using an existing library.

Interactive animation controls: Refine movement and test your character directly in Hyper3D.

And here's where things get really interesting.

Traditional auto-rigging systems are often designed around familiar character structures.

Humans. Quadrupeds. Standard skeleton templates.

But what happens when your character has six arms, three tails, or an unnecessarily complicated pair of dragon wings?

Usually, you start editing the rig manually.

Hyper3D is trying to turn that process into a conversation.

Generate the initial skeleton.

Then ask:

"Add a flexible tail with several bones."

Or:

"Add bones to the ears so they can move independently."

The system adapts the skeleton structure based on your instructions.

And once the rig is ready, you can immediately test it with animation.

The platform includes more than 250 motion presets, so you can quickly see how your character behaves when walking, running, jumping, or performing other actions.

You can also import your own compatible animations.

But here's the important distinction.

A generated skeleton doesn't automatically mean a production-ready character.

Complex deformations, skin weights, joint placement, and unusual anatomy still need inspection.

And the more unconventional your creature becomes, the more likely you'll need manual adjustments.

Still, the direction is fascinating.

We've already seen AI generating 3D geometry, textures, and animations.

Now it's becoming increasingly capable of creating and modifying the structural systems that make those characters move.

And instead of simply accepting whatever skeleton the model generates, you can tell it what needs to change.

Imagine going from a generated character to a working animated creature without spending hours manually building its rig.

We're not completely there yet.

But the gap between AI-generated 3D models and usable game characters keeps getting smaller.

And somewhere, a traditional character rigger is probably staring at this demonstration with a complicated mixture of excitement and professional anxiety.

A toast to the riggers and character setup artists.

Your next coworker might be a text prompt.
