items.videoDescription:
What if waiting for your favorite Twitch streamer could actually help save a forest?

Not by donating money. Not by watching an advertisement.

Just by paying attention.

Meet FireCatchers, one of the smartest examples of creative marketing I've seen recently.

Developed by Havas Play and Sapeurs-Pompiers de France, the campaign transforms Twitch's ordinary "Starting Soon" screens into a real-time wildfire detection network.

And the idea is brilliantly simple.

Here's how it works:

Live forest cameras: Instead of a boring waiting screen, viewers see live footage from wildfire-prone areas in France.

Community-powered detection: Gamers watch for suspicious smoke while waiting for their stream to begin.

Instant reporting: If someone spots something unusual, they report the camera number in Twitch chat.

Human verification: When multiple viewers flag the same camera, an alert goes to the local emergency operations center for verification.

Real-world impact: Viewers become part of an early-warning system that can help firefighters respond faster.

The campaign launched in July 2025 with four French Twitch creators.

And according to the campaign's published results, it achieved:

600,000 followers reached through participating creators

786 additional streamers joining voluntarily

2,190 hours of additional live surveillance

5 fires detected

But here's why I find this particularly interesting from a marketing perspective.

This isn't advertising disguised as entertainment. It's entertainment infrastructure repurposed for something genuinely useful.

Havas Play didn't interrupt the audience with another banner.

They found a moment when people were already paying attention and gave that attention a purpose.

They didn't ask gamers to become passive supporters of a campaign.

They gave them an actual role.

And suddenly, an ordinary Twitch waiting screen became a community-powered public safety tool.

That's a pretty powerful lesson for brands, marketers, and anyone working on partnerships.

The best brand collaborations don't just ask for attention. They give people something meaningful to do with it.

Sometimes the most creative media placement isn't about finding a new place to advertise.

It's about discovering what an existing space could become.

items.excerpt: Sometimes AI feels less like technology and more like a magician that can take you straight back to childhood. Let me tell you a story. I was eight years old when I got my first PlayStation. It was New Year's Eve. I open
items.videoDescription:
Sometimes AI feels less like technology and more like a magician that can take you straight back to childhood.

Let me tell you a story.

I was eight years old when I got my first PlayStation.

It was New Year's Eve. I opened the box and couldn't believe my eyes.

A PlayStation One.

A completely unexpected gift. And something I'd wanted more than almost anything in the world.

The next morning, January 1st, snow was falling outside.

I was sitting on a patterned carpet, putting my very first game disc into my brand-new console.

Sheep, Dog 'n' Wolf.

A wonderfully ridiculous game featuring Ralph Wolf, Sam Sheepdog, Looney Tunes humor, clever puzzles, and occasionally infuriating challenges.

I loved it.

Fast-forward to November 2, 2026.

Me. OpenAI Codex. GPT-6 Astra.

And one little experiment.

What if I could bring that exact childhood experience back to life on my Mac?

Well, apparently, modern AI coding agents can do quite a lot in 90 minutes.

Here's what Codex accomplished:

Found the original Windows version of Sheep, Dog 'n' Wolf.

Created a Mac port so I could run the game on my computer.

Improved the graphics with antialiasing, resolution adjustments, and lighting enhancements.

Translated the game into Russian, including a custom-generated language selection screen.

Created Russian voice acting for the entire game using Gemini TTS.

Added a little Easter egg: A sign in the starting area promoting my YouTube channel.

Yes, that sign you can see in the screencast.

And the whole thing took approximately an hour and a half.

Not weeks. Not months.

Ninety minutes.

Of course, this wasn't a complete remake built from scratch. It was an AI-assisted port and enhancement of the original game.

But that's precisely what makes it so special.

I wasn't trying to create something new. I wanted to experience something old again.

The same characters. The same absurd humor. The same puzzles.

Just running on my Mac, with better visuals and a language I could choose.

And suddenly, for a little while, I was that eight-year-old kid sitting on the carpet again.

I spend a lot of time experimenting with AI coding agents, automation, creative tools, and new technologies.

But every now and then, one of those experiments reminds me why I fell in love with computers in the first place.

Not because of productivity. Not because of benchmarks. Not because of how many tokens a model can process.

Because sometimes a computer can do something that feels like magic.

And on November 2, 2026, Codex gave me back a tiny piece of my childhood.

A magician suddenly appeared in my Codex window.

And for once, I didn't ask it to write another line of business software.

items.videoDescription:
Ever asked Claude Code or Codex to build a beautiful website?

And somehow ended up with the same generic SaaS landing page?

Purple gradients. Rounded cards. Predictable layouts. We've all been there.

Well, someone just made it much easier to give your AI coding agent better design taste.

Meet GradientDeck UI, a free library of more than 1,280 real website designs, each with a downloadable DESIGN.md file.

And this is a genuinely useful resource for anyone building websites with AI.

Here's the idea.

Instead of asking your AI agent to "make something modern and beautiful," you give it a real design system extracted from a website you actually like.

What's inside the library?

1,286 real website references: SaaS products, portfolios, creative studios, e-commerce, fintech, and more.

Color palettes: Primary colors, backgrounds, accents, and contrast rules.

Typography: Font families, sizes, weights, and hierarchy.

Spacing and layout: Margins, padding, content widths, and proportions.

Component styling: Buttons, cards, borders, and other interface patterns.

Design guidelines: Instructions that help AI agents maintain a consistent visual language.

And the best part?

Every reference comes with a ready-to-use DESIGN.md file.

No registration. No subscription. Completely free to browse and download.

Here's how to use it with Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor:

Step 1: Visit GradientDeck UI and find a website whose visual style you like.

Step 2: Download or copy its DESIGN.md file.

Step 3: Save that file in your project's root directory.

Step 4: Tell your AI coding agent:

"Build a responsive landing page for my product. Read DESIGN.md first and follow its typography, colors, spacing, and component guidelines. Adapt the visual style to my content and branding without copying the original website."

That's it.

Your agent now has a concrete visual reference instead of another vague instruction to make everything look premium.

And here's what I particularly like about this approach.

You're not downloading someone else's website code.

You're giving your agent a structured description of its visual design.

That means you can borrow the visual principles while creating completely different layouts, content, and components.

Want the typography of a beautiful editorial website?

The spacing of a minimalist portfolio?

The color system of a polished fintech product?

Find an example, grab the design guidelines, and start experimenting.

Of course, a DESIGN.md file won't automatically turn every AI-generated website into an award-winning design.

You'll still need good content, visual judgment, and a few iterations.

And you should avoid copying distinctive branded assets or reproducing another company's website too closely.

But this is a much better starting point than asking AI to invent a complete design language from scratch every single time.

Because maybe AI coding agents don't need another thousand design prompts.

Maybe they just need better references.

And 1,286 real websites should keep them busy for a while.

Explore GradientDeck UI:
https://ui.gradientdeck.com/

items.excerpt: Ever wanted to learn something new, only to discover that the recommended course is 40 hours long? You bookmark it. Watch the introduction. Promise yourself you'll finish it someday. And never open it again. Well, someon
items.videoDescription:
Ever wanted to learn something new, only to discover that the recommended course is 40 hours long?

You bookmark it.

Watch the introduction.

Promise yourself you'll finish it someday.

And never open it again.

Well, someone built a Claude Code skill specifically for people like us.

Meet Claudemy, a free, open-source AI learning tool that transforms almost any topic into a personalized course of short, podcast-style lessons.

And the concept is surprisingly practical.

You tell Claude what you want to learn. It builds an entire course around your request.

Not just a summary. Not a random collection of articles.

An actual learning program with research, audio lessons, practical exercises, and references.

Here's what Claudemy creates:

12 short lessons: Approximately two minutes each.

Podcast-style audio: Two AI hosts discuss the subject instead of delivering another boring lecture.

Research-backed content: Claude examines 20–40 relevant web pages.

Multiple perspectives: Compares expert opinions and identifies disagreements.

Lesson summaries: Each lesson includes a three-line explanation of the key idea.

Practical exercises: Small, actionable tasks that help you apply what you've learned.

Source references: Links to the original research, articles, and documentation.

Personal playbook: A collection of the most useful takeaways from the entire course.

And here's what makes it particularly interesting.

Claudemy doesn't simply ask an AI model to invent a course from its existing knowledge.

It actually researches the topic.

First, it identifies the important subtopics.

Then it searches the web, reads relevant sources, compares different opinions, and organizes everything into a logical learning sequence.

The system even checks that cited sources were actually accessed during research.

And before generating the entire course, it produces one sample lesson and asks for your feedback.

That way, you can adjust the style or difficulty before the remaining lessons are created.

Want to learn something specific?

Try:

"Teach me negotiation."

"Create a beginner's course on Three.js."

"Teach me how to design better AI agent workflows."

"Explain behavioral economics through practical examples."

You can even ask Claudemy to build a course based on a particular expert's writing.

And the whole thing becomes approximately 25 minutes of audio you can listen to like a podcast.

Each lesson ends with something concrete to try.

Because understanding a concept and actually being able to use it are two very different things.

How to install Claudemy in Claude Code:

Open Claude Code and run:

/plugin marketplace add assafkip/claudemy
/plugin install claudemy@claudemy

Then simply ask:

Teach me negotiation

Claudemy will start researching and building your course.

What about audio generation?

For natural two-host conversations, Claudemy supports ElevenLabs.

You'll need an ElevenLabs API key and available credits.

On macOS, you can also use the built-in system voices for free.

The skill itself is free and MIT licensed, although Claude usage and optional premium speech generation have their own costs.

And here's why I particularly like this project.

AI has made information incredibly accessible.

But access to information isn't the same as learning.

You can ask ChatGPT almost anything, but that doesn't automatically give you a structured path toward understanding a subject.

Claudemy tries to solve that problem.

Research the topic.

Break it into manageable pieces.

Explain the important concepts.

Give you something to practice.

Then move on.

It's less like asking a chatbot a question and more like having a tiny educational production studio working just for you.

Of course, AI-generated lessons still need critical evaluation, especially for technical, medical, financial, or legal topics.

But for exploring new skills and getting an introduction to unfamiliar subjects?

This is a pretty compelling format.

Maybe the future of online education isn't another marketplace with thousands of courses we'll never finish.

Maybe it's being able to say:

"I want to understand this."

And getting a course made specifically for you.

Claudemy on GitHub:
https://github.com/assafkip/claudemy

Free and open source under the MIT license.

items.title: NVIDIA GR00T 2: Robots Learn New Tasks From Just 5 Demos
items.excerpt: NVIDIA just introduced GR00T 2, a new world-action AI model that helps robots learn physical skills from human videos and adapt to unfamiliar tasks with just five demonstrations. In NVIDIA's experiments, GR00T 2 achieved
items.videoDescription:
NVIDIA just introduced GR00T 2, a new world-action AI model that helps robots learn physical skills from human videos and adapt to unfamiliar tasks with just five demonstrations.

In NVIDIA's experiments, GR00T 2 achieved 95% average success across 50 evaluated robot tasks after five demonstrations and only 30 minutes of fine-tuning on a single RTX 5090.

This is a major step toward robots that can learn from watching humans instead of requiring extensive task-specific programming.

What makes GR00T 2 different?

• World-action modeling: predicts future video and robot actions together, learning how the physical world changes as a robot moves.

• Massive training dataset: 402,730 hours of human first-person video, 10,184 hours of handheld-gripper demonstrations across 2,897 tasks, and 23,500 hours of robot teleoperation.

• Zero-shot capabilities: 40% average success on 50 evaluated tasks without demonstrations on the target robot.

• Rapid adaptation: 95% average success after five demonstrations and a 30-minute LoRA fine-tune on one NVIDIA RTX 5090.

• Dexterous manipulation: 85% success inserting NVIDIA GB300 memory modules and 65% assembling a toy truck using robotic hands.

• Real-world reinforcement learning: success rates reaching 88–96% across three contact-rich manipulation tasks.

• Open robotics data: NVIDIA has released 100,000 hours of human video from its Human-1M dataset on Hugging Face.

The bigger breakthrough is the ability to transfer skills from human videos and other robots into entirely different robotic bodies.

GR00T 2 doesn't just predict what action to take next. It also predicts what the world should look like after that action.

These are NVIDIA's reported research results on selected evaluation tasks, not proof that the system can master any physical task with five demonstrations. Model code is scheduled for release in December 2026.

items.videoDescription:
SpaceX is preparing to attempt something that has never been done before.

Catch an entire orbital rocket system using giant mechanical arms. Both stages. On the same mission.

During SpaceX's Q3 2026 earnings presentation, Elon Musk and Gwynne Shotwell confirmed an ambitious plan for the upcoming Starship Flight 15, currently targeted for November 2026.

And this time, catching the Super Heavy booster isn't enough.

They want to catch Starship itself, too.

Here's the plan:

Super Heavy booster: Return to Starbase and be caught by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms, nicknamed "Mechazilla chopsticks."

Starship spacecraft: Return from orbit, survive atmospheric reentry, and be caught by the tower instead of splashing down in the ocean.

Both stages recovered: A potential historic milestone toward a fully reusable orbital launch system.

SpaceX is already working with the FAA on regulatory approval for returning and catching both stages at Starbase.

And Elon Musk sounds surprisingly optimistic.

He described the chances of success as "more likely than not."

Of course, catching a massive spacecraft returning from orbit is a completely different challenge from recovering a booster.

And success is far from guaranteed.

But if SpaceX pulls this off, it could mark a major breakthrough in reusable rocket technology.

Why does this matter?

Because the ultimate goal isn't simply landing rockets.

It's building a transportation system where both stages can be recovered, refurbished, and launched again, eventually operating more like aircraft than disposable spacecraft.

That could dramatically change the economics of reaching orbit and support future missions to the Moon and Mars.

In this video, you'll see:

SpaceX's official animation of the planned Starship tower catch

The proposed Flight 15 recovery sequence

Highlights from Starship Flight 14, which successfully reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites

Flight 15 is currently expected in November 2026, pending regulatory approval and launch readiness.

One giant rocket. Two extraordinary catches.

Fingers crossed. This is going to be quite a show.

items.excerpt: ElevenLabs is back with another impressive update. And this time, it's not just about making AI voices sound more human. Meet ElevenLabs SFX v3, a new AI model that generates complex sound effects, atmospheric soundscape
items.videoDescription:
ElevenLabs is back with another impressive update.

And this time, it's not just about making AI voices sound more human.

Meet ElevenLabs SFX v3, a new AI model that generates complex sound effects, atmospheric soundscapes, and even musical and vocal elements from a single text prompt.

And the results sound pretty incredible.

Here's the problem it solves.

Great sound design is rarely just one sound.

Imagine a football stadium. The crowd is cheering, a ball hits the ground, someone blows a whistle, and suddenly the entire audience starts booing.

Previously, generating that sequence accurately could take multiple attempts.

Now SFX v3 is designed to understand all those instructions in a single prompt.

What's new in ElevenLabs SFX v3:

Multiple sounds in one prompt: Generate layered audio scenes with several events happening in sequence.

Better prompt following: More accurately reproduce the timing and relationships between sounds.

Improved music and vocals: Generate more convincing musical phrases and vocal performances alongside sound effects.

More natural audio: Cleaner, richer sound with fewer unwanted artifacts.

Better high-frequency sounds: More realistic whistles, chimes, bells, and resonant effects.

API integration: Bring AI-generated sound effects directly into your applications and creative workflows.

And it's already available through ElevenCreative and ElevenAPI, although access may depend on your account and region.

Why does this matter?

Because AI video generation has been advancing ridiculously fast, but creating convincing sound for those videos is still a separate challenge.

A cinematic scene needs footsteps, wind, mechanical noises, environmental ambience, music, and dozens of tiny audio details that make the world feel real.

Now imagine describing that entire soundscape to an AI model instead of assembling every element manually.

That's where ElevenLabs is heading.

First, they made AI voices remarkably convincing.

Then came music generation.

And now they're pushing further into cinematic sound design.

I wouldn't claim that ElevenLabs has solved every audio problem. But they're building an increasingly comprehensive toolkit for AI-powered audio production.

Soon, the hardest part of making a movie might not be creating the visuals or the sound.

It might be deciding what happens in the movie.

items.title: All Tests Passed. Why AI Code Can Still Be Wrong
items.excerpt: The tests are green. The patch can still miss the requirement that matters. InfraDev studies coding-agent changes to AI infrastructure. This short explainer shows why checking the expected output is different from checki
items.videoDescription:
The tests are green. The patch can still miss the requirement that matters.

InfraDev studies coding-agent changes to AI infrastructure. This short explainer shows why checking the expected output is different from checking memory, state, or communication—and how additional probes can expose a missing promise.

In the paper’s evaluation, 102 submissions passed every official test; 33 of them did not pass the added probes. That is approximately 32% of that subset, not a universal failure rate for AI-generated code.

CHAPTERS
00:00 Why passing tests can miss the promise
00:19 What InfraDev evaluates
00:31 Three different promises
00:42 Hidden checks, clear requirements
00:57 The 102 / 33 result
01:11 Same output, different transfer
01:25 What to measure

PRIMARY SOURCE
Deng et al., “InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?” arXiv:2610.36589v1, 27 October 2026.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36589

The transfer animations are original simplified illustrations. Their toy block counts are not experimental measurements. This video does not reproduce the multi-GPU benchmark or show a real agent run.

Created with AI-assisted narration and original explanatory graphics. Original minimal sound design.

items.excerpt: Here's something most people watching this channel probably don't know about me. I spent 12 years of my life working in augmented and virtual reality. Not as a developer. Pretty much everything else you can imagine doing
items.videoDescription:
Here's something most people watching this channel probably don't know about me.

I spent 12 years of my life working in augmented and virtual reality.

Not as a developer. Pretty much everything else you can imagine doing while running an AR/VR development studio.

And I absolutely loved it.

Actually, I still do.

I've been waiting for years for AR and VR to finally take the next big leap. Not necessarily in software or the underlying technology, but in hardware.

Because the biggest problem with mixed reality has never been a shortage of ideas. It's been finding hardware you'd actually want to wear.

Then I came across this video.

Someone had vibe-coded a snapshot application for their Pico XR headset.

Nothing revolutionary, perhaps. Just a developer using modern AI coding tools to build something for mixed reality.

But watching it triggered something I hadn't felt in quite a while.

That overwhelming urge to start building things in XR again.

I still have plenty of ideas gathering digital dust in the deepest corners of my Google Drive.

Projects I wanted to build years ago. Experiments. Interactive environments. Things that never quite made it beyond the concept stage.

And now we have something we didn't have back then.

Powerful AI coding agents that can turn ideas into working software without requiring you to master the sacred runes of programming.

Claude Code, Codex, and other agentic development tools have dramatically lowered the barrier to building software.

For someone like me, who spent years creating technology products without being a hands-on programmer, that's a pretty exciting development.

But there's still one problem.

I don't want to build these experiences for another bulky, uncomfortable headset.

And the lighter alternatives often come with compromises in performance, capabilities, or the actual mixed reality experience.

What I really want is something I've been waiting for since roughly 2016.

Powerful, lightweight, portable mixed reality glasses.

Something you can wear comfortably, take anywhere, and use to create and explore experiences beyond a flat screen.

And here we are, almost a decade later.

Still waiting.

AI has made building immersive software easier than ever. Now I just need the hardware to catch up.

Come on, XR industry.

Give us the glasses already.

I have a decade's worth of ideas waiting to get out of Google Drive.

items.title: Telegram Bots Can Now Run Interactive HTML Widgets Inside Messages
items.excerpt: Telegram just introduced interactive HTML widgets for bots, turning ordinary chat messages into live dashboards, control panels, and mini-apps. And the entire widget fits into just 4 KB of compressed code. This is part o
items.videoDescription:
Telegram just introduced interactive HTML widgets for bots, turning ordinary chat messages into live dashboards, control panels, and mini-apps.

And the entire widget fits into just 4 KB of compressed code.

This is part of Telegram Bot API 10.4, and it could fundamentally change how we build AI agents and automation interfaces.

I already tested it with Hermes, my AI agent.

I built a live system-monitoring widget that displays my computer's status and updates every second. After pinning the widget in the Telegram chat, I can access the machine's current status directly from the pinned message.

Tap it, and an interactive HTML/JavaScript dashboard opens with detailed system information.

No separate monitoring app required.

Here's what's new:

• Interactive HTML widgets: embed custom interfaces directly inside Telegram bot messages.

• 4 KB compressed: lightweight HTML, CSS, and JavaScript interfaces, with up to 32 KB of uncompressed source.

• Live data updates: bots can update widget state without sending a new message every time.

• Buttons and interactions: build dashboards, controls, polls, calculators, and other interactive experiences.

• AI agent dashboards: monitor autonomous agents, background tasks, and system health directly in Telegram.

• Native rendering: Telegram runs widgets in a sandboxed environment rather than loading a traditional website.

• Bot API integration: widgets can send requests to their bot and receive responses.

There are some important limitations. Widgets cannot make direct network requests, and production support is currently limited to private bot chats.

Telegram also prevented me from recording the widget screen on my phone, so I can't show my own Hermes example yet.

But the possibilities are obvious.

Instead of scrolling through endless text reports from AI agents, we can give every bot a compact, interactive dashboard with real-time status information and controls.

Time to redesign all those Telegram bot menus, monitoring systems, and automated reports.

https://t.me/BotNews/122

https://core.telegram.org/bots/widgets

items.title: Claude Code: Sonnet + Opus + Haiku. A Smarter AI Agent Setup
items.excerpt: What if you could make Claude Code more efficient by giving each AI model a different job? Instead of using the most expensive model for everything, try a smarter multi-model setup: Sonnet does the coding. Opus provides
items.videoDescription:
What if you could make Claude Code more efficient by giving each AI model a different job?
Instead of using the most expensive model for everything, try a smarter multi-model setup:
Sonnet does the coding. Opus provides expert advice. Haiku explores the codebase.
Three models. Three roles. One coordinated workflow.

Here's how it works:
- Claude Sonnet: Your main coding agent. Handles implementation, edits, testing, and everyday development.
- Claude Opus: Your senior advisor. Reviews complex decisions, helps solve difficult problems, and provides guidance when Sonnet gets stuck.
- Claude Haiku: Your research assistant. Explores repositories, reads files, searches for dependencies, and reports findings.

The goal? Better resource allocation, potentially lower costs, and less unnecessary work for your most powerful models.

Step 1: Install the multi-model configuration
npx claude-code-templates@latest --setting model/sonnet-opus-advisor-haiku-subagents

During installation, choose where the settings should apply: User, Project, or Local.

Step 2: Make your Haiku subagents read-only
Here's an additional improvement I recommend.
When Haiku subagents investigate your codebase, they don't necessarily need permission to modify anything.
Let them research. Let Sonnet make the changes.

You can enforce this behavior using two Claude Code hooks:
Subagents Explore Only: Uses SubagentStart to instruct subagents to investigate and report findings without modifying files.
Subagent Read Only Guard: Uses PreToolUse to block common file-writing tools and state-changing commands when invoked by subagents.

Install both:
npx claude-code-templates@latest --setting hooks/subagents-explore-only --hook security/subagent-read-only-guard

Your main agent keeps its normal permissions, while research subagents work under additional restrictions. Note that the guard does not cover every possible write mechanism, including write-capable MCP tools.

 DEV Community
Why does this matter?
Because more powerful AI models aren't always the answer.
Sometimes the biggest improvement comes from giving the right task to the right model.
Let Haiku do the research.
Let Sonnet do the work.
Let Opus handle the hard questions.
Save this configuration and try it in your next Claude Code session.

https://github.com/davila7/claude-code-templates

items.excerpt: Snapchat just opened its platform to games built with PlayCanvas. And this could be a surprisingly interesting opportunity for indie developers, creative coders, and people building games with AI agents. Because apparent
items.videoDescription:
Snapchat just opened its platform to games built with PlayCanvas. And this could be a surprisingly interesting opportunity for indie developers, creative coders, and people building games with AI agents. Because apparently, Snapchat is becoming another place where you can publish your vibe-coded creations.

And here's how it works.
1. Build your game with PlayCanvas. PlayCanvas is an open-source JavaScript game engine supporting 2D and 3D graphics, with technologies including WebGL, WebGPU, and Gaussian splatting.

2. Connect your AI coding agent. Here's where things get interesting. PlayCanvas has an official MCP server for its visual editor.

Your agent can help:
Create and organize scene objects.
Write game logic in JavaScript.
Import and configure assets.
Set up cameras, lighting, and animations.
Inspect the scene and iterate on the result.
Or you can skip the visual editor entirely and build directly with the PlayCanvas Engine.

3. Publish your game to Snapchat. Once the game is ready, package it as a ZIP file and upload it through Snapchat's My Lenses portal.

There are some technical requirements:
9:16 portrait orientation
8 MB maximum ZIP size
1 MB maximum index.html size
All assets must be included in the package.

After review, the game becomes available inside Snapchat.
Players can discover it through Lenses or open it using a Snapcode.

4. Or just describe your game to Easy Lens. And Snapchat has its own AI game creator.

For example: "Create a 3D arcade game where a tiny spaceship flies through an endless neon city, dodging obstacles and collecting energy."
Easy Lens plans the project, writes the code, and builds a playable browser preview.

According to Snap's latest quarterly results:
977 million monthly active users
Over 175 million monthly Game Lens users, according to Snap's previously published engagement figures
More than 30 million paid subscribers across its subscription products
And yes, there's a monetization program. Meet Lens+ Payouts.
Approved developers can publish exclusive Lenses and receive a share of subscription revenue based on engagement.

Those 977 million users are not your monetizable audience. And neither are all 30 million paid subscribers.

Snapchat's Lens+ Payouts program primarily rewards engagement from Lens+ subscribers and subscriptions driven by your Lens.
Snap hasn't publicly disclosed the exact Lens+ subscriber count.

In other words, millions of plays don't automatically mean millions of dollars.

One PlayCanvas game, Snake Showdown, reportedly reached over 7 million plays from more than 1.8 million players within its first four weeks.

Another game, Bitmoji Ski, reportedly reached 6 million impressions per day.

Official PlayCanvas announcement and publishing guide: https://blog.playcanvas.com/snapchat-now-supports-playcanvas-games/
Create games with Snapchat Easy Lens: https://easylens.snapchat.com/web-lenses

items.title: HyperFlow H3 Flash: 14B AI Video + Stereo Audio in 6 Steps | ComfyUI & GGUF
items.excerpt: VIDEO REBIRTH just compressed MiniMax-H3 from roughly 31 billion parameters to under 14 billion, and made it generate video AND sound in just six sampling steps. Meet HyperFlow H3 Flash, the latest release in the HyperFl
items.videoDescription:
VIDEO REBIRTH just compressed MiniMax-H3 from roughly 31 billion parameters to under 14 billion, and made it generate video AND sound in just six sampling steps.

Meet HyperFlow H3 Flash, the latest release in the HyperFlow family. It's designed for faster, more accessible AI video generation without sending audio off to a separate model afterward.

And the performance numbers are getting interesting.

Here's what makes HyperFlow H3 Flash special.

1. A 54% smaller model

The developers reduced the original MiniMax-H3 transformer to approximately 13.7B parameters for text, image, and keyframe-guided generation, or 13.9B for reference-to-video.

The architecture uses structural pruning and low-rank factorization to make the model significantly smaller.

2. Just SIX generation steps

Instead of running dozens of denoising steps, HyperFlow offers three presets:

4 steps: Maximum speed.

6 steps: Balanced default.

8 steps: Higher-quality generation.

All with CFG set to 1.0.

3. Video and stereo audio generated together

And this is particularly interesting.

HyperFlow produces synchronized video and audio in the same generation process.

The default output is:

1344 × 768 resolution

24 FPS

32 kHz stereo audio

5.2 to 15-second clips

No separate sound-effects model required.

4. Real-time generation on NVIDIA Blackwell

According to the developers, an optimized NVIDIA SOL-H3 configuration supports real-time inference using four Blackwell accelerators.

For a 5.2-second clip at six steps, the published benchmarks report:

4 × NVIDIA B200: 8.7 seconds

1 × H200: 36 seconds

RTX 5090: Approximately 92 seconds

RTX 4090: Approximately 152 seconds with GGUF

RTX 3090: Approximately 315 seconds with GGUF

So yes, the system can approach real-time operation on specialized infrastructure.

But your RTX 4090 isn't suddenly generating video in real time.

Not yet, anyway.

5. Local generation with ComfyUI

Here's the part I'm particularly interested in.

HyperFlow H3 Flash supports INT8 and GGUF quantization.

The Q4_K_M transformer checkpoint weighs approximately 9.1 GB.

That makes local deployment possible on consumer GPUs, including RTX 3090 and RTX 4090 configurations with 24 GB VRAM.

Just remember that 9.1 GB is the transformer file size, not the total memory required for generation.

And the standard RTX 5080 has only 16 GB VRAM, so don't assume the published 24 GB performance figures apply to it.

6. Four creative workflows

The model supports:

Text-to-video

Image-to-video

First-and-last-frame animation

Reference-to-video

You can use existing images to guide composition, appearance, and movement instead of relying entirely on text prompts.

But here's the bigger picture.

We're watching video generation move toward smaller, more efficient models.

And that's important.

Because generating beautiful videos in a massive data center is one thing.

Running useful video models locally, experimenting with different workflows, and actually integrating them into creative pipelines is another.

Six steps. A much smaller transformer. Synchronized stereo audio.

That's a genuinely interesting combination.

Of course, there's a licensing catch.

The inference code is open source, but the model weights use the MiniMax H3 Community License. Users in the EU, UK, US, and South Korea need prior authorization from MiniMax.

So this is an open-weight release, not an unrestricted open-source model.

Still, it's another significant step toward making AI video generation more accessible.

Maybe the next big breakthrough in AI video won't be another 100-billion-parameter model.

Maybe it'll be making existing models ten times more efficient.

Model weights and benchmarks:
https://huggingface.co/VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash

GitHub, installation and ComfyUI workflows:
https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash

#HyperFlow #MiniMaxH3 #ComfyUI #AIVideo #LocalAI #GenerativeAI #VideoRebirth

items.title: Vercel CEO Built a Vinyl Player That Generates Sound From Physics
items.excerpt: Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch just built an incredibly detailed vinyl record player simulation using WebGL2, Web Audio, and real-time physics. But here's the fascinating part: it doesn't simply play an audio file with a vin
items.videoDescription:
Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch just built an incredibly detailed vinyl record player simulation using WebGL2, Web Audio, and real-time physics.

But here's the fascinating part: it doesn't simply play an audio file with a vintage filter.

It converts music into the physical geometry of a vinyl groove, then simulates a stylus tracking that groove 384,000 times per second.

The sound you hear is calculated from the electrical signal that this movement would induce in a real phono cartridge.

And yes, you can scratch the record like a DJ.

Here's how the simulation works:

• Physical groove generation: audio is converted into a spiral stereo groove with millions of geometric samples.

• 384,000 samples per second: a simulated stylus continuously follows the groove walls to reconstruct the audio signal.

• Realistic cartridge physics: models stylus contact, cantilever movement, tracking force, friction, and tonearm mechanics.

• Natural vinyl imperfections: crackle, pops, surface noise, and distortion emerge from simulated dust, scratches, and groove geometry.

• Wow and flutter: speed variations, off-center records, and mechanical imperfections affect the resulting sound.

• Inner-groove distortion: high frequencies become less accurate near the center of the record, just like on real vinyl.

• Interactive turntable: drop the needle, change playback speed, scratch the record, or even knock the table to make the stylus skip.

• Custom vinyl records: upload your own audio and let the simulation cut it into a virtual record.

• WebGL2 visualization: the spinning vinyl, groove geometry, and stylus are rendered directly in the browser.

• Open-source code: the entire project is available on GitHub under the MIT license, so you can modify it, experiment with the physics, or deploy your own version.

The simulation even includes different stylus shapes, adjustable tracking force, anti-skating, dust, scratches, and record warping.

The really impressive part is that vinyl imperfections aren't simply layered onto the audio as prerecorded effects.

They arise from the interaction between the simulated needle and the record's geometry, although some physical parameters are manually calibrated.

This is an unusually creative combination of computer graphics, digital signal processing, mechanical simulation, and browser technology.

And it's a great example of how sophisticated physical systems can be modeled using JavaScript and modern web APIs.

Try the interactive vinyl simulator:
https://vinyl-gl.vercel.app/

Open-source GitHub repository:
https://github.com/rauchg/vinyl

Created by Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel.

items.videoDescription:
Meet DAWN, a new AI VFX foundation model from British startup PXLD that composites real actors into entirely different environments while preserving their original performances.

No AI-generated faces. No rewritten expressions. No replacing the actor with a synthetic version.

DAWN introduces a different approach to AI compositing: world harmonisation.

Instead of regenerating an entire video, the model is designed to preserve the original footage while adapting lighting, shadows, reflections, and the surrounding environment.

Key capabilities demonstrated and announced by PXLD:

• Hair-level detail: preserving individual hair strands, fine edges, and subtle facial expressions.

• Performance preservation: keeping the actor's original identity, movement, and facial performance intact.

• Dynamic AI relighting: adapting illumination, shadows, and reflections to match a new environment.

• Flexible environments: placing real footage into photographs, videos, 360° panoramas, and 3D scenes.

• Spatial lighting control: positioning light sources around the scene without relying on text prompts.

• Film-scale ambitions: PXLD claims support for unlimited clip lengths and workflows ranging from smartphone footage to high-end cinema production.

For compositors working in Nuke, After Effects, or professional VFX pipelines, the implications could be significant.

Less manual masking. More control over lighting. And most importantly, the original performance stays the original performance.

DAWN is currently being introduced through early access. Its production capabilities and limitations still need independent validation.

items.excerpt: What if you could animate any object in a photo simply by drawing where you want it to move? No complicated keyframes. No manual masking across hundreds of frames. Just select an object, draw its trajectory, and let AI h
items.videoDescription:
What if you could animate any object in a photo simply by drawing where you want it to move?

No complicated keyframes. No manual masking across hundreds of frames.

Just select an object, draw its trajectory, and let AI handle the animation.

Meet H3 Motion, a new open-source motion control application powered by MiniMax H3 and ComfyUI.

And it's a pretty interesting alternative to traditional text-to-video generation.

Here's the idea.

Instead of writing a prompt and hoping the AI understands exactly how an object should move, you can control the motion directly.

Here's what H3 Motion can do:

Object selection: Identify subjects using SAM 3.1 segmentation.

Motion paths: Draw exactly where an object should travel through the scene.

Scale animation: Make objects grow, shrink, or flip as they move.

AI background reconstruction: Remove the original subject and fill the empty space.

Video editing: Select a region of existing footage and regenerate what happens inside it.

Reference images: Upload or generate visual references to guide the result.

Audio control: Preserve, reference, or replace the original video's sound.

And here's where things get interesting.

H3 Motion isn't powered by a single AI model.

It's an entire coordinated pipeline.

Step 1: SAM 3.1 finds the object.

Select a subject by name or refine its mask manually.

Step 2: Qwen3-VL understands the scene.

The vision-language model describes the selected object and provides context for the next stages.

Step 3: Qwen Image 2.1 removes the original.

The model reconstructs the background so the object can move without leaving an empty hole behind.

Step 4: You direct the movement.

Draw a motion path, set keyframes, and adjust the object's size, position, and orientation.

Step 5: MiniMax H3 generates the animation.

Using an adapted Time-to-Move workflow, H3 turns your motion instructions into a video with sound.

And it works with existing videos, too.

Draw a mask around the area you want to change, describe what should happen, and let H3 regenerate that part of the scene.

The application then composites the generated result back into the original footage.

This is particularly interesting for object replacement, creative video editing, visual effects, and controlled character animation.

Why does this matter?

Because one of the biggest frustrations with AI video generation is the lack of precise control.

You can describe the perfect scene in a prompt.

But getting an object to move exactly where you want it?

That's another story.

H3 Motion gives you a more direct way to control that movement.

Less guessing with prompts. More actual creative direction.

Of course, it's still an experimental tool.

The workflow depends on multiple AI models, a properly configured ComfyUI environment, and a capable GPU. Complex movements and imperfect masks can still produce artifacts.

And there's an important distinction: the application is open source under AGPL-3.0, but its underlying models have separate licenses and usage restrictions.

Still, this is exactly the direction I'd love to see AI video tools moving.

Not just generating random beautiful footage.

Giving creators actual control over what happens inside the frame.

Because the future of AI filmmaking shouldn't be about prompting until you get lucky.

It should be about directing the scene.

items.title: Instagram Edits for Mac: Claude & Codex Can Edit Videos via MCP
items.excerpt: Instagram just launched Edits for macOS, a free CapCut alternative with built-in MCP support that lets Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Meta's Muse edit videos directly inside the app. I connected Claude, asked it to edit
items.videoDescription:
Instagram just launched Edits for macOS, a free CapCut alternative with built-in MCP support that lets Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Meta's Muse edit videos directly inside the app.

I connected Claude, asked it to edit several videos, and tested how useful this actually is.

The results? Interesting technology, but not exactly a revolution in AI video editing.

Here's what Instagram Edits offers:

• Free video editor: CapCut-style timeline editing with no watermarks and free 4K exports.

• Built-in MCP server: connect AI coding agents directly to the editor through the Model Context Protocol.

• Hundreds of editing tools: agents can manipulate clips, transitions, text, audio, effects, and other timeline elements.

• Easy agent setup: copy-ready connection commands for Claude Code, Codex, and Meta Muse directly in the settings.

• Visual timeline: watch your AI agent make changes inside a real video editor.

• Multi-track editing: audio waveforms, color grading, keyboard shortcuts, and support for multiple aspect ratios.

• Manual and AI workflows: switch between editing by hand and giving instructions to an agent.

BUT HERE'S THE PROBLEM.

After testing several edits with Claude, I found the MCP workflow dramatically slower and less effective than letting an AI coding agent edit the same kind of footage directly with FFmpeg.

In my experiments, the Edits workflow was roughly 10x slower, with noticeably worse results. That's a personal comparison, not a controlled benchmark.

Edits is perfectly reasonable for basic Instagram Reels, Shorts, captions, and simple transitions.

But it isn't a replacement for After Effects, advanced motion graphics, or professional compositing workflows.

DaVinci Resolve also has agent integration options, with a much more powerful editing environment. Adobe, meanwhile, continues investing heavily in generative AI features.

Which raises an interesting question:

Why make AI agents operate hundreds of buttons inside a video editor when they can manipulate the media directly through code?

The best workflow might not need a traditional editing interface at all.

Instagram Edits is currently available for macOS. Windows and Linux versions aren't available yet.

Download Instagram Edits:
https://edits.instagram.com/

What would you choose for AI-assisted video editing: Claude + MCP + a visual timeline, or Claude + FFmpeg?

#InstagramEdits #ClaudeCode #AIVideoEditing

items.title: TenPix Cloth: New GPU Cloth Simulator for 3ds Max | Tearing, Soft Bodies & Realistic Fabric
items.excerpt: What if you could simulate complex clothing, realistic fabric collisions, tearing, and even soft-body muscles directly inside 3ds Max? Without constantly switching between different simulation applications? Meet TenPix C
items.videoDescription:
What if you could simulate complex clothing, realistic fabric collisions, tearing, and even soft-body muscles directly inside 3ds Max?

Without constantly switching between different simulation applications?

Meet TenPix Cloth, the first product from 10pix Studio, a new GPU-accelerated cloth simulation system designed specifically for Autodesk 3ds Max.

And the results look seriously impressive.

Here's what makes TenPix Cloth interesting.

Instead of introducing an entirely separate simulation environment, the plugin works directly through 3ds Max's familiar modifier stack.

Twenty specialized modifiers let you build sophisticated fabric simulations while keeping everything inside your existing 3D workflow.

Here's what it can do:

GPU cloth simulation: Uses NVIDIA RTX graphics cards to accelerate complex fabric simulations.

True geometry collisions: Cloth interacts with actual mesh surfaces instead of relying exclusively on simplified collision volumes.

Self-collision: Fabric folds interact without simply passing through each other.

Layered clothing: Simulate jackets, shirts, trousers, and other overlapping garments.

Realistic fabric materials: Control stretching, bending, friction, weight, and material behavior.

Stitching and tearing: Sew garments together, create seams, and simulate fabric ripping under stress.

Animated characters: Attach clothing to moving characters and preserve selected deformations.

Soft-body simulation: Experiment with deformable materials, muscle contractions, and soft tissue.

Alembic export: Cache simulations for use in professional animation and VFX pipelines.

MAXScript integration: Automate simulation workflows using scripts.

And here's the particularly interesting part.

TenPix doesn't limit itself to cloth.

Its experimental soft-body system can simulate deformable objects such as rubber, jelly, fat, and simple muscle structures.

You can even define muscle fibers that contract and produce visible bulging.

It's not a complete anatomical simulation system, but it's a promising addition to a cloth-focused workflow.

And the integration with 3ds Max goes beyond the modifier stack.

TenPix includes a dedicated graph interface for managing simulation groups, support for standard forces such as wind, and Deadline integration for recording simulation caches on render farms.

For studios already using 3ds Max, keeping cloth simulation close to character animation, scene management, and rendering could be genuinely useful.

Now for the price.

TenPix Cloth is currently available for $150, discounted from its regular $200 price until December 31, 2026.

It's a perpetual license for one computer, including one year of updates and support.

And yes, there's a free demo.

The demo includes the full modifier system, with two main limitations:

Maximum 25,000 vertices per scene

Simulation limited to the first 100 frames

Alembic export requires the paid license.

System requirements:

Autodesk 3ds Max 2024–2027

Windows 10 or 11

NVIDIA RTX 20-series through RTX 50-series

Of course, a GPU solver doesn't automatically guarantee faster performance in every scene. Dense collision geometry and complex layered garments still need proper testing.

But here's what I particularly appreciate.

TenPix isn't another standalone application trying to replace the tools 3D artists already use.

It's a specialized plugin designed to fit into an established professional workflow.

And personally, I'd love to see more development like this.

Better simulations. Better integration. Less switching between applications.

Sometimes the most useful innovation isn't reinventing the entire 3D pipeline. It's making one part of it significantly better.

One is Claude Fable 5.2, Anthropic's frontier model designed for complex reasoning, coding, and long-running engineering tasks.

The other is GLM-5.3-Flash, Z.ai's more affordable model optimized for efficient coding and agentic workflows.

And the result was interesting.

For this particular task, GLM-5.3-Flash turned out to be surprisingly capable.

Is Fable 5.2 more powerful overall? That's not what this experiment measures.

The practical question is whether you actually need that extra power for every creative coding and animation task.

Sometimes, a good-enough result at a much lower cost is exactly what you need.

As AI agents become increasingly capable of creating 3D environments, animations, and visual content, choosing the right model for the job may matter more than simply choosing the most powerful one.

items.videoDescription:
AI coding agents can build entire applications.

But why do their UI animations still look like they were designed by a programmer who discovered gradients yesterday?

Well, someone decided to fix that.

Meet Stageshow, a new open-source design skill created by Benji Taylor, Head of Design for X and SpaceXSI.

And this might be one of the most useful skills for anyone creating websites, product demos, motion graphics, or marketing visuals with AI agents.

The idea is surprisingly simple.

Instead of asking Claude Code or Codex to "make a beautiful animation" and hoping for the best, Stageshow teaches the agent how an experienced product designer actually approaches the work.

Composition. Visual hierarchy. Typography. Spacing. Motion. Timing. Storytelling.

All those tiny decisions that separate polished product design from generic AI-generated UI.

Here's what Stageshow can create:

Animated product demos: Beautiful interactions for SaaS landing pages and homepage hero sections.

Faux UI: Realistic-looking interfaces created entirely with code, not screen recordings.

Motion graphics: Seamless loops, transitions, animated dashboards, and product walkthroughs.

Bento grids: Carefully composed feature presentations and marketing visuals.

Device mockups: Browser windows, desktop applications, smartphones, and macOS-style interfaces.

Animated cursors: Realistic movements, clicks, hovering, dragging, and element interactions.

Infographics: Technical diagrams and visual explanations for articles, documentation, and presentations.

Design-system integration: Use your actual brand colors, typography, spacing, and component styles. But here's where things get interesting.

Stageshow doesn't just provide a collection of pretty components. It gives AI agents an actual design methodology.

Here's how the workflow works:
Step 1: Choose the format. Static illustration or animation? Seamless loop or one-time sequence? Desktop or mobile?
Step 2: Establish the visual direction. Light, dark, blueprint, glass, or a custom theme based on your product's design system.
Step 3: Tell a visual story. Break the interaction into three to five meaningful moments.
Step 4: Study a reference. Choose the closest example from the included library and adapt its composition to your product.
Step 5: Build the interface. Use real content only where it matters. Simplify everything else.
Step 6: Choreograph the animation. Coordinate transitions, cursor movement, camera zooms, and overlapping scenes. Make loops actually seamless.
Step 7: Review the result. The agent renders the animation, examines individual frames, checks mobile layouts, detects visual jumps, and fixes problems.
And the best part?
The final result is an ordinary React component.

Install Stageshow with one command:
npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow
It works with Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Gemini, and other compatible coding agents.

Then try a prompt like this:
"Create a polished, seamlessly looping product demo for my SaaS homepage. Show a user interacting with our analytics dashboard, discovering an important metric, and opening a detailed report. Use our existing design system and the Stageshow skill. Build it as a reusable React component."

And here's why I particularly like this approach.

AI models are already excellent at writing code.

But great visual design isn't just about technical implementation.

It's about knowing what to show, what to hide, where to direct attention, and when an animation should simply stop moving.

Benji has essentially packaged years of accumulated design judgment into instructions, examples, components, and verification tools that AI agents can follow.

And then released it for everyone to use.

Of course, it won't magically turn every AI-generated interface into an award-winning design. Benji himself acknowledges that most results still benefit from a few rounds of feedback.

But it's a much better starting point than asking an agent to "make it look premium."

This is exactly the kind of tool I find useful for creating feature illustrations, animated infographics, and visual content for SEO articles.

Instead of spending hours designing every graphic manually, you can give an AI agent a consistent visual system and let it handle the implementation.

The future of AI-assisted design might not be about models developing taste from scratch.

It might be about experienced designers turning their judgment into reusable skills.

And honestly, having someone like Benji Taylor open-source his design taste is a pretty generous contribution to that future.

items.title: SKY-001: The AI World Model That Builds Real CAD Designs, Part by Part
items.excerpt: What if AI could do more than generate a 3D model? What if it could actually figure out how to build one? Meet SKY-001 by Skyfall AI, a new engineering world model designed to turn text prompts and reference images into
items.videoDescription:
What if AI could do more than generate a 3D model?
What if it could actually figure out how to build one?
Meet SKY-001 by Skyfall AI, a new engineering world model designed to turn text prompts and reference images into detailed mechanical assemblies.
And the team behind it has a fascinating history.
Back in 2017, Microsoft acquired Maluuba, an AI startup founded by Sam Pasupalak and Kaheer Suleman.

That was a year before OpenAI released GPT-1.
Now the founders are back with Skyfall AI. And instead of building another large language model, they've created something very different.
An AI model that reasons about how physical objects are constructed.

Here's how SKY-001 works:
- Starts with a text description or reference image
- Generates an initial 3D design
- Breaks complex objects into individual components
- Decomposes assemblies down to tiny screws and fasteners
- Creates 2D engineering sketches and 3D construction sequences
- Assembles the components into a complete mechanical structure
- Supports CAD-oriented workflows, including demonstrations involving Autodesk Fusion
And the results are pretty wild.
According to Skyfall AI's own benchmarks:
- 51× faster than GPT-6 Astra on CAD construction tasks
- 150× cheaper per CAD construction case
- Comparable geometric accuracy: 79.7% versus Astra's 79.1%
- Even larger speed improvements on certain BIM tasks

These are company-reported results, not yet independently verified. SKY-001 is currently a research preview with waitlist access.
But here's the part that really caught my attention.
Watch the moment when individual components start coming together, piece by piece, until they form a complete machine.
This isn't just AI producing a pretty 3D mesh.
It's attempting to understand the structure of an engineered object and generate the steps needed to construct it.
And that's a fundamentally different direction for generative AI.

We've seen models that write code, generate images, create videos, and simulate virtual worlds.
Now we're starting to see models designed to engineer objects in the physical world.
From generating pixels to designing machines.
That's a pretty significant leap.

https://skyfall.ai/sky-001
Technical research and benchmarks:
https://skyfall.ai/blog/introducing-sky-001

items.title: Bambu Lab H3C Is INSANE! 9 Print Heads, 6-Second Swaps & AI-Designed Hardware
items.excerpt: What if you could design an entire electronic device with AI and then manufacture its physical components at home? Well, November 2026 is making that future look considerably closer. Bambu Lab just introduced the H3C, it
items.videoDescription:
What if you could design an entire electronic device with AI and then manufacture its physical components at home?

Well, November 2026 is making that future look considerably closer.

Bambu Lab just introduced the H3C, its first third-generation 3D printer.

And on the very same day, OpenAI demonstrated a physical device designed almost entirely by GPT-6 Astra.

Coincidence? Probably.

An interesting glimpse of where hardware development is heading? Absolutely.

First, meet the Bambu Lab H3C.

This isn't just another 3D printer with slightly better resolution.

It's a machine built around a completely new tool-changing architecture called Swaptek.

Here's what makes it interesting:

9 independent PrintTools: Each has its own filament path, heater, and nozzle.

6-second material changes: Swaptek switches materials without repeatedly unloading and reloading filament.

Multiple nozzle sizes: Combine fine-detail 0.2 mm printing with larger nozzles for faster production.

Multi-material printing: Mix colors, rigid plastics, flexible TPU, and specialized materials in a single print.

Built-in filament management: AMS 3H handles feeding, storage, and active drying.

More than printing: Optional CutTool, DrawTool, and DebossTool attachments extend the machine's capabilities.

Automatic calibration: The printer manages tool alignment, bed leveling, and other setup operations.

And here's my favorite detail.

Changing materials takes approximately six seconds.

Not because the printer has suddenly learned to move at ridiculous speeds.

But because all nine printing tools keep their own filament loaded and can be preheated before the next change.

The actual mechanical tool swap takes just 3.4 seconds.

That's some seriously clever engineering.

The technical specifications are impressive too:

Build volume: 330 × 320 × 325 mm

Maximum nozzle temperature: 350°C

Heated chamber: up to 65°C

Up to 9 dedicated printing tools

Optional expansion to 24 materials with additional AMS hardware

The optional cutting, drawing, and debossing tools use the same mounting architecture, although 2D operations and 3D printing currently require separate workflows.

And the price?

$2,499 for the H3C with AMS 3H.

Not exactly pocket change, but surprisingly interesting for a machine with this level of automation.

Now here's where AI enters the picture.

On November 3, OpenAI published an experiment demonstrating how GPT-6 Astra helped design a complete physical device.

Not just a 3D enclosure.

The entire product.

Astra worked on:

The mechanical enclosure and internal structures

Electronic component selection

Printed circuit board design

User interface and interaction design

Firmware and software integration

The result was a small device designed to communicate with Codex.

Two OpenAI employees completed the design experiment in under a week, and a contract manufacturer produced a small batch of prototypes in less than a month.

The process still required engineering reviews and manufacturing corrections, but the direction is fascinating.

Now put these two developments together.

On one side, AI agents are becoming capable of designing increasingly complex physical products.

On the other, machines like Bambu Lab H3C are making multi-material manufacturing more accessible.

Imagine describing an idea to an AI agent and receiving a complete package:

A 3D enclosure.

A PCB design.

Firmware.

Assembly instructions.

And printable parts ready for your own machine.

We're not at fully autonomous home manufacturing yet.

But we're getting much closer to a world where the distance between having an idea and holding a working prototype becomes dramatically smaller.

And I have to admit something.

I've wanted a Bambu Lab 3D printer for quite a while.

I keep following the technology, watching demonstrations, and imagining what I could build with one.

But somehow, I still haven't convinced myself to take the plunge.

With powerful AI coding agents and machines like the H3C, that decision is getting increasingly difficult to postpone.

Because the most exciting thing about AI might not be what it creates on our screens.

It might be what it helps us build in the physical world.

items.videoDescription:
Apparently, the internet has rediscovered pixel art.

Over the weekend, X (Twitter) was flooded with 8-bit animations, isometric dioramas, and tiny top-down RPG worlds.

And naturally, I couldn't resist.

So I gave Claude Opus a little creative challenge.

Take some iconic scenes from the 1995 cult classic Hackers and turn them into endlessly looping pixel art animations.

If you've been following me for a while, you probably know I have a particular weakness for this movie.

The computers. The ridiculous hacking interfaces. The cyberpunk fashion. The soundtrack. Angelina Jolie and Jonny Lee Miller looking impossibly cool while doing things that had absolutely nothing to do with real hacking.

Peak 1990s cyberculture.

And now, thirty-one years later, I'm revisiting that world through AI-generated pixel art.

Here's the idea:

Reimagine scenes from Hackers (1995) in a retro pixel art aesthetic.

Capture the atmosphere of 1990s cyberpunk and early internet culture.

Create small, animated environments inspired by classic video games.

Make the animations loop seamlessly, so they can run forever.

Let Claude handle the creative coding and animation.

No traditional frame-by-frame drawing. Just a favorite old movie, an AI coding agent, and a sudden attack of pixel nostalgia.

And I have to admit, there's something strangely satisfying about turning a movie that once represented the future of computers into something that looks like it belongs on a 1990s game console.

The future of 1995, recreated by the AI of 2026, in the graphics of 1985.

We've officially come full circle.

Now I'm wondering which other cult movies deserve the pixel art treatment.

Which 90s movie would you turn into a looping pixel art world?

An unofficial AI-assisted creative experiment inspired by Hackers (1995). Not affiliated with the film's creators or rights holders.

items.videoDescription:
What if AI could generate an entire world while you're exploring it?
Not a video. Not a traditional game. An interactive environment that responds to your actions in real time.
Meet Odyssey-3, a new AI world model that generates environments from text prompts or images and lets you explore them as they evolve.
And yes, you can apparently become a seal, a cat, or someone kayaking through an AI-generated world. Walking like a normal human is also an option, although considerably less interesting.

What Odyssey-3 can do:
- Generate interactive 3D-like environments from text prompts
- Use images as starting points for new worlds
- Let you explore in first-person or third-person view
- Move the camera independently
- Introduce new events while the world is being generated
- Predict how objects move and interact using learned physics
But here's where things get interesting.

Odyssey-3 Pro scored 66.1 on Physics-IQ Verified, achieving the highest reported video-to-video benchmark result using best-of-8 sampling.
The benchmark tests how accurately AI models predict the continuation of real physical experiments, covering everything from fluid dynamics to optics and mechanics.
And Odyssey isn't building this technology just for entertainment.

The company is exploring applications in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and AI agents that need to understand and interact with physical environments.
I tried Odyssey-3 Flash in the browser.
The waiting time was around five minutes. Then I got roughly five minutes to explore before being sent back to the queue.
Five minutes to play God. Five minutes to wait. Apparently, even AI-generated universes have capacity limits.
Still, this is a fascinating glimpse of a future where worlds aren't designed in advance. They're generated as you experience them.

items.title: Skylight: Turn Your Ceiling Into a Live Night Sky with Raspberry Pi | Open Source DIY
items.excerpt: Ever looked at your ceiling and thought, "You know what this room needs? The entire night sky." Well, someone actually built it. Meet Skylight, a beautiful open-source DIY project that transforms an ordinary ceiling into
items.videoDescription:
Ever looked at your ceiling and thought, "You know what this room needs? The entire night sky."

Well, someone actually built it.

Meet Skylight, a beautiful open-source DIY project that transforms an ordinary ceiling into a living window to the sky above your home.

Not a prerecorded star animation. Not another decorative galaxy projector.

The actual sky above your location, recreated in real time.

And the result is absolutely mesmerizing.

Here's what Skylight can do:

Live aircraft tracking: Watch planes flying over your home, leaving glowing trails across your ceiling.

Real stars and constellations: See the night sky calculated for your exact location.

Moon and planets: Follow their positions as they move across the sky.

Satellite tracking: Watch satellites, including the International Space Station, pass overhead.

Flight information: Discover aircraft details and where passing planes are heading.

Customizable visuals: Adjust colors, brightness, orientation, and the information displayed.

Phone controls: Configure everything directly from your smartphone.

And here's the really interesting part.

When an actual aircraft passes over your house, its corresponding light moves across your ceiling.

You can hear the plane outside, look up, and watch its virtual counterpart glide overhead.

So how does it work?

The hardware is surprisingly simple.

1. Raspberry Pi

A small computer runs Skylight and renders the sky visualization.

2. An upward-facing projector

Projects the generated sky onto your ceiling. A relatively inexpensive 1080p projector is sufficient for a dark room.

3. Optional USB radio receiver

An RTL-SDR receiver picks up ADS-B signals transmitted by nearby aircraft.

This allows Skylight to track planes directly, without relying on an internet flight-tracking service.

Don't have a radio?

No problem. Skylight can use a free online aircraft data feed instead.

4. Your smartphone

Once the software is running, open its control panel on your phone.

Set your location, calibrate the projection, choose what to display, and enjoy your very own indoor observatory.

And the best part?

Skylight is completely free and open source under the MIT license.

No subscriptions. No proprietary hardware. No expensive smart-home ecosystem.

Just a Raspberry Pi, a projector, and a little curiosity.

The project also includes optional camera tracking for automatically following aircraft, although that requires additional hardware.

Why do I love projects like this?

Because it's technology doing something wonderfully unnecessary and beautiful.

Nobody really needs a real-time visualization of the International Space Station slowly crossing their bedroom ceiling.

But once you've seen it, an ordinary white ceiling starts to feel like a terrible waste of space.

And imagine falling asleep while the actual stars, planets, and airplanes above your home quietly move across the room.

We spend so much time staring down at screens.

Someone finally gave us a good reason to look up.

Now I just need to find a ceiling I'm willing to sacrifice to another DIY experiment.

Explore Skylight and see the real demonstration:
https://skylightceiling.com/

Source code and installation guide:

items.title: Explore Tokyo in Manga Style! Free Interactive 3D City & Background Generator
items.excerpt: What if you could turn real streets into beautiful manga backgrounds? Not by drawing them manually. Not by generating random AI images. By exploring an actual city through an interactive, stylized 3D world. Meet Dokodemo
items.videoDescription:
What if you could turn real streets into beautiful manga backgrounds?

Not by drawing them manually. Not by generating random AI images.

By exploring an actual city through an interactive, stylized 3D world.

Meet Dokodemo Rokehan, a free browser-based tool that transforms real-world locations into manga-style environments using geographic data.

And it's surprisingly addictive.

Here's how it works.

Choose a location on the map, enter an address, or provide GPS coordinates.

The application uses OpenStreetMap data and elevation information to reconstruct buildings, roads, trees, and terrain in 3D.

Then you can explore the environment, move the camera, adjust the lighting, and find the perfect composition.

Here's what you can do:

Explore real cities: Recreate streets and neighborhoods based on actual map data.

Control the camera: Choose aerial views, street-level perspectives, or cinematic angles.

Change visual styles: Switch between color, grayscale, manga line art, and screentone rendering.

Adjust the atmosphere: Experiment with lighting, shadows, fog, and color palettes.

Customize the composition: Adjust camera height, focal length, and viewing direction.

Export your work: Save images as PNG, vector line art as SVG, or 3D scenes as GLB, FBX, and OBJ.

And here's the interesting part.

This isn't a traditional AI image generator.

The application uses Three.js and procedural graphics to reconstruct and render environments from real geographic data.

The buildings are simplified representations, not exact architectural scans, but the results can be beautiful.

And it's free. No registration required.

The tool was originally created for manga artists who need location references and backgrounds without spending hours drawing every building.

But honestly, I'm not even a manga fan.

I just found myself wandering around Tokyo, changing camera angles, experimenting with the lighting, and enjoying the virtual city.

And it reminded me of something I used to love.

In-game photography.

There was a time when I could spend ages looking at photographs people captured inside GTA San Andreas.

Not screenshots of gameplay.

Actual virtual photography, with carefully chosen compositions, lighting, and atmosphere.

There's something fascinating about treating a digital environment as a real place worth exploring through a camera.

And Dokodemo Rokehan brought back a little of that feeling.

It's part manga background generator, part virtual location scout, and part digital photography playground.

You can even walk through the reconstructed streets or fly above them.

Of course, geographic coverage and building details depend on the available map data. The scenery isn't a perfect replica of the real world.

But that's almost part of the charm.

Sometimes you don't need an entire video game.

Just a virtual city, a camera, and the freedom to wander around looking for beautiful compositions.

And honestly, that's a pretty wonderful way to waste an afternoon.

items.title: Luma AI Photo Reframe: Expand Any Image to 2K with Generative AI | AI Outpainting
items.excerpt: Ever taken the perfect photograph, only to realize it doesn't fit the format you actually need? A beautiful portrait that should have been landscape. A product shot that needs more breathing room. Or a cinematic composit
items.videoDescription:
Ever taken the perfect photograph, only to realize it doesn't fit the format you actually need?

A beautiful portrait that should have been landscape.

A product shot that needs more breathing room.

Or a cinematic composition that would look much better if the camera had captured a wider scene.

Well, Luma AI just released Photo Reframe, a new generative outpainting tool that expands images beyond their original boundaries.

And the results look pretty impressive.

Here's how it works.

Upload your original image.

Choose the size and aspect ratio of your new canvas.

Then position the original photograph wherever you want inside that canvas.

And let AI generate everything that wasn't there before.

Not just stretching pixels or adding blurred borders.

The model attempts to create entirely new visual content that matches the original photograph.

Here's what Photo Reframe can do:

Custom aspect ratios: Adapt images for landscape, portrait, square, and other formats.

Flexible positioning: Move your original image anywhere within the new composition.

Generative outpainting: Expand the environment beyond the original frame.

2K output: Generate high-resolution images suitable for many digital creative workflows.

Perspective matching: Attempt to maintain the geometry and visual composition of the original scene.

Lighting consistency: Extend shadows, highlights, and environmental illumination.

Texture continuity: Reconstruct plausible surfaces, materials, and background details.

Depth of field: Match the photographic look of the original image.

And here's what I particularly like.

You're not simply asking AI to make an image wider.

You're directing the composition.

Want more space above your subject for a headline?

Move the original image down.

Need a horizontal banner from a vertical product photograph?

Expand the canvas and let AI reconstruct the surroundings.

Want to turn an ordinary photograph into a more cinematic wide shot?

Give the composition some room to breathe.

For designers, marketers, photographers, and content creators, that's genuinely useful.

Think about how often we need the same visual in different formats:

YouTube thumbnails

Social media posts

Website hero images

Advertising banners

Product presentations

Editorial illustrations

Instead of cropping important details out of the image, you can now attempt to generate the missing space around them.

But there's an important distinction.

AI outpainting doesn't recover the actual environment beyond your photograph.

It invents a plausible continuation.

And while Luma aims to preserve the original lighting, perspective, and textures, complex architecture, reflections, and geometric structures can still produce inconsistencies.

Still, this is a very useful direction for AI-assisted image editing.

Because sometimes you don't want to generate an entirely new picture.

You already have the picture you want.

You just wish you'd taken one step back before pressing the shutter.

Now AI can attempt to take that step for you.
