items.title: MOSS-Live Is Here! Full-Duplex AI Voice Assistant + New Open-Source AI Models Coming
items.excerpt: Remember MOSS-Image, the impressive open-source 5-billion-parameter image generator released by OpenMOSS in October? Well, apparently, generating images was just the beginning. The Chinese AI team is back with MOSS-Live,
items.videoDescription:
Remember MOSS-Image, the impressive open-source 5-billion-parameter image generator released by OpenMOSS in October?

Well, apparently, generating images was just the beginning.

The Chinese AI team is back with MOSS-Live, a real-time voice assistant that can listen, speak, understand video, and perform tasks simultaneously.

And they've got quite a few more models in development.

First, meet MOSS-Live.

Most traditional voice assistants work like walkie-talkies.

You speak. They listen. You stop. They answer.

MOSS-Live takes a different approach.

It's a full-duplex conversational AI system.

That means it can keep listening while it's speaking, creating a much more natural conversation.

Here's what makes it interesting:

Natural interruptions: Understands the difference between a genuine interruption and a casual "uh-huh."

Smarter pauses: Gives you time to think instead of assuming you've finished speaking.

Conversation memory: Can resume its response from where it stopped after an interruption.

Simultaneous translation: Translates speech while you're still talking.

Camera and screen understanding: Processes live visual information alongside audio.

Background agents: Delegates complex research and tasks while continuing the conversation.

Proactive interaction: Can respond to relevant events without waiting for a new question.

Imagine talking to your AI assistant while it researches something, checks your screen, translates a conversation, and continues working.

Without having to constantly interrupt the interaction.

MOSS-Live is currently available in beta, including through a real-time API. The API documentation lists limited-time free access.

But here's where things get even more interesting.

OpenMOSS isn't building just another voice assistant.

It's building an entire family of multimodal AI models.

Here's what the team has already released:

MOSS-Image: An open 5B image generation model with layout control and text rendering.

MOSS-TTS: Speech synthesis, voice cloning, and expressive speech generation.

MOSS-Audio: Understanding speech, environmental sounds, and music.

MOSS-VL: Image and video understanding, including real-time visual streams.

MOVA: An open-source model that generates synchronized video and audio together.

MOVA is particularly interesting.

Released in January 2026, it generates both moving images and their accompanying sound in a unified model.

And the weights are available on Hugging Face.

Now for what's coming next.

During a recent Reddit AMA, the MOSS development team shared several upcoming projects.

1. MOSS-Anime

A specialized image generation model focused on anime aesthetics, with a faster Turbo version also planned.

2. MOSS Image Editing

A new model designed for editing images and working with visual references, potentially combining both capabilities.

3. MOSS-TTS 2.0

A major speech generation update focused on expressive styles and fine-grained emotional control.

The team is targeting November 2026.

4. A New Compact AI Video Model

This one might be the most interesting.

OpenMOSS says it's training an experimental model that generates video and synchronized audio together.

The goal is better motion, improved audio-video alignment, and a smaller architecture that could eventually run on consumer GPUs.

And that would be a pretty significant development for local AI video generation.

Of course, these are development plans, not finished releases.

The video model's final size, hardware requirements, performance, and release date haven't been confirmed.

And as we've learned from several ambitious AI model roadmaps, there's a considerable difference between promising something and actually shipping it.

But here's what I find fascinating about OpenMOSS.

Instead of focusing all its efforts on building another general-purpose chatbot, the team is developing specialized models for different ways humans communicate and experience the world.

Speech. Sound. Images. Video. Real-time interaction.

And increasingly, those capabilities are coming together.

The interesting future of AI might not be one gigantic model doing absolutely everything.

It might be a coordinated system of specialized models that can see, hear, speak, create, and act.

OpenMOSS seems rather interested in that future.

Now let's see how much of this roadmap actually ships.

items.title: Viggle Image Swap: Replace Entire People in Photos with Qwen-Image-2.1 LoRA
items.excerpt: Face swap? Cute. Viggle wants to replace the ENTIRE person. Meet Viggle Image Swap, a new LoRA for Qwen-Image-2.1 that takes a character sheet and replaces someone in an existing photo. Not just the face. Hair, body, and
items.videoDescription:
Face swap? Cute. Viggle wants to replace the ENTIRE person.

Meet Viggle Image Swap, a new LoRA for Qwen-Image-2.1 that takes a character sheet and replaces someone in an existing photo.

Not just the face. Hair, body, and clothing too, while trying to preserve the original pose, expression, camera angle, lighting, and background.

And the interesting part is how much control you get.

Here's how it works:

Character sheets: Start with a 1536 × 1024 reference image. A portrait goes on the left, with front, side, and back views on the right.

Full character replacement: Give it a source photo and identify the person you want to replace.

Group photos: Use --left to target specific people and --kept to leave others untouched.

Local inference: Run the included inference/swap.py script using Hugging Face Diffusers.

And yes, you can use a real face photograph in the portrait section of the character sheet, provided you have the necessary permission.

Now for the technical stuff.

Under the hood, Viggle Image Swap uses a rank-256, bf16 LoRA running on QwenImage21Pipeline.

Standard inference takes just SIX denoising steps, with CFG set to 1.0.

There's also a --turbo mode.

It runs two steps with the swap model, then switches to Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo for another six steps to produce sharper details.

And the developers made a rather clever optimization.

They replaced a heavy Conv3d patch-embedding operation in the vision encoder with equivalent matrix multiplication.

The result?

Approximately 30 seconds saved per input image, according to Viggle.

No changes to the output. Just less unnecessary computation.

But here's a small reality check.

Viggle reports generation times of approximately 2.2 seconds per image on an NVIDIA B200.

That's impressive.

It also requires around 46 GB of peak GPU memory in the benchmarked configuration.

So don't expect exactly the same performance from your gaming laptop.

There are also some limitations.

The original person's clothing can occasionally survive the swap. Poses may drift, and Turbo sometimes brings back unwanted details from the source image.

Still, I really like where this is going.

Instead of generating an entirely new scene and hoping the composition stays consistent, you can preserve an existing image and replace individual characters.

For visual storytelling, character concept art, and compositing experiments, that's a much more controlled workflow.

And with support for multiple people, it becomes even more interesting.

Imagine replacing the entire cast of a photograph while keeping the original composition.

Hollywood, but with considerably fewer casting meetings.

One important detail: the model weights use the Qwen Research License, which limits use to research and evaluation. Commercial applications require separate permission. The inference code itself is Apache 2.0.

Viggle Image Swap, model weights, examples, and inference code:
https://huggingface.co/Viggle/Viggle-Image-Swap

items.excerpt: OpenAI just launched Businesses in ChatGPT, allowing companies to claim their business profiles, manage product information, and even create their own AI agents directly inside ChatGPT. This could fundamentally change ho
items.videoDescription:
OpenAI just launched Businesses in ChatGPT, allowing companies to claim their business profiles, manage product information, and even create their own AI agents directly inside ChatGPT.

This could fundamentally change how customers discover businesses and shop using AI.

Instead of relying entirely on third-party reviews and website summaries, businesses can now provide verified information, including product prices, availability, and service details.

Here's what's new:

• Business Profiles: companies can claim and verify their presence in ChatGPT, update their information, and give customers a dedicated business profile to explore.

• Product Feeds: retailers can provide current product catalogs, pricing, and availability directly through Business Hub.

• Business Agents: eligible companies can launch their own AI assistants to answer customer questions, explain products, and help shoppers compare options.

• In-ChatGPT Conversations: when a business appears in a ChatGPT response, users can open its profile and, if available, start a separate conversation with its Business Agent.

• Business Analytics: companies can track aggregated mentions, website clicks, and discovery topics to understand how customers find them through ChatGPT.

• Privacy Protection: businesses don't receive private ChatGPT conversations or individual Business Agent chats. Insights are aggregated and subject to privacy thresholds.

• Shopify Integration: merchants can connect their stores through Shopify or Business Hub, with eligible products already integrated through Shopify Catalog.

• Global Business Claims: eligible businesses in countries where ChatGPT operates can apply to claim their profiles. Business Agents are initially available to eligible ecommerce and online service companies in the United States.

The bigger picture?

AI search is becoming a new customer discovery channel.

For businesses, being found through ChatGPT may soon be as important as appearing in traditional search results.

But claiming a profile doesn't guarantee higher rankings, recommendations, or sales. ChatGPT's independent answers remain separate from conversations with business-controlled agents.

OpenAI is also introducing sponsored Business Agents as destinations for clearly labeled ChatGPT ads.

items.title: RelayVSR: Near Real-Time AI Video Upscaling in ComfyUI | 1080p, 4K & 29 FPS
items.excerpt: Remember when upscaling a short AI video meant waiting several minutes, or sometimes even longer? Well, things are getting considerably faster. ComfyUI just added support for RelayVSR, an open-source AI video upscaler ca
items.videoDescription:
Remember when upscaling a short AI video meant waiting several minutes, or sometimes even longer?

Well, things are getting considerably faster.

ComfyUI just added support for RelayVSR, an open-source AI video upscaler capable of processing 1080p footage at nearly 30 frames per second.

And the technology behind it is genuinely interesting.

Meet RelayVSR, a streaming video super-resolution system developed by researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China.

Unlike traditional generative upscalers, it doesn't run a massive diffusion model on every single video frame.

Instead, it makes the expensive AI model work only when necessary.

Here's how it works.

Step 1: Generate detailed reference frames

A large generative model creates high-quality references at selected keyframes.

Step 2: Reconstruct everything between them

A much smaller network called the Dual-Memory Video Transformer transfers visual details from those reference frames to the rest of the video.

It remembers both the generated references and the recent motion context.

Step 3: Keep the video consistent

A reinforcement learning technique called Video-Aware Reference Optimization (VARO) helps prevent visual errors from accumulating across frames.

The result is a system designed to upscale long videos without repeatedly running expensive generative inference on every frame.

And the performance numbers are impressive.

According to the researchers' benchmarks, on a single NVIDIA A100 80GB:

RelayVSR: 29.29 FPS at 1080p

FlashVSR-Tiny: 7.80 FPS

RelayVSR GPU memory: 13.82 GB

FlashVSR-Tiny GPU memory: 24.45 GB

First-frame latency: Just 0.327 seconds

That's approximately 3.75× faster, while using considerably less GPU memory.

But here's an important distinction.

The nearly 30 FPS benchmark was measured on an NVIDIA A100, not a typical consumer graphics card.

And 13.82 GB of VRAM usage doesn't mean every 16 GB GPU can achieve the same speed.

The architecture supports efficient streaming, but performance still depends on hardware, resolution, configuration, and video content.

Now for the interesting part for ComfyUI users.

RelayVSR support has been merged into ComfyUI, and the team has published optimized model weights.

Available configurations include:

4× video upscaling: Higher-resolution reconstruction using the x4 model.

2× video upscaling: A lighter alternative based on LightX2V.

INT8 quantization: Reduced model memory requirements.

Streaming processing: Designed for longer video sequences.

Open-source inference: Run the models locally instead of relying on a commercial upscaling API.

The approach can be used for enhancing low-resolution footage, AI-generated videos, animations, and other visual material.

And yes, 4K output is possible with suitable input resolutions and hardware, although the published near-real-time benchmark is for 1080p.

Want to try it?

Download the ComfyUI-ready weights:

https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/RelayVSR

Place the diffusion models and VAE files in their corresponding ComfyUI model directories, update to a build that includes RelayVSR support, and configure your workflow.

But here's what I find most interesting.

We're watching AI video production move toward increasingly practical workflows.

Generating impressive footage is one thing.

But actually using that footage in a production pipeline requires resolution, temporal consistency, predictable performance, and reasonable hardware requirements.

And RelayVSR addresses several of those problems at once.

Instead of making one giant AI model process everything, the researchers combined a powerful model with a much smaller, specialized one.

The big model creates the important details.

The small model handles the repetitive work.

And the entire system becomes dramatically more efficient.

It's a familiar lesson from agentic AI, now applied to video processing.

Maybe the future of generative video isn't just bigger models.

Maybe it's smarter ways to make different models work together.

And getting close to real-time generative upscaling is a pretty significant step in that direction.

items.videoDescription:
Apparently, Google has decided that Claude Opus and GPT-6 shouldn't have all the fun building video games.

Meet Google Playground, an experimental AI-powered game creation platform that turns simple text prompts into actual playable games.

And you don't need to know how to code.

Just describe the game you want, and Google's AI starts building it.

Want a retro racing game?

A tower defense simulator?

A strange little RPG where cats fight monsters?

Apparently, that's a perfectly reasonable request now.

Here's what Google Playground can do:

Text-to-game: Describe your idea and generate a playable browser game.

Conversational editing: Change the rules, characters, physics, or environment through follow-up prompts.

2D and 3D games: Experiment with different genres and visual styles.

Instant testing: Play your creation directly in the browser.

Game remixing: Start from existing templates or community creations.

Multiplayer: Selected game genres support multiplayer and leaderboards.

Easy sharing: Send your game to friends using a link or publish it in the Explore gallery.

And here's the interesting part.

Google isn't building another traditional game engine.

It's creating an environment where the entire game development process starts with a conversation.

Behind the scenes, Playground combines Gemini, Nano Banana, and Lyria, alongside a specialized game-generation system.

So you can describe an idea, test the result, discover what doesn't work, and ask the AI to fix it.

All without manually writing the code.

But Google has bigger plans.

The company is also working with Unity on Unity Spark, an upcoming integration intended to bring more sophisticated gameplay mechanics, high-fidelity 3D environments, and professional game development capabilities to the platform.

For now, Playground is an early experiment.

Availability:

Launched October 7, 2026

Currently available in the United States

Users must be 18 or older

Free game creation comes with limited weekly usage

Paid Google AI plans provide higher creation limits

Games can be played on desktop and mobile browsers

And here's what I find fascinating.

A year ago, building even a simple browser game could mean spending days configuring an engine, writing code, creating assets, and fixing bugs.

Now you can describe an idea and start experimenting almost immediately.

Of course, there's still an enormous difference between generating a simple playable prototype and creating a genuinely good game.

But the barrier between imagining a game and actually playing it keeps getting smaller.

And with Claude, Codex, Kimi, and now Google all moving into AI-assisted game creation, this is becoming a very interesting field.

At this rate, the biggest challenge in game development won't be writing the code.

It'll be coming up with something worth playing.

items.excerpt: What if AI agents could use almost any website without spending half their time clicking buttons and waiting for pages to load? And what if that made them dramatically faster and cheaper? Meet Pomerado, a new Y Combinato
items.videoDescription:
What if AI agents could use almost any website without spending half their time clicking buttons and waiting for pages to load?

And what if that made them dramatically faster and cheaper?

Meet Pomerado, a new Y Combinator startup that's taking a completely different approach to browser automation.

And the results are pretty ridiculous.

Here's the problem.

Most AI agents use websites the same way humans do.

They open a browser, find buttons, click around, read the screen, and repeat.

It works. But it's slow, expensive, and surprisingly fragile.

Pomerado does something smarter.

Instead of forcing your AI agent to navigate the same interface every time, it explores the website once and builds a reusable API or MCP integration.

Then your agent can call that integration directly.

No endless screenshots. No repeated visual navigation. No unnecessary reasoning about where to click next.

And when the website changes?

Pomerado's managed platform can detect broken integrations and automatically repair them.

Now for the really interesting part.

In a demonstration involving onboarding two employees across several business systems:

Codex Computer Use: 21 minutes 22 seconds, $41.01

Pomerado: 8 minutes 16 seconds, $0.03

That's approximately 2.6× faster and 1,367× cheaper in this particular test.

Yes. Three cents instead of forty-one dollars.

These are company-reported results, not independent benchmarks, but they're certainly worth investigating.

What else can Pomerado do?

Turn websites without public APIs into reusable tools

Connect to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible agents

Work with legacy CRMs, ERPs, internal dashboards, and business portals

Handle authenticated workflows, including two-factor authentication

Generate integrations from natural-language instructions

Automatically repair broken integrations through its managed cloud service

And here's the best part.

The core technology is open source under the MIT license.

You can build and run integrations locally, although creating them requires an OpenAI API key. The hosted service adds authentication management, hosting, and automatic maintenance.

This could be a significant development for agentic automation.

Because the future of AI agents might not involve making them better at clicking buttons.

It might involve teaching them to stop clicking buttons altogether.

And honestly, that's a much more interesting direction.

items.excerpt: Runway just launched Sightline, a new AI-powered tool that generates complete 360-degree environments from text prompts and lets you frame cinematic shots using a virtual camera. Instead of generating a completely new ba
items.videoDescription:
Runway just launched Sightline, a new AI-powered tool that generates complete 360-degree environments from text prompts and lets you frame cinematic shots using a virtual camera.

Instead of generating a completely new background for every shot, Sightline creates one panoramic location that you can explore from different viewing angles.

And you can export the environment for use in 3D and VFX workflows.

Available through Runway App Studio, Sightline introduces a different approach to AI-assisted filmmaking: generate the location first, then choose your shots.

Here's what Sightline can do:

• Text-to-360° environments: describe a location and generate a spherical panoramic scene.

• Consistent camera angles: frame multiple shots from the same environment without regenerating the entire location.

• Virtual cinematography: choose focal lengths from 14mm to 85mm, adjust camera direction, tilt, and roll.

• Cinematic framing: capture shots in 16:9, 2.39:1, 1.85:1, 4:3, 1:1, or 9:16.

• High-resolution output: save camera views at up to 2160p, with additional upscaling options.

• Lighting presets: generate locations with dawn, daylight, dusk, or nighttime atmosphere.

• Orbit shot sets: automatically capture multiple views at different angles and export them together.

• Seamless panorama tools: inspect and correct visible panorama seams.

• 3D environment export: download equirectangular panoramas or cubemap faces for use as backdrops and environment textures in Blender, Unreal Engine, and compositing pipelines.

• Reference images: guide location generation using existing images or Runway assets.

The interesting part is the shift from generating individual images to creating reusable virtual locations.

For AI filmmakers, that means more consistent backgrounds, better shot planning, and fewer unpredictable changes between camera angles.

But there's an important distinction.

Sightline generates panoramic environments, not fully reconstructed 3D scenes with editable geometry, depth maps, or unrestricted camera movement.

You can rotate and frame a virtual camera inside the panorama, but moving it through the scene won't reproduce the parallax of real 3D geometry.

It's closer to an AI-generated virtual set or environment map than a complete 3D world.

Still, for previsualization, virtual production, AI filmmaking, and VFX backgrounds, this could be a genuinely useful workflow.

items.videoDescription:
Someone just brought the golden age of DOS file managers back to life. Except this time, they're running AI agents.

Meet AI-Commander, a new open-source terminal interface built by developer Mikhail Malyshev.

And I have to admit, this thing gives me an unreasonable amount of childhood joy.

Remember Norton Commander?

The blue screens. The silver dialog boxes. The function keys. The beautiful feeling that you were operating a serious computer just by pressing F2.

Well, imagine that aesthetic combined with modern AI coding agents.

That's AI-Commander.

It's a multi-harness TUI designed to bring different AI agent runtimes into one familiar, old-school interface.

Here's what it can do.

1. Multiple AI agent backends

Instead of creating another AI model or agent framework, AI-Commander acts as a frontend for existing agent harnesses.

The current public implementation includes:

OpenCode: Connects through its server API, streams responses, and retrieves available models.

Hermes Agent: Runs through the Hermes CLI, streams output, and manages conversations.

More harnesses planned: The architecture is designed for additional integrations, including DeepSeek's agent harness.

The idea is to make different agent runtimes accessible through a consistent interface.

2. A proper old-school terminal UI

And this is where the nostalgia really kicks in.

You get:

Conversation history in a sidebar

A central chat window

A message composer

Classic Norton Commander-inspired dialogs

Function-key controls

A built-in file browser

Full mouse and keyboard navigation

Russian and English interface languages

It looks like 1995. But the things running inside it belong to 2026.

3. Live agent activity

AI-Commander doesn't just display the final answer.

It supports streaming text, reasoning output, tool calls, Markdown, and code blocks.

You can switch between available models and configure defaults for different harnesses.

There's also support for file and image attachments.

And yes, you can browse files using an interface inspired by Norton Commander.

Which might be the most emotionally satisfying way to attach a screenshot to an AI agent ever invented.

4. Built entirely in Rust

The project uses:

Rust for the application

Ratatui for the terminal interface

Crossterm for terminal interaction

Tokio for asynchronous operations

No browser window pretending to be a desktop application.

No giant web frontend just to display a chat conversation.

A native terminal application with a lightweight architecture.

And it feels refreshingly fast.

5. Designed to support more agents

The architecture uses a pluggable backend interface.

Each new harness gets its own adapter while the rest of the UI stays consistent.

That's particularly interesting because the AI agent ecosystem is becoming increasingly fragmented.

Claude Code.

Codex.

OpenCode.

Hermes.

DeepSeek's experimental agent harnesses.

Everyone has their own runtime, configuration, interface, and way of handling sessions.

But what if you could use your favorite agents without constantly switching interfaces?

That's the idea behind AI-Commander.

Of course, it's still an early-stage project.

The publicly available code currently implements OpenCode and Hermes. Broader support, including DSH, remains part of the development direction rather than a finished integration.

But that's also what makes it interesting.

It's a small, open-source project with a clear idea and plenty of room to grow.

And honestly, I love that someone decided the future of AI agents should look like a DOS application from the 1990s.

We've spent years making developer tools look increasingly polished and complicated.

Rounded corners.

Glass effects.

Animated sidebars.

Entire Chromium instances just to display some text.

And then someone says: What if we simply brought Norton Commander back?

Perfect.

No notes.

Well, maybe a few GitHub issues.

AI-Commander is available on GitHub.

If you like the project, give it a star, open an issue, suggest your favorite agent harness, or contribute.

And if you're old enough to remember Norton Commander, consider this a perfectly valid excuse to feel twelve years old again.

GitHub repository:
https://github.com/mb-mal/ai-commander

Created by: Mikhail Malyshev (@tsingular)

#AICommander #RustLang #OpenCode #HermesAgent #AIAgents #TerminalUI #OpenSource #VibeCoding

items.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Destroyed GPT-6 & Gemini in an AI Sailing Race | The Autopilot Experiment
items.excerpt: Someone built a sailing simulator, put the world's leading AI models behind the wheel, and discovered something fascinating about how these models actually solve problems. Or, more accurately, behind the rudder. Develope
items.videoDescription:
Someone built a sailing simulator, put the world's leading AI models behind the wheel, and discovered something fascinating about how these models actually solve problems.

Or, more accurately, behind the rudder.

Developer Abhishek (@shekitup) created a 3D sailing simulator using Claude Code.

The physics, wind, water, coastline, boats, and simulation environment were largely written by Claude.

Then he decided to make the frontier models race each other.

And things got interesting.

The first experiment: Let AI models sail the boats themselves.

The competitors included:

Claude Opus 5.5

GPT-6 Astra

Gemini 4 Argon

Qwen 3.5-9B

Every five seconds of simulated time, each model received 23 numerical values describing the environment.

Boat speed.

Heading.

Wind direction.

Wind strength.

Distance and direction to the next checkpoint.

And so on.

The model then had to decide how to adjust the rudder and sails.

No visual input. No sailing instructions. Just numbers and decisions.

And the results?

Gemini 4 Argon won.

GPT-6 Astra finished second.

Claude Opus 5.5 couldn't complete the race.

And the little Qwen model apparently decided that sailing was overrated and headed straight for the beach.

Not exactly a glorious day for Claude.

But then came the second experiment.

The developer teased Opus about losing.

And Claude suggested a different approach.

What if, instead of manually steering the boats through repeated language-model calls, each model wrote its own autopilot?

Now that's an interesting idea.

The frontier models were tasked with generating actual navigation code.

Code that could read the simulated environment, make steering decisions, adjust the sails, and navigate the course automatically.

And then the autopilots were tested on tracks the models had never seen before.

No memorizing the route.

No pre-programmed solution for a particular course.

The code had to generalize to unfamiliar sailing conditions and layouts.

And this time, Claude Opus 5.5 absolutely dominated.

According to the developer, Opus not only outperformed GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon, but was also the only model whose autopilot successfully completed every unseen track.

Which is a spectacular turnaround.

Claude couldn't sail the boat particularly well.

But it could write software that sailed the boat extremely well.

And that's what makes this experiment so interesting.

There's a fundamental difference between using an LLM to make every individual decision and using an LLM to design a system that makes those decisions.

In the first approach, the model has to repeatedly interpret the environment and decide what to do next.

In the second, it can build a reusable control algorithm.

Once written, that algorithm executes without needing another expensive language-model inference every five seconds.

In other words, Claude stopped trying to be the captain and became the engineer.

And apparently, that was a much better career choice.

Of course, this is an informal developer experiment, not a standardized scientific benchmark.

We don't have enough independent testing to conclude that Opus is universally better at robotics, control systems, or navigation.

But the result illustrates something important about AI agents.

Sometimes the best way to solve a problem isn't to ask an AI to perform the task continuously.

It's to ask the AI to build a tool that performs the task reliably.

And that's a distinction worth remembering as we build increasingly autonomous systems.

The most capable AI agent might not be the one making the most decisions.

It might be the one smart enough to automate those decisions away.

Also, congratulations to Qwen.

I hope the beach was nice.

items.videoDescription:
OpenAI just released Images 2.6, and ChatGPT can finally generate animated GIFs.
Naturally, I immediately tried to break it. But first, the official news.

ChatGPT Images 2.6 introduces:
Animated GIF generation: Create looping animations from text prompts or still images.
Saved reference images: Reuse your face, characters, pets, and other visual references across conversations.
50% faster image generation: According to OpenAI's announcement.
Better editing consistency: Preserve character appearance, clothing, products, and other details across revisions.
Two image models: GPT-Image-2.6 Flare for speed and Sunburst for higher-quality generation.
Developer features: Animated GIF output, image markup, SVG generation, and adjustable complexity through the API.
Both Flare and Sunburst are already available in the API. And yes, you can now ask ChatGPT to animate a character, create a looping reaction, or bring a reference image to life.
Sounds wonderful.

So I decided to see what happens when you push this thing beyond the beautiful examples in the announcement.
Here's what I discovered.

First, resolution.
I tried generating GIFs at different sizes.
1024 × 1024: Couldn't get it to work.
883 × 883: Only managed two frames.
308 × 308: A much more practical result with 16 frames.
These are results from my experiments, not universal resolution limits published by OpenAI.

Then I started increasing the frame count.

And things got interesting.

16 frames: The sweet spot.

The animation was relatively coherent, movement looked reasonable, and the result was actually usable.

64 frames: Things started getting weird.

The animation became unstable.

Objects began jumping around, the composition drifted, and even when I explicitly requested a static camera, the entire image started shaking.

128 frames: Structural collapse.

Characters and background elements increasingly lost their consistency.

256 frames: Congratulations. You've invented a new form of digital suffering.

The animation basically fell apart.

Motion, geometry, continuity, everything.

At that point, I wasn't testing an animation tool anymore.

I was documenting the gradual destruction of visual reality.

And there's an important technical distinction here.

The current public OpenAI image API documentation specifies 2 to 16 frames per GIF, with nine frames as the default.

Yet in my ChatGPT experiments, I was able to request and receive much longer animations, including 128 and 256 frames.

Being able to request that many frames, however, doesn't mean the model can maintain useful visual consistency across them.

And based on my tests, it definitely can't.

Now for the interesting part: Reference Images.

I uploaded a photo of my own face.

And suddenly, the results became noticeably more stable.

Less random visual noise.

Better character consistency.

The reference helped the model maintain recognizable features instead of constantly reinventing them.

In some of the higher-resolution results, I even got a few visual flashbacks to Sora.

Not always in a good way.

But the difference was significant.

Another limitation worth knowing:

ChatGPT can edit GIFs it generated itself, but it currently doesn't support editing an arbitrary animated GIF that you upload.

You can upload a still image and animate it, though.

And now for the genuinely interesting news.

While experimenting with my own face, I started looking into OpenAI's rules for generating real people.

Because remember when AI image generators seemed terrified of anything resembling an actual human being?

Well, the situation is more nuanced than that.

There's no longer a blanket technical prohibition on generating images of adult public figures.

OpenAI explained this approach in its earlier native image generation system card.

Instead of blocking all depictions of public figures, the company introduced more targeted safeguards.

That means certain historical, educational, artistic, or satirical depictions can be generated.
OpenAI's Service Terms still prohibit reproducing someone's likeness without express consent and the necessary rights.
The rules also prohibit using visual capabilities to identify people or extract private or sensitive information about them. And there are additional restrictions around harmful, deceptive, and exploitative content.

Official Images 2.6 announcement: https://openai.com/index/introducing-images-2-6/
ChatGPT image generation and GIF documentation: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11084440-images-in-chatgpt
Image generation API documentation: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/image-generation
OpenAI Service Terms: https://openai.com/policies/service-terms/
OpenAI's earlier policy explanation on public figures: https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/4o-native-image-generation/public-figures

items.videoDescription:
We have officially reached a new milestone in AI-generated content.
AI can now produce videos faster than humans can watch them.
And the internet is responding exactly as you'd expect.
With infinite AI slop.
AI infrastructure company fal.ai has developed H3 Max and H3 Max Turbo, optimized versions of MiniMax's H3 video generation model.
And the numbers are ridiculous.

According to fal's benchmarks:
- 5 seconds of video in just 0.44 seconds with H3 Max Turbo at 480p.
- 10 seconds of video in approximately 1 second.
- 15 seconds of video in just 1.71 seconds.
- Video generation can now run significantly faster than real-time playback.

That's not a typo. The AI can generate the next clip before you've finished watching the previous one. Fal.ai
And someone has already figured out what to do with this extraordinary technological achievement.
Infinite Slop.

Developer Pieter Levels created an AI-powered TV experiment where videos are generated continuously, viewers suggest what should appear next, and the stream can keep producing new content.
No actors. No cameras. No production crews.
Just prompts, GPUs, and an endless supply of increasingly questionable entertainment.
The project is called Infinite Slop, which might be the most accurate product name in the history of artificial intelligence. skunkworks.levels.io
And here's the funny part.

I've already come across about five similar AI-generated streams today.
We spent decades developing technologies that allow us to create moving images almost instantly.
And apparently, the first thing we're doing with them is building television channels that never run out of nonsense.
The future of entertainment is here. Unfortunately, it has no OFF button.

items.title: Viggle Remake: Open-Weight AI Video Editing vs Higgsfield Miracle
items.excerpt: Viggle AI just released Viggle-Remake, an open-weight video-to-video editing system built on MiniMax-H3 that brings cinematic AI video transformations to local GPUs. Think Higgsfield Miracle-style video editing, but with
items.videoDescription:
Viggle AI just released Viggle-Remake, an open-weight video-to-video editing system built on MiniMax-H3 that brings cinematic AI video transformations to local GPUs.

Think Higgsfield Miracle-style video editing, but with downloadable model weights, ComfyUI support, and AI agent automation through MCP.

Viggle has also demonstrated a recreation of the visual editing approach behind Higgsfield's viral Miracle promo.

Instead of generating an entirely new video from scratch, Viggle-Remake transforms existing footage while aiming to preserve its original motion, camera movement, timing, and soundtrack.

Here's what makes it interesting:

• Two specialized LoRA models: Swap replaces characters and actors, while Edit adds or removes objects and changes backgrounds, weather, lighting, and visual styles.

• MiniMax-H3 foundation: built on a powerful video generation architecture with dedicated video-to-video editing capabilities.

• Agentic video editing: Claude Code, Codex, or other MCP-compatible agents can orchestrate the editing pipeline.

• Automatic shot processing: the agent detects cuts, creates reference keyframes, renders individual segments, checks results, and assembles the finished video.

• Long-form video support: processes footage in windows of 90–345 frames at 24 fps, then combines segments into longer sequences.

• ComfyUI integration: official custom nodes, ready-made workflows, and support for quantized int8 and GGUF models.

• Local GPU support: manual ComfyUI workflows are available for 12–24 GB VRAM GPUs.

• RTX 5090 agent workflow: a single 32 GB GPU can run the automated pipeline at 1280×736 with approximately 60 GB of system RAM.

• Smaller LoRA checkpoints: rank-128 and rank-64 alternatives reduce adapter storage requirements.

The biggest difference isn't just the video editing model.

It's the combination of video-to-video generation, local inference, and autonomous AI agents capable of managing an entire editing workflow.

But there are limitations.

Viggle-Remake isn't real-time. The developers report approximately 28 minutes to render a 345-frame window at 1280×736 on an RTX 5090. The model also requires substantial storage and memory, and results may contain artifacts or temporal drift.

Its weights are available under the MiniMax H3 Community License, while the supporting inference and agent code is Apache 2.0.

Higgsfield Miracle remains a separate, closed product. Similar editing capabilities don't establish equivalent performance.

https://huggingface.co/Viggle/Viggle-Remake

Official ComfyUI documentation:
https://huggingface.co/Viggle/Viggle-Remake/blob/main/COMFYUI.md

How does an AI agent turn an idea into a finished video? This two-minute Framewright lesson follows the process: brief, scenes, tools, narration, checks, precise revisions, and a publication-ready package.

Two fictional AI-generated presenters briefly appear in the opening, giving the synthetic voices visible personalities. The dialogue explains the workflow through real examples: an animated dog story, a PlayMCP game used for a book promo, and a manga-style Nantes scene revised after feedback.

Framewright is an experimental open-source collection of workflows, project memory, and local tools for a video studio run with an AI agent. The agent operates selected tools in your environment. Technical checks, creative approval, and publication remain separate decisions.

Try it: choose one idea and write three scenes. For each, note what you will say, what viewers will see, and where the material comes from.

items.title: GPT-6 Astra vs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: Same Prompt, $7 vs $0.90. Who Did Better?
items.excerpt: What happens when you give two powerful AI models exactly the same creative challenge? One developer decided to find out. They tested GPT-6 Astra against DeepSeek V4.1-1017 Flash, using the same prompt and maximum reason
items.videoDescription:
What happens when you give two powerful AI models exactly the same creative challenge?

One developer decided to find out.

They tested GPT-6 Astra against DeepSeek V4.1-1017 Flash, using the same prompt and maximum reasoning settings.

And the results were genuinely surprising.

The numbers:

GPT-6 Astra: 20 minutes, $7.00

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: 1 hour 40 minutes, $0.90

Astra finished 5 times faster, but cost almost 8 times more.

And here's where things get interesting.

Astra's result was impressively detailed, carefully composed, and surprisingly original. It showed a level of visual creativity that you don't always see from GPT models.

DeepSeek took a completely different approach.

Its environment was absolutely stunning, with beautiful scenery and atmosphere. But there was one small problem.

The koi fish.

Let's just say the fish weren't quite as convincing as the rest of the scene.

So which model wins?

Astra delivered speed, precision, and originality at a premium price.

DeepSeek delivered remarkable environmental design at a fraction of the cost, but needed significantly more time and struggled with some details.

Of course, this is a single creative experiment, not a comprehensive benchmark.

But it illustrates something important about AI-assisted creative work.

The most expensive model doesn't necessarily produce the most interesting result. And the cheapest model isn't necessarily the best value if time matters.

Sometimes the real question isn't which AI model is smarter.

It's which one you actually prefer looking at.

What would you choose: the $7 result in 20 minutes or the $0.90 result in 100 minutes?

#GPT6 #DeepSeek #Astra #AICoding #VibeCoding #GenerativeAI #AIComparison

items.title: Starship Flight 15: SpaceX Will Attempt TWO Mechazilla Catches! November 13 Launch
items.excerpt: SpaceX has officially announced the target date for Starship Flight 15: no earlier than November 13, 2026. And this could be one of the most important rocket launches in history. Because for the first time, SpaceX plans
items.videoDescription:
SpaceX has officially announced the target date for Starship Flight 15: no earlier than November 13, 2026.

And this could be one of the most important rocket launches in history.

Because for the first time, SpaceX plans to do something that sounds slightly ridiculous.

Launch an entire orbital-class rocket, deploy satellites, and catch BOTH stages back at the launch site.

Yes. Both of them.

With the giant mechanical arms of the Mechazilla launch tower in Texas.

Here's the mission plan.

1. The first double tower catch in history

After liftoff from Starbase, Super Heavy Booster 22 will separate from Starship and return to the launch site.

Approximately 6 minutes and 35 seconds after launch, SpaceX plans to catch the booster using Mechazilla's mechanical arms.

But that's only the beginning.

The upper stage, Ship 42, will continue into orbit.

And unlike previous missions, it won't simply splash down in the ocean.

SpaceX intends to bring Starship all the way back to the same launch tower.

If successful, this would mark the first recovery of both stages of an orbital-class launch system during a single mission.

2. More than 22 hours in space

Starship is expected to complete approximately 14 orbits around Earth, flying at an altitude of about 275 kilometers.

The entire mission is planned to last more than 22 hours.

Then comes the difficult part.

Starship will perform a deorbit burn, survive atmospheric reentry, fly back toward Texas, and transition from its familiar bellyflop orientation into a vertical landing.

And instead of touching down on landing legs, it will attempt to position itself between Mechazilla's arms.

The planned ship catch is approximately 22 hours and 32 minutes after liftoff.

Imagine watching a rocket launch on Friday and returning the next day to watch the rest of it land.

3. Twenty-six operational Starlink V3 satellites

Flight 15 isn't just another test of the launch vehicle.

Starship is scheduled to deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites into low Earth orbit.

Unlike the earlier experimental deployments, these satellites are intended to enter operational service after completing their orbital checks.

According to SpaceX, the batch could provide network capacity comparable to approximately ten Falcon 9 launches carrying Starlink V2 Mini satellites.

And three of the satellites have an additional assignment.

They'll carry cameras to photograph Starship's heat shield from orbit.

Those images will help engineers assess the vehicle before its return to Earth.

4. An upgraded heat shield

One of the biggest challenges for Starship has always been surviving atmospheric reentry.

For Flight 15, SpaceX is continuing its work on the thermal protection system.

The design includes:

Improved attachment mechanisms in vulnerable areas.

Additional protection against hot plasma penetrating behind the tiles.

Wider use of curved heat-shield tiles to reduce heating between them.

Updated thermal protection around critical structural areas.

All of this matters because Starship must survive reentry well enough to perform a controlled return to the tower.

5. The FAA still has a say

And here's the catch.

Well, the bureaucratic one.

Flight 15 is still awaiting final regulatory approval from the FAA.

The current target is Friday, November 13, with the launch window opening at 4:45 PM Central Time (22:45 UTC). But that date isn't guaranteed.

The mission involves an unprecedented attempt to return a massive orbital spacecraft to its launch site, so safety and licensing requirements are particularly important.

Launch schedule and mission tracking: https://nextspaceflight.com/launches/details/8403/
Texas Herald, live coverage announcements: https://t.me/starbasepost
SpaceX official website: https://www.spacex.com/

items.title: Mago Studio Is Now Open Source! A Complete Local AI Filmmaking Studio with MiniMax H3
items.excerpt: What if you could run an entire AI filmmaking studio on your own computer? Not just another text-to-video generator. A complete production environment with scripts, storyboards, characters, video editing, version history
items.videoDescription:
What if you could run an entire AI filmmaking studio on your own computer?

Not just another text-to-video generator.

A complete production environment with scripts, storyboards, characters, video editing, version history, and project management.

And what if you could modify the entire thing yourself?

Meet Mago Studio, a local-first AI production platform that has just released its source code.

And honestly, this is the kind of AI creative software I'd love to see more of.

Here's what makes Mago Studio interesting.

Most AI video generators have one annoying problem.

You generate a clip. Then another. Then another.

Eventually, you have 200 renders sitting in one enormous history panel, and absolutely no idea which one belongs to which project.

"Don't worry, I'll organize everything tomorrow."

Of course you will.

Mago Studio takes a different approach.

It treats AI filmmaking as an actual production workflow.

1. Mago Director: From Script to Finished Video

Start with an idea or screenplay and turn it into a structured video project.

Develop scripts with an AI writing assistant.

Create characters and reference images.

Generate shot lists and storyboards.

Maintain visual consistency between scenes.

Review individual shots, compare takes, and assemble your final cut.

2. Mago Transform: AI-Powered Video Editing

Already have footage?

Use AI to transform it.

Restyle existing videos.

Replace characters or modify their appearance.

Change lighting and visual atmosphere.

Edit specific frame ranges.

Apply masks to individual areas.

Compare results and refine them through multiple iterations.

3. Actual Project Management

This might be my favorite feature.

Mago includes version history, organized projects, individual shots, review tools, and a frame-accurate editing workflow.

You can experiment without losing track of your previous results.

A revolutionary concept, apparently, in AI video generation.

And here's what's running under the hood.

Mago supports several AI models through ComfyUI:

Qwen3.8 27B: Scriptwriting, casting, shot descriptions, and prompt optimization.

Qwen3-VL 4B: Understanding and describing images and video.

MiniMax H3: Local video generation and transformation.

Wan 2.2 and Wan VACE: Additional animation and video editing workflows.

Qwen Image and Qwen Image Edit: Image generation and editing.

FLUX 2 Klein: Additional image generation options.

You can use local models, connect an existing ComfyUI installation, or switch to paid Mago Cloud services when you need more computing power.

And here's the best part.

The source code is now available under the AGPL-3.0 license.

Which means developers can study the architecture, modify the interface, extend the pipelines, and integrate additional models.

You can even ask Claude Code or Codex to help customize the application.

Want another video model? Add it.

Need a different workflow? Build one.

Want an even darker dark mode?

Apparently, nothing can stop you now.

But there's one more thing I appreciate.

The interface actually looks like something designed for creative professionals.

Not another developer dashboard with 400 mysterious sliders, a dozen disconnected nodes, and a user experience apparently designed to test your patience.

Sorry, Automatic1111.

A few practical details:

Windows, macOS, and Linux are supported.

Local rendering uses ComfyUI and your own GPU.

Windows includes a guided local setup for supported NVIDIA hardware.

macOS and Linux users currently need to connect their own ComfyUI installation.

Local workflows can operate offline without a Mago account.

Cloud models require an account and paid credits.

The Windows local setup lists 8 GB VRAM as its minimum, but the basic model installation needs approximately 63 GB of free disk space. More advanced pipelines require additional resources.

And model licenses still apply independently of the application's open-source license.

But the bigger picture is what matters.

We've spent the last few years getting better and better AI models.

Now we desperately need better creative workflows around them.

Proper project management. Reproducible settings. Editing. Versioning. Human creative control.

Mago Studio is an interesting step toward treating AI video generation like actual filmmaking instead of an endless slot machine for random clips.

And that might be more valuable than yet another model promising slightly better cinematic lighting.

items.videoDescription:
We may have just witnessed one of the strangest AI experiments of 2026.
Researchers connected a simulated fruit fly brain to Odyssey-3, an AI world model capable of generating interactive virtual environments in real time.
And then they let it explore.
No real landscapes. No physical insect. Just a digital simulation of a biological brain navigating a world generated by another artificial intelligence.
Think about that for a second.
A brain modeled after a living creature is exploring places that have never existed.

Here's what makes this fascinating:
- The brain: A software simulation inspired by the neural circuitry of a fruit fly.
- The environment: Odyssey-3, a generative AI model that creates interactive worlds.
- The experiment: The simulated fly appears to navigate these artificial environments autonomously.
- The bigger picture: AI-generated worlds could become experimental environments for studying biological and artificial intelligence.

Odyssey shared the demonstration on October 17, 2026.
The technical details haven't been published yet, so we don't know exactly how faithfully the fly's brain is simulated or how its neural activity controls movement.
But even as an early experiment, the concept is extraordinary.
We're connecting simulations of biological nervous systems to environments imagined by artificial intelligence.
One AI creates the universe. A simulated biological brain explores it.
Science fiction is having a very difficult time keeping up.

items.title: YouTube to TikTok: One Master or Two Layouts? We Tested Both
items.excerpt: Can a YouTube video become a TikTok simply by cropping its centre—or does it need a separate layout? We tested both workflows on two different 90-second animated films. A used independent landscape and portrait compositi
items.videoDescription:
Can a YouTube video become a TikTok simply by cropping its centre—or does it need a separate layout? We tested both workflows on two different 90-second animated films.

A used independent landscape and portrait compositions. B was built as a 4K landscape master with its essential story inside a self-contained vertical centre, then cropped from that encoded master.

What we measured:
• Portrait composition/export: A 142.75s; B 40.47s.
• Landscape + portrait exports combined: A 390.61s; B 331.40s.
• B needed more full-stage source rendering and corrections in this pair.

These are tool elapsed times for specific phases, not total labour or monetary savings. The two stories and their correction loads were different. Both visual approaches were accepted for reuse; this is a practical production comparison, not proof that cropping always wins. Audience results remain separate.

items.excerpt: What if you could talk to ChatGPT, Claude, or your AI coding agents without making a single sound? No keyboard. No microphone. Not even whispering. Just silently move your mouth, and your thoughts become text. Well, almo
items.videoDescription:
What if you could talk to ChatGPT, Claude, or your AI coding agents without making a single sound?

No keyboard. No microphone. Not even whispering.

Just silently move your mouth, and your thoughts become text.

Well, almost.

Meet The Subvocal Company, a Y Combinator startup building what might become one of the most interesting new interfaces for the AI era.

And the internet has gone absolutely crazy over it.

Here's how Subvocal works.

The device looks like a relatively ordinary pair of glasses.

But instead of using cameras to read your lips, it uses sensors designed to detect the tiny physical movements associated with silent speech.

An AI model then translates those signals into written text.

And the numbers are pretty wild.

200+ words per minute: The typing speed claimed for the company's prototypes.

Silent input: No audible speech required.

No cameras: The system doesn't rely on visual lip-reading.

AI integration: Designed for tools like ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cursor, and everyday applications.

Minimal movement: Users deliberately articulate words, but the movements can be barely noticeable.

Personal calibration: A short setup process helps the system adapt to each user.

And no, it doesn't actually read your mind.

You still need to intentionally form the words, just without speaking aloud.

The startup was founded by Aarush Yadav and Arnav Kumar, two Georgia Tech students who began experimenting with the technology at a Stanford hackathon.

Now they're part of Y Combinator's Fall 2026 batch, with approximately $1.3 million in pre-seed funding.

But here's why I find this particularly interesting.

AI agents are changing how we interact with computers.

When your computer can write code, research, build applications, and perform complex tasks, typing every instruction starts to feel like an unnecessary bottleneck.

Voice input is faster.

But talking to your computer in a crowded office, on a train, or during a meeting?

Not always ideal.

Subvocal is trying to combine the speed of speaking with the privacy of typing.

Of course, there's a catch.

The technology is still in development. The claimed 200+ WPM performance hasn't been independently verified, and the company hasn't published a detailed accuracy benchmark or disclosed its complete sensing architecture.

Whether it works reliably outside controlled demonstrations remains to be seen.

But you can already reserve a pair.

Early-bird price: $499

Refundable deposit: $199

Estimated shipping: Q1 2027

Preorders currently available in the United States

And yes, you'll probably look like the strangest person in the office.

But imagine sitting silently at your desk while an entire army of AI agents follows your instructions.

Your coworkers think you're doing nothing. Your AI agents think you're running a company.

Honestly, that sounds like a pretty interesting future.

How many follow-ups would you send before giving up on your dream customer?

Three? Five? Maybe ten?

Well, Harry Stebbings sent 53 emails to Marc Benioff, the CEO of Salesforce.

And for 52 weeks, he got absolutely nothing.

Not a single reply.

If you don't know Harry, he's the founder of 20VC, one of the most influential venture capital podcasts, and the man behind a VC firm that raised a $400 million fund.

He started his podcast at just 18.

I've known of Harry since my student days in London, back when I was struggling to sell the first subscriptions to my startup, Jammy, while he was already making waves in the startup ecosystem.

And his approach to cold outreach is a masterclass in persistence.

Here's what he did:

Every Sunday evening, at the same time, Harry emailed Marc Benioff asking him to appear on his podcast.

But he didn't just send the same boring "Just following up" message 53 times.

He did his homework.

Every email included a different, highly personalized P.S.

Benioff's favorite whiskey

His favorite vacation destinations

His food preferences

Salesforce's latest quarterly results

Personal details that demonstrated genuine research

He even A/B tested different approaches.

The result after 52 weeks? Absolutely nothing.

Until one particular email mentioned Benioff's favorite Macallan whiskey.

And suddenly, Marc replied.

He agreed to appear on the show.

Benioff later acknowledged that Harry had emailed and texted him nearly 100 times before getting a yes.

His conclusion?

"Persistence pays."

And that's the lesson for startup founders.

Especially if you're selling to mid-market or enterprise customers with a relatively small target account list.

You can't afford to give up after a couple of unanswered emails.

But here's the important distinction.

Persistence isn't sending the same message over and over. It's finding a new reason to be relevant every time.

My favorite GTM formula for 2026:

Founder-Led + Signal-Based + Multichannel + Creative Storytelling + AI

Research your accounts. Understand their priorities. Find meaningful signals. Make every interaction count.

And respect clear boundaries. Persistence should never become harassment.

Now open your CRM and look at your biggest opportunity.

How many attempts did you make before giving up?

Because Harry was apparently just getting warmed up.

items.title: Viggle Remake Is Open! AI Character Replacement with MiniMax H3 + ComfyUI
items.excerpt: What if you could take an existing video, replace the actors, change the environment, or completely redesign the scene while keeping the original performance? And what if you could run the entire process on your own GPU?
items.videoDescription:
What if you could take an existing video, replace the actors, change the environment, or completely redesign the scene while keeping the original performance? And what if you could run the entire process on your own GPU?

Meet Viggle Remake, a new open-weight AI video editing system built on MiniMax H3.
Viggle has released its model adapters, inference code, ComfyUI workflows, quantized models, and even an MCP server for AI coding agents. And this is a pretty interesting development for AI-assisted filmmaking.

Instead of generating a completely new video from scratch, Viggle Remake starts with existing footage.

The model attempts to preserve the original camera movement, timing, character actions, and soundtrack while changing whatever you specify.

Two specialized AI models handle the work.

1. Recast: Replace characters in existing videos

The swap mode lets you replace one or several people or characters using visual references.

Imagine taking a dance video and replacing the performers with entirely different characters.

The choreography remains.

The camera movement remains.

Even the original soundtrack stays.

2. Edit: Transform objects and environments

The edit mode handles everything else:

Change clothing and costumes

Replace or remove objects

Add new elements to a scene

Change backgrounds and locations

Modify lighting and weather

Transform the overall visual style

Both modes are implemented as separate LoRA adapters for MiniMax H3.

And here's where things get technically interesting.

Viggle didn't release another enormous foundation model.

Instead, the developers published two specialized LoRAs that extend the existing MiniMax H3 video model.

Each full-rank adapter is approximately 2.67 GB.

The original MiniMax H3 model is considerably larger, requiring roughly 144 GB of model files in the reference configuration.

That's not exactly friendly to consumer hardware.

But Viggle has prepared smaller versions.

The release includes:

INT8 models: Approximately 21 GB each

GGUF Q8: Approximately 22.3 GB

GGUF Q6: Approximately 17.6 GB

GGUF Q4: Approximately 14.3 GB

ComfyUI workflows: Ready-made graphs for character replacement and video editing

CPU offloading: Options for running on GPUs with significantly less memory

The documentation describes configurations down to 12 GB VRAM, although these require compromises in speed and substantial system memory.

So yes, you can experiment without renting an expensive GPU server.

Just don't expect instant results on a mid-range graphics card.

But here's my favorite part.

Viggle Remake also includes an MCP server for Claude Code, Codex, and other compatible AI agents.

And that changes the workflow considerably.

Instead of manually editing every shot, you can give an agent a longer video and describe what you want.

The agent can:

Analyze the footage and identify individual shots.

Divide the video into manageable segments.

Prepare reference frames and editing instructions.

Run the appropriate model for each segment.

Review the generated results.

Assemble everything into a finished video while preserving the original soundtrack.

The underlying model handles relatively short video windows, typically around 12 seconds.

The agent handles the longer sequence.

In one demonstration, Viggle recreated a 116-second music video containing 69 cuts.

That's a rather different proposition from generating isolated five-second clips.

And this is what I find most interesting.

We're watching AI video tools evolve from standalone generators into components of complete production pipelines.

Generate the assets.

Prepare the references.

Modify individual shots.

Check continuity.

Assemble the final edit.

And increasingly, let an AI agent coordinate the process.

Of course, there are limitations.

Complex non-human characters, fine details, and long uninterrupted shots can still produce artifacts or inconsistencies.

The model also cannot independently verify whether a person has consented to having their likeness used. Only use footage and identities you have permission to modify, and clearly label synthetic results.

And while the inference code is Apache 2.0, the model weights use the MiniMax H3 Community License, with additional conditions for commercial use.

But the direction is fascinating.

We're moving from AI that generates videos to AI that can help reshoot existing footage without bringing everyone back to the studio.

And now the tools behind that workflow are becoming available to independent developers.

That's a pretty significant step for open-weight AI filmmaking.

https://huggingface.co/Viggle/Viggle-Remake

ComfyUI setup and ready-made workflows:
https://huggingface.co/Viggle/Viggle-Remake/blob/main/COMFYUI.md

Try Viggle Remake online:
https://viggle.ai/models/viggle-remake

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 Made a 4K CGI Film With Blender & Python for $5.75
items.excerpt: Claude Fable 5.2 just created an entire 4K CGI short using Python, Blender, RunPod, and ElevenLabs, starting from a single prompt. The reported GPU rendering cost? Just $5.75. In an experiment by Riley Brown, Claude was
items.videoDescription:
Claude Fable 5.2 just created an entire 4K CGI short using Python, Blender, RunPod, and ElevenLabs, starting from a single prompt.

The reported GPU rendering cost? Just $5.75.

In an experiment by Riley Brown, Claude was asked to create an animated room with a MacBook, some vibe-coding magic, and Clawd, Anthropic's little mascot.

Instead of generating video frames with a diffusion model, Claude wrote Python scripts to construct and animate an actual 3D scene inside Blender.

And the level of detail is remarkable.

Here's what Claude reportedly built:

• Procedural 3D environment: an entire room, desk, lighting setup, MacBook, and animated Clawd character, constructed through Python.

• Detailed MacBook: 77 individually modeled and animated keyboard keys, synchronized with the typing displayed on screen.

• A working screen animation: Claude built a web page resembling the Claude interface, captured it as 1,345 sequential images, and used them as animated textures on the laptop display.

• Frame-accurate keyboard animation: individual keys move when their corresponding letters appear on screen.

• 13 cinematic shots: camera compositions and movements generated programmatically.

• Animated lighting: a simulated sun moves from golden hour through nighttime and into sunrise.

• Cloud GPU rendering: Claude orchestrated a 4K render across 10 rented GPUs on RunPod.

• Rendering cost: approximately $5.75 for GPU rendering, completed in about 52 minutes.

• AI-generated audio: music and sound effects created using ElevenLabs.

• Automated post-production: color grading, titles, and final video assembly.

The interesting part isn't simply that Claude generated a good-looking animation.

It's that the entire production was built through code.

The geometry exists in Blender. The cameras are editable. The lighting can be modified. The animation can be adjusted and rendered again.

This is fundamentally different from generating a video directly with a text-to-video model.

For independent filmmakers, motion designers, and VFX artists, AI agents capable of controlling traditional 3D software could dramatically change production workflows.

Of course, $5.75 is the reported GPU rendering cost, not the total cost of model inference, development time, or all production services.

And one initial prompt doesn't necessarily mean the same results can be reproduced without existing context or further iteration.

Still, the technical possibilities are fascinating.

items.title: Echo-3: Turn iPhone Videos Into Photorealistic 3D Worlds | AI Gaussian Splatting
items.excerpt: What if you could turn your apartment, office, or entire building into an explorable 3D world using nothing but your phone? No expensive 3D scanner. No specialized camera. Not even LiDAR. Just walk around, record your su
items.videoDescription:
What if you could turn your apartment, office, or entire building into an explorable 3D world using nothing but your phone?

No expensive 3D scanner. No specialized camera. Not even LiDAR.

Just walk around, record your surroundings, and let AI reconstruct the entire space.

Meet Echo-3 by SpAItial, a new AI world model that transforms ordinary iPhone footage into photorealistic 3D environments using Gaussian Splatting.

And the results look pretty incredible.

Here's how it works.

Open the SpAItial app on your iPhone and spend a few minutes walking around your space.

Record the walls, furniture, ceiling, floor, and everything else you want to reconstruct.

Then upload your capture and let Echo-3 do its thing.

The result? A 3D environment you can freely explore, share, and measure.

But here's where things get really interesting.

Echo-3 doesn't just reconstruct what your camera recorded. It also attempts to recreate what your camera missed.

If an object was partially hidden, or you didn't capture every corner of a room, the model uses learned spatial information to generate plausible missing regions.

In other words, it combines 3D reconstruction with generative AI.

And that's a pretty significant difference from traditional photogrammetry.

What makes Echo-3 interesting:

No LiDAR required: Works with supported iPhones using ordinary camera footage.

Photorealistic reconstruction: Creates explorable Gaussian Splatting scenes.

AI scene completion: Attempts to fill in missing and partially obscured areas.

Real-world scale: SpAItial claims metric-scale geometry and measurements.

Large environments: Supports rooms, apartments, factories, multi-floor buildings, and outdoor spaces.

Browser-based viewing: Explore and share reconstructed environments through a web link.

Of course, there's a catch.

AI-generated geometry isn't necessarily accurate geometry.

When Echo-3 fills in missing parts of a scene, it's making predictions. Those predictions may look convincing without matching the actual physical space.

So while this is exciting for visualization, virtual tours, digital environments, and creative production, don't treat the generated results as a replacement for verified architectural measurements.

And there's another important detail.

The capture happens on your iPhone, but the reconstruction is processed in the cloud.

The app is available for iOS, with a one-month introductory free trial for eligible new subscribers. After that, paid plans and credit limits apply.

Android support is planned.

But Echo-3 isn't your only option.

If you're interested in turning real environments into Gaussian Splats, here are four more tools worth exploring.

Postshot by Jawset

A powerful Windows application for local 3D reconstruction using photos and video. Supports NVIDIA GPUs, virtual camera animation, rendering, and After Effects integration.

https://www.jawset.com/

Polycam

One of the most accessible ways to capture real-world spaces using a phone. Supports Gaussian Splatting, spatial scanning, 3D viewing, and exporting.

https://poly.cam/

Nerfstudio

An open-source toolkit for users who want more technical control over reconstruction, camera trajectories, keyframes, and rendering.

https://docs.nerf.studio/

Splatframes

A specialized Windows tool that combines video, photography, and optional LiDAR data into Gaussian Splat scenes. Includes camera animation, keyframes, and professional video export options.

https://splatframes.com/

And here's why I find this entire field fascinating.

We've spent decades building virtual worlds manually.

Modeling geometry. Creating textures. Adjusting lighting. Rebuilding real environments piece by piece.

Now we're approaching a future where capturing a physical space might be as simple as recording a short video.

And AI can help turn that recording into something you can walk through.

Imagine what this means for architecture, real estate, filmmaking, game development, virtual production, and mixed reality.

The real world is becoming something we can capture, reconstruct, and eventually modify like a digital scene.

And that's a pretty interesting direction for spatial computing.

Explore Echo-3:
https://spaitial.ai/echo-3

Official technical announcement:
https://spaitial.ai/blog/echo-3-release

items.videoDescription:
Trois paquets. Quatre indices. Une seule solution. Saurez-vous retrouver qui a pris quoi ?

Mettez sur pause pour chercher : la réponse arrive seulement à la fin.

Ce court film illustré vous propose une énigme tirée de Les petites affaires du port : trois personnes ont retiré trois paquets à trois heures différentes. À vous de reconstituer l’histoire.

Lucien Morel a passé sa carrière dans la police. Aujourd'hui retraité, il n'a rien perdu de son intérêt pour les détails qui ne collent pas, les témoins trop sûrs d'eux et les conclusions un peu hâtives.

Lorsque son petit-fils Milo, quatorze ans, l'accompagne en train jusqu'au Parc des Lanternes, les souvenirs de l'ancien commissaire deviennent le point de départ d'un jeu de raisonnement. Une heure de rendez-vous, un colis mystérieux, un itinéraire inattendu, quelques pièces ou une simple erreur de calcul : les petites affaires du quotidien peuvent cacher de vrais défis.

D'autres personnages se joignent à la conversation. Chacun apporte ses questions, ses idées et sa manière de raisonner. Milo découvre vite qu'un ancien commissaire n'a pas toujours le dernier mot.

40 énigmes pour exercer sa logique et son sens de l'observation

• Quarante énigmes de difficulté croissante : déduction, logique, calcul, observation et stratégie.
• Une histoire suivie, des personnages attachants et des dialogues malicieux.
• Deux indices progressifs pour chaque énigme.
• Des solutions détaillées qui expliquent le raisonnement.
• Des illustrations en noir et blanc inspirées des récits policiers classiques.

Aucune connaissance policière ni mathématique avancée n'est nécessaire. Chaque énigme contient les informations utiles. Certaines se résolvent de tête ; d'autres méritent un carnet, un crayon et quelques minutes de réflexion.

À feuilleter, annoter et reprendre à son rythme : dans le train, en vacances ou le temps d'une soirée tranquille. Un livre illustré pour les adultes qui aiment les mystères, le suspense léger et le plaisir de trouver eux-mêmes la solution.

Prenez un crayon. Le train attendra.

Livre broché : https://www.amazon.fr/dp/B0HQ9MX1M9
