items.title: Why GLB Is Perfect for AI Agents | 3D Animation with Three.js, No Blender Required
items.excerpt: If you're creating 3D animations with AI agents, there's one file format you should seriously consider: GLB. And the interesting part is that your agent might not need Blender at all. Just a 3D model, some JavaScript, an
items.videoDescription:
If you're creating 3D animations with AI agents, there's one file format you should seriously consider: GLB. And the interesting part is that your agent might not need Blender at all. Just a 3D model, some JavaScript, and a browser.

Let me explain. GLB is the binary container format for glTF 2.0, an open standard developed by the Khronos Group for delivering 3D scenes and assets. Think of it as a convenient package containing the information needed to reconstruct an entire 3D scene.

Inside, you can have:
Scene hierarchy: Objects, components, and their relationships.
Geometry: Vertices, triangles, and other mesh data.
Materials and textures: How everything should look.
Animations: Keyframes, transforms, and movement.
Named objects: Individual components that can be accessed and manipulated through code.
And the entire scene can be packaged into a single .glb file.

Here's why this matters for AI agents.
Three.js has excellent support for glTF 2.0 through its GLTFLoader.
An agent can load a GLB model, inspect its scene hierarchy, find specific objects by name, and manipulate them directly with JavaScript.

Imagine a model containing a human skeleton.
Instead of moving thousands of individual vertices, the agent can identify objects such as: Skull Spine Rib cage Pelvis Individual vertebrae Left and right arms Then it can animate, rotate, highlight, or hide those components independently. It's almost like working with a digital construction kit.
Of course, this requires the GLB to contain properly separated and named objects. Not every downloaded model is organized that way. But when it is, the workflow becomes remarkably straightforward. And here's my favorite part.

The agent doesn't necessarily need to open a traditional 3D application.
It can:
1. Load the GLB model.
2. Write a Three.js scene.
3. Position the camera and lights.
4. Animate individual objects through code.
5. Render a frame in the browser.
6. Inspect the result and make corrections.

With browser automation and image inspection tools, the agent can even iterate visually on its own output.
Write code. Render. Look. Adjust. Repeat.

Hugging Face is becoming a useful source of ready-to-use 3D assets. There are datasets containing furniture, household objects, mechanical components, scanned artifacts, architectural elements, and much more. And some of them are surprisingly unusual.

For example, this entire animation was built using real anatomical data.

I used the CT Anatomy GLB dataset by CodePawl, available on Hugging Face.

The underlying medical data originates from TotalSegmentator, a research dataset developed at University Hospital Basel in Switzerland.

Researchers annotated 117 anatomical structures across 1,228 real clinical CT scans.

We're talking about actual medical imaging data, not anatomically questionable models invented by a text-to-3D generator.

The GLB collection converts a small selection of those segmented scans into structured 3D assets.

The published subset contains:

7 reconstructed anatomical scans

20 additional organ and body-part assets

Individually named anatomical structures

Optimized GLB geometry suitable for browser visualization

You can inspect individual organs, isolate anatomical systems, animate components, and build educational visualizations. And that's exactly what makes this format so useful. 

The AI agent doesn't need to invent the anatomy. The geometry already exists.

Its job is to understand the scene, write the animation, control the camera, and produce the final visual. That separation of responsibilities is important.

Generative AI is excellent at helping write code and construct workflows. But it doesn't always need to generate every asset from scratch.

Sometimes the most reliable approach is to combine existing structured 3D data with an agent that knows how to manipulate it. And that's why I think formats like GLB deserve much more attention in AI-assisted creative workflows.

items.title: Hermes Agent v0.23.0: Browser UI, /Rewind, Smarter AI Agents & Lower Token Costs
items.excerpt: What if your AI agent could work across your terminal, desktop, browser, and messaging apps without constantly losing context or duplicating tasks? And what if multiple agents could collaborate in the same conversation w
items.videoDescription:
What if your AI agent could work across your terminal, desktop, browser, and messaging apps without constantly losing context or duplicating tasks? And what if multiple agents could collaborate in the same conversation while you controlled exactly how much they were allowed to spend?

Meet Hermes Agent v0.23.0, codenamed The Hearth Release, from Nous Research.

Here's what's new.
1. Your entire AI workspace now runs in a browser
The Hermes Desktop experience is now available through a web interface.
Same conversations. Same agents. Same plugins and settings.
You can access your workspace from another computer, over your local network, or through an authenticated public URL.
No need to install the desktop application on every device.
The web interface is disabled by default, so you need to enable it in your settings.

2. One gateway. One conversation. No duplicate agents.
Previously, different Hermes interfaces could launch separate agent processes against the same conversation.
That could lead to duplicated actions, inconsistent histories, and unnecessary resource consumption.
Now a single gateway manages each conversation on its host.
The CLI, terminal UI, desktop, browser, editors, bots, and scheduled tasks connect to the same session.
Your conversation stays consistent, no matter where you access it.

3. /Rewind: Go back without destroying your work
Ever wish you could return to an earlier message, change your instructions, and try a completely different approach? Now you can.
Use: /rewind
Or press Escape twice in the terminal interface.
Choose an earlier message, edit it, and start a new branch of the conversation.
The original session remains intact.

4. Group Chats with automatic agent routing
This might be one of my favorite improvements.
Hermes Group Chats can now decide which agent should handle a message.
Instead of manually addressing every specialist, a lead agent or automatic router can select the appropriate participant.

The system can route messages, maintain shared context, and prevent agents from getting stuck replying to one another forever.
Because apparently, even AI agents need someone to stop an unnecessary meeting.

5. Spending limits for paid tools
This is a particularly welcome improvement.
Paid MCP tools can now expose their costs before execution.
Hermes shows the price of a tool call, tracks the conversation's spending, and asks for approval when a configured budget is exceeded.
Even in YOLO mode. So your AI agent can't casually spend your entire API budget generating 3D models and cinematic videos without asking.

6. A much larger plugin ecosystem
The Hermes plugin catalog has grown from approximately 600 to more than 1,050 integrations.
New official plugins include:
Meshy for AI-powered 3D generation
ElevenLabs for music and sound effects
X Chat integration
Reverse-engineering tools
Additional sandboxing and automation capabilities
Plugins can also be updated together, with optional automatic updates.

7. Smaller, faster, and more efficient
Nous Research has also made substantial improvements under the hood.
Approximately 1,570 fewer prompt tokens per one-shot call
Shared prompt caching for recurring scheduled jobs
Faster file operations
Improved memory management for long-running gateways
A smaller built-in skill set, reduced from 58 to 44
Better performance for large conversation histories

These optimizations are particularly useful if you run Hermes continuously rather than launching it for occasional tasks. And here's the bigger picture.

We're gradually moving beyond AI agents that live inside one chat window.

The next generation of agent platforms needs shared sessions, persistent context, coordinated specialists, cost controls, and interfaces that work across multiple devices.

Hermes v0.23.0 is moving in exactly that direction.

Not just a smarter chatbot.

A more complete environment for running AI agents as an ongoing system.

Of course, this is a major release, so existing users should check the migration notes. Some browser tools have changed, and several built-in capabilities have moved into plugins.

But I particularly like the philosophy behind this update.

The future of personal AI might not be one giant agent doing everything.

It might be a small team of specialized agents working together, remembering what they've done, and knowing when to ask for your approval.

And ideally, not setting your API budget on fire while you're sleeping.

https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent

items.title: Ultra Water: Insane Real-Time Ocean Simulation in Three.js | Free Open Source
items.excerpt: Someone just built an incredibly realistic ocean simulation using Three.js and WebGL2. And then decided to give away the entire source code. For free. Meet Ultra Water, an open-source, high-performance ocean renderer tha
items.videoDescription:
Someone just built an incredibly realistic ocean simulation using Three.js and WebGL2.

And then decided to give away the entire source code.

For free.

Meet Ultra Water, an open-source, high-performance ocean renderer that brings surprisingly sophisticated water physics and visual effects directly into your browser.

And honestly, the results look fantastic.

Here's what Ultra Water can do:

Realistic ocean waves: FFT-based simulation with four wave cascades, from large ocean swells to tiny ripples.

Breaking waves: Waves interact with the shoreline, producing realistic surf and foam.

Water reflections: Dynamic reflections, refraction, and sunlight scattering.

Underwater rendering: Light shafts, caustics, atmospheric effects, and underwater views.

Floating objects: Boats, barrels, and other objects respond to waves through buoyancy and drag.

Interactive controls: Experiment with camera angles, lighting, and rendering quality.

Real-time performance: The developer reports over 200 FPS across several scenes on an RTX 3060.

Yes, that's a consumer GPU rendering complex water effects in a browser.

The published benchmarks show approximately 303 FPS for open ocean and 212 FPS underwater, measured at 3.3 megapixels on an RTX 3060.

Of course, those are the developer's measurements, not guaranteed performance on every computer.

But there's more.

The same developer also released Ultra Elements, a collection of 39 real-time elemental spells and visual effects built with Three.js.

Fireballs. Lightning. Ice. Explosions. Magical shields. Particle effects.

Each spell has customizable parameters, colors, and presets.

And the interesting part?

You can give this code to Claude Code, Codex, or another AI coding agent and ask it to create entirely new effects for your game.

For example:

"Study the Ultra Elements codebase and create a new magical water spell with swirling particles, realistic splashes, and a glowing impact effect. Follow the existing architecture and make the effect customizable."

Instead of asking an AI agent to invent everything from scratch, you're giving it a working rendering system and a collection of examples to build upon.

That's a much better starting point.

And this is what I love about open-source creative coding.

One developer builds an impressive technical foundation.

Another turns it into a game.

Someone else creates a completely new visual effect.

And AI coding agents make it increasingly easy to experiment with and extend these systems.

Want realistic water or custom magic effects in your next Three.js project?

You probably don't need to start from zero anymore.

Try the interactive water demo:

A preview can look right while an export still needs checking. I tested whether picture and sound stay together when Premation changes video speed.

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 Built a Game in 8 Hours. Here's the Real Breakthrough
items.excerpt: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are here. AI can now build playable games from a single prompt, work on complex projects for hours, and coordinate increasingly sophisticated software systems. But does that mean game deve
items.videoDescription:
Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are here. AI can now build playable games from a single prompt, work on complex projects for hours, and coordinate increasingly sophisticated software systems.

But does that mean game development is dead?

Not even close. And that's not the most interesting part.

Let's look at three actual AI game development experiments instead of another round of "AI just replaced game developers" headlines.

EXPERIMENT 1: BLENDER TO THREE.JS

Claude Opus 5.5 attempts to recreate a Blender 3D scene in Three.js, comparing the rendered result against a visual reference.

Try it yourself:
https://claude.ai/artifact/XgM7ai2k4DRyXrUXjLGDng

EXPERIMENT 2: RECONSTRUCTING A 3D ENVIRONMENT

Another Blender-to-Three.js reconstruction experiment.

Pay attention to the details the model has to interpret or invent when reproducing the reference.

Interactive example:
https://claude.ai/artifact/7NnuK9iVSvVsuwkzNSHht8

EXPERIMENT 3: ONE-PROMPT GAME DEVELOPMENT

A game reportedly built by Claude Fable 5.2 from a single initial prompt, with approximately eight hours of agent execution and around $550 in AI costs.

Play it:
https://claude.ai/artifact/BGY1SztrAYcJQHSsnHHGmp

The interesting question isn't whether these examples look as polished as a professional AAA game.

They don't need to.

The real breakthrough is the ability to develop increasingly complex software systems through extended autonomous work.

Here's the distinction:

• Visual fidelity: AI still struggles with sophisticated art direction, convincing materials, detailed character surfaces, and the kind of visual polish professional artists achieve through experience.

• Complex systems: models are becoming increasingly capable of building interconnected mechanics, procedural environments, state management, physics interactions, and application logic.

• Long-running agents: frontier models can work on engineering tasks for extended periods, iterating, testing, debugging, and coordinating subagents.

• System architecture: the ability to maintain relationships between components matters more as projects become larger.

• AI-assisted 3D development: Blender, Three.js, and coding agents make it possible to construct playable environments without manually building every element.

• Cost and iteration: a one-prompt game costing around $550 is an interesting experiment, but it isn't equivalent to a finished commercial game.

And here's where things get interesting.

Creating a beautifully detailed monster is one challenge.

Building a monster with complex skeletal animation, physics, procedural movement, behavioral systems, damage mechanics, and interactions with an entire game world is another.

AI models are becoming increasingly useful at the second challenge.

They may produce technically sophisticated rigs and interactions while still struggling with the precise artistic direction needed for convincing skin, decay, materials, and detailed character design.

For now, the most productive approach may be to use AI agents for complex systems while relying on experienced artists for visual quality.

Eventually, generating beautiful graphics may become much cheaper and easier too.

But a convincing game world is more than a collection of beautiful assets.

It's the relationships between its mechanics, physics, rules, characters, and systems that make the world feel alive.

These three examples are demonstrations, not controlled benchmarks. The eight-hour runtime and approximately $550 cost are creator-reported figures.

Official Anthropic announcement:
https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2

So, is AI about to replace game developers?

Or is the real opportunity to build games with a level of systemic complexity that previously required much larger teams?

items.title: Three.js r187 Is INSANE! 2 Billion Triangles at 60 FPS in a Browser | Claude Opus 5.5
items.excerpt: Remember when rendering millions of polygons required expensive workstations, specialized software, and a considerable amount of patience? RenderMan veterans, this one's for you. Someone just built a browser-based 3D sce
items.videoDescription:
Remember when rendering millions of polygons required expensive workstations, specialized software, and a considerable amount of patience?

RenderMan veterans, this one's for you.

Someone just built a browser-based 3D scene containing almost TWO BILLION triangles, running at 60 FPS.

And the entire environment was created with the help of Claude Opus 5.5.

Meet BILLION, an impressive graphics experiment by Sara Chen (@sara_kumodeck), showcasing the new MeshletDrawingPipeline introduced in Three.js r187.

And the numbers are ridiculous.

1,967,478,960 triangles.

In a desktop browser.

At 60 frames per second.

So how is that even possible?

The secret is GPU-driven rendering using something called meshlets.

Instead of treating enormous 3D models as single objects, the new pipeline divides geometry into small clusters of 64 triangles.

Then the GPU decides which clusters actually need to be rendered.

Here's what makes Three.js r187 so interesting:

Meshlet rendering: Large meshes are divided into 64-triangle clusters.

GPU-driven culling: Invisible clusters are skipped before rendering.

Level of Detail (LOD): Distant geometry automatically switches to simplified versions.

Occlusion culling: Geometry hidden behind other objects can be excluded.

Indirect drawing: The GPU handles much of the rendering workload without constant CPU intervention.

WebGPU acceleration: Modern browser graphics APIs make these techniques possible.

And here's the really impressive comparison.

In the developer's demonstration:

Meshlets enabled: Approximately 60 FPS

Traditional rendering: Approximately 20 FPS

Same scene. Same hardware.

That's a threefold performance improvement in this particular test.

There's also a button to visualize individual meshlets, making it possible to see how the GPU organizes the scene.

And here's an important technical detail.

The scene contains nearly two billion triangles, but the GPU doesn't actually draw all of them every frame.

That's precisely the point.

Meshlet culling and LOD dramatically reduce the amount of geometry that needs to be processed.

The developer also reports that preparing the meshlets and LOD structures takes approximately 16–21 seconds on a desktop computer.

And if WebGPU isn't available, the demo falls back to a smaller WebGL2 version containing approximately 13.5 million triangles.

But here's what I find even more fascinating.

The entire canyon environment was generated procedurally.

No imported 3D models. No external textures.

Just code, mathematical noise, Three.js, and Claude Opus 5.5.

Which raises a rather interesting question.

What happens to traditional 3D production when powerful coding agents can generate complex environments directly in a modern rendering engine?

Of course, Blender, Maya, Houdini, Cinema 4D, and RenderMan aren't going anywhere.

Professional 3D production involves much more than generating geometry.

But for interactive experiences, procedural environments, browser games, and creative experiments, the combination of LLMs and modern rendering technology is becoming increasingly powerful.

And the barrier to creating ambitious 3D worlds keeps getting lower.

Almost two billion triangles. A browser. And an AI coding agent.

Not bad for something running in a tab.

Try the BILLION demo:
https://r187-meshlet.kumodeck.app/

https://threejs.org/changelog/?r187

https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/pull/35191

Apparently, CapCut couldn't just sit back and watch creators automate their video editing workflows with Claude Code and DaVinci Resolve.

So now CapCut is coming directly to ChatGPT.

Announced at CapCut World LA on October 24, 2026, the new integration lets creators edit videos using natural language instead of manually doing everything on a timeline.

And the demonstration looks pretty interesting.

Here's how it works:

Upload your footage: Give ChatGPT your video clips and explain what you want.

Describe the edit: Ask for a fast-paced highlight reel, specific transitions, or a particular visual style.

Generate a first cut: CapCut helps assemble your footage into an editable timeline.

Make changes through chat: Ask for titles, captions, different timing, or other adjustments.

Keep creative control: Continue refining the project in CapCut.

No need to manually arrange every single clip just to get a first draft.

And here's another interesting detail.

Among the people involved in the announcement was Sam Yam, OpenAI's Head of Creator Product and former Patreon co-founder and CTO.

Which makes me think this is probably just the beginning.

We're already seeing AI agents write code, generate animations, and automate increasingly complex creative workflows.

Now professional video editing is becoming another area where natural language can replace part of the traditional interface.

CapCut's new ChatGPT integration is expected to enter open beta in November 2026, across mobile, desktop, and web.

Pricing and regional availability haven't been fully announced yet.

Meanwhile, there's another interesting development for video creators.

Blackmagic Design just launched a rare 20% discount on DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.

Regular price: $295

Sale price: $236

You save: $59

Offer ends: November 20, 2026

And unlike most professional editing software, DaVinci Resolve Studio uses a one-time purchase model instead of a recurring subscription.

You get professional editing, color grading, Fusion motion graphics, Fairlight audio tools, and powerful AI features.

Personally, I find both developments fascinating.

On one side, AI is becoming part of the video editor.

On the other, creators are using coding agents to automate workflows around existing professional tools.

The real question isn't whether AI will change video editing.

It's how much of the timeline we'll still be editing manually in a couple of years.

items.title: Spline + ChatGPT: Create Interactive 3D Scenes Just by Prompting | Codex Plugin
items.excerpt: What if you could create an entire interactive 3D scene without opening Blender, writing Three.js code, or manually building every object? And what if you could edit the result directly inside ChatGPT? Meet the new Splin
items.videoDescription:
What if you could create an entire interactive 3D scene without opening Blender, writing Three.js code, or manually building every object?

And what if you could edit the result directly inside ChatGPT?

Meet the new Spline plugin for ChatGPT and OpenAI Codex.

And this is exactly the kind of AI integration I've been waiting for.

Here's the idea.

Instead of asking ChatGPT to generate 3D code and hoping everything renders correctly, you connect it directly to a real 3D design application.

Spline's editor opens right next to your conversation.

You describe what you want, and ChatGPT builds the scene while you watch.

Here's what you can create:

Interactive 3D scenes: Objects, materials, lighting, cameras, and animations.

Product configurators: Interactive 3D products with customizable colors and materials.

3D interfaces: Animated music players, dashboards, and product demonstrations.

Interactive games: Simple playable 3D experiences.

Websites and app interfaces: Design layouts using Spline's Hana editor.

AI-generated assets: Create 3D models and images directly within your workflow.

Shareable experiences: Publish your finished scene and get a public link.

But here's where things get really interesting.

You and ChatGPT can edit the same project together.

Ask ChatGPT to create a 3D chair configurator.

Then manually rotate the chair, change its material, or adjust the lighting in the Spline editor.

Now tell ChatGPT:

"Add three color options and animate the chair when users select a different material."

ChatGPT reads the updated project and continues working from your changes.

No starting over. No losing your manual edits.

And the result isn't just another AI-generated image or video.

It's a real, editable Spline project saved to your account.

You can open it later, modify it manually, continue the conversation, or publish it online.

How to get started with ChatGPT:

Open the Spline plugin in ChatGPT's plugin directory.

Connect your Spline account.

Describe the 3D scene or interface you want.

Watch the editor build it.

Continue refining the same project through conversation.

No installation. No API key.

The integration uses Spline's hosted MCP server and includes the Spline Agent Skill, which teaches ChatGPT how to work with the editor.

And yes, it works with OpenAI Codex too.

You can install the same plugin or connect the MCP server manually:

codex mcp add spline --url https://mcp.spline.design/mcp
codex mcp login spline

The plugin works across Spline plans, including Free, although AI actions count toward your plan's daily usage limits.

Why do I find this exciting?

Because we're finally seeing AI agents integrate with actual creative software instead of constantly reinventing simplified versions of it.

You don't need another AI-generated mockup that becomes useless the moment you want to change something.

You need editable projects.

Real tools.

And an AI agent that can collaborate with you inside them.

The future of creative AI shouldn't be about replacing designers with prompts.

It should be about giving designers tools that can turn ideas into working, editable experiences much faster.

And Spline's integration with ChatGPT and Codex is a very interesting step in that direction.

https://chatgpt.com/plugins/spline

Official documentation:
https://docs.spline.design/generate/plugins/chatgpt

items.title: Do You Believe in Life After Death? This Interactive 3D Visualization Explores 130,000 Answers
items.excerpt: What happens after we die? It's one of humanity's oldest questions. And someone decided to turn 130,000 people's answers into an interactive 3D experience. Meet Life After Death?, a fascinating data visualization created
items.videoDescription:
What happens after we die?

It's one of humanity's oldest questions. And someone decided to turn 130,000 people's answers into an interactive 3D experience.

Meet Life After Death?, a fascinating data visualization created by Alvin Chang for The Pudding.

The project draws on survey responses from nearly 130,000 people across 23 countries, exploring how our beliefs about death, religion, and the afterlife differ across cultures and generations.

But instead of presenting another collection of boring charts, Chang built something much more interesting.

A virtual room filled with 1,500 people.

Each little character represents a real survey respondent, positioned according to their age and beliefs.

And the entire room is interactive.

Here's what you can explore:

Belief in the afterlife: See how people differ in what they believe happens after death.

Age and generations: Explore how beliefs vary across age groups.

Individual responses: Click on a character to learn more about their answers.

Interactive categories: Switch between survey questions and watch the characters change colors or move into new groups.

Global perspectives: Discover patterns across different countries and cultures.

The underlying research comes from the Global Flourishing Study, with additional historical context from international values surveys.

And here's what I find particularly beautiful about this project.

It turns statistics back into people.

Instead of looking at abstract percentages, you're surrounded by hundreds of tiny human figures, each representing someone with their own perspective on one of life's biggest mysteries.

It's part data journalism, part interactive art, and part philosophical exploration.

And a wonderful example of how creative coding and data visualization can make complex research feel surprisingly personal.

130,000 answers. 23 countries. One question nobody can definitively answer.

What do you believe?

Explore the interactive visualization:
https://pudding.cool/2026/10/lifeafter/

Created by Alvin Chang for The Pudding.

#DataVisualization #InteractiveArt #CreativeCoding #LifeAfterDeath #DataJournalism #Shorts

items.title: Why a Realistic Robot Simulation Can Still Be Wrong
items.excerpt: Two identical blocks. The same starting speed. Different stopping distances. A robot simulation can look convincing and still get the physics wrong. This short explainer examines the Real2Sim challenge through Google's A
items.videoDescription:
Two identical blocks. The same starting speed. Different stopping distances. A robot simulation can look convincing and still get the physics wrong.

This short explainer examines the Real2Sim challenge through Google's Argon robotics demonstration and our own MuJoCo friction experiment: what must a digital twin match beyond its appearance?

We look at geometry, cameras, mass, inertia, friction, collision shapes and joints—and why contact timing and forces matter when comparing a simulation with recorded behaviour.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Same start, different outcome
0:13 Google's Real2Sim demonstration
0:30 The visible layer
0:41 Hidden physical properties
0:52 Our MuJoCo friction experiment
1:09 Compare with measurements
1:24 What the demonstration does—and doesn't—prove
1:38 The question a useful twin must answer

SOURCES
Google Developers — Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics, 13 October 2026:
https://developers.googleblog.com/gemini-4-argon-for-robotics/

MuJoCo — official project and Python documentation:
https://mujoco.org/
https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/stable/python.html

ABOUT THIS VIDEO
The block comparison is an independent toy experiment calculated in MuJoCo, not a reproduction of Google's robot or a real-object calibration. The robot-arm graphics are explanatory diagrams. Google's results are attributed to its developer demonstration; we do not claim that any video can automatically become a validated simulator.

Created with AI-assisted writing and synthetic English narration, original animated graphics, and an original quiet sound bed. No third-party demonstration footage is used.

items.videoDescription:
A great shot. One wrong detail. Should you edit it or regenerate everything?

Google says Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash can create 15-second clips and refine them through follow-up requests. This short illustrated guide looks at a practical question: after an edit, what happens to the subject, camera and action?

I use an original robot-and-umbrella miniature to explain a single-change workflow: keep the original, request one change, compare the result, then count every output needed to reach an accepted shot.

The pricing example uses Google's published 720p video-output table: 5,792 tokens per second at $12 per million video tokens. That is approximately $1.04 for 15 seconds, or $3.13 for three such outputs. Input and other charges are extra. Prices were checked on 9 November 2026 and may change.

These visuals are our own AI-assisted illustrations and local animation. They are not Gemini Omni-generated video, a model-quality benchmark, or a bill from our own API test. We have not tested how many attempts a particular Omni shot needs, or whether a follow-up request reduces its total cost.

items.title: Free Figma MCP Without the 20-Call Limit! | Claude Code, Codex & Cursor
items.excerpt: I wanted to give my AI coding agent access to Figma. Meet Figma Console MCP, a free tool developed by Southleft that lets Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, and other AI agents work directly with Figma. It uses Figma's P
items.videoDescription:
I wanted to give my AI coding agent access to Figma.

Meet Figma Console MCP, a free tool developed by Southleft that lets Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, and other AI agents work directly with Figma.

It uses Figma's Plugin API instead of relying exclusively on the official MCP server.

That means its local design operations aren't subject to the official 20-call monthly MCP quota.

Pretty much everything you'd expect from a serious Figma integration:

Create designs: Frames, shapes, text, components, and complete interface layouts.

Edit existing files: Change colors, typography, spacing, positioning, and other properties.

Manage design systems: Read and modify variables, tokens, components, and styles.

Build prototypes: Work with supported interactions and prototype connections.

Real-time monitoring: Track selections, document changes, and console output.

Visual debugging: Capture screenshots and inspect design elements.

Design-to-code workflows: Extract design specifications and compare them with your implementation.

FigJam support: Create diagrams, flowcharts, tables, and collaborative boards.

And it currently offers around 130 MCP tools in its full local setup.

That's a pretty serious toolkit.

But how does it actually work?

The project uses something called Figma Desktop Bridge.

It's a local plugin running inside the Figma desktop application.

Your AI agent communicates with an MCP server, which connects to the plugin through WebSocket.

The plugin then uses Figma's native Plugin API to inspect and modify your design.

In other words, your AI agent gets direct access to Figma's design functionality without clicking around the interface like a human.

And because the connection is local, it can also monitor changes as you work.

Want to try it?

Here's the basic setup.

Step 1: Install Figma Desktop

Download the macOS or Windows application:

https://www.figma.com/downloads/

Step 2: Get Figma Console MCP

Open the GitHub repository:

https://github.com/southleft/figma-console-mcp

You can configure the MCP server manually or ask your AI coding agent to follow the installation instructions.

For example:

"Set up figma-console-mcp from southleft/figma-console-mcp for my coding environment. Follow the official installation guide, configure the Figma Desktop Bridge, and verify the connection. Ask before modifying existing Figma files or changing global settings."

Step 3: Configure the connection

The recommended local setup requires Node.js 18+, an MCP-compatible AI client, and a Figma personal access token.

Keep your token in the appropriate local configuration. Don't paste it into public repositories or share it in conversations.

Step 4: Import the Desktop Bridge plugin

Open Figma Desktop and navigate to:

Plugins → Development → Import plugin from manifest

Select the manifest generated by Figma Console MCP.

After importing, open your design file and run:

Plugins → Development → Figma Desktop Bridge

Step 5: Start designing with AI

Now ask Claude Code or Codex something like:

"Open my current Figma design, inspect the existing layout, and create a new dashboard screen using the same typography, spacing, and color system."

Or:

"Review the components in this file and identify inconsistencies in the design system."

Or simply:

"Create a responsive SaaS landing page directly in Figma."

And here's the best part.

You can continue editing the design manually while your AI agent works with the same file.

No exporting screenshots after every change.

No manually transferring design specifications back and forth.

Now, one important caveat about the word "unlimited."

The local Plugin API connection avoids Figma's official MCP monthly call quota for those operations.

But Figma's separate REST API limits, account permissions, and your AI model's usage costs still apply where relevant.

So it's not literally unlimited access to every Figma feature.

And there's one notable difference from the official integration.

Figma Console MCP doesn't provide Figma's native Code Connect functionality, which links design components directly to their corresponding code components.

Still, for everyday AI-assisted design, editing, and design-system management, it's a remarkably capable alternative.

First, companies introduce AI integrations.
Then developers discover the limitations. Then someone builds an open-source alternative that gives users more control over their own workflows.

Figma Console MCP is another example of that shift.

Figma Console MCP on GitHub:
https://github.com/southleft/figma-console-mcp

Official installation guide:
https://github.com/southleft/figma-console-mcp/blob/main/docs/setup.md

Figma Desktop:
https://www.figma.com/downloads/

Official Figma MCP limits:
https://developers.figma.com/docs/figma-mcp-server/rate-limits-access/

Free and open source under the MIT license.

items.title: 109M vs 72B: Why Better Training Pairs Matter
items.excerpt: What if better AI starts with better training pairs, rather than just a bigger model? This short visual explainer looks at a 2026 preprint by Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun. Their 109M-parameter text JEPA achieved st
items.videoDescription:
What if better AI starts with better training pairs, rather than just a bigger model?

This short visual explainer looks at a 2026 preprint by Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun. Their 109M-parameter text JEPA achieved stronger alignment with image representations than the language models evaluated, including Qwen2.5-72B, on the reported WIT-1024 test.

That is a specific representation-alignment result—not proof that the smaller model is generally smarter or can replace a conversational assistant.

A dog, a bicycle and three descriptions help explain good views, representation space and why the relationships between examples matter. Real paper excerpts and a redrawn chart show where the reported numbers come from.

READ THE FULL ARTICLE
https://abvx.xyz/writing/lecun-jepa-109m-vs-72b-platonic-representations

CHAPTERS
00:00 109M vs 72B: the question
00:21 The paper and JEPA
00:49 How training pairs work
01:01 The alignment results
01:16 What this does not prove
01:26 The takeaway

RESEARCH
Randall Balestriero & Yann LeCun — Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs, arXiv:2610.39302v1, 29 October 2026:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39302

Minyoung Huh, Brian Cheung, Tongzhou Wang & Phillip Isola — The Platonic Representation Hypothesis, ICML 2024:
https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/huh24a.html

VISUALS & PRODUCTION
PDF excerpts: Balestriero & LeCun, CC BY4.0. Cropping/highlights added; chart redrawn from Table 3. The point-space geometry is explanatory, not measured embeddings. The realistic dog-and-bicycle scene and thumbnail are AI-generated illustrations. English narration is synthetic; it does not impersonate either researcher. Original instrumental music is reused from our studio library.

items.excerpt: A rooftop becomes a canvas: explore Pokras Lampas’s 177 m² calligraphy work at the Barkli DAN residence in Kazan. This short art film combines aerial footage, moving photographs, English narration and an original electro
items.videoDescription:
A rooftop becomes a canvas: explore Pokras Lampas’s 177 m² calligraphy work at the Barkli DAN residence in Kazan. This short art film combines aerial footage, moving photographs, English narration and an original electronic soundtrack.

The artist brings contemporary Cyrillic calligraphy into conversation with architecture and Tatar cultural heritage. Six words express three ideas: glory, writing and inspiration. Concentric bands of blue, black and white turn the roof into a composition that changes as the camera moves from its geometric whole to the detail of individual letters.

According to the artist’s statement supplied for this film:
• 177 square metres of calligraphy
• 15 metres in diameter
• Three months of preparation
• Fourteen days of painting

ARTWORK
Artist: Pokras Lampas
Location: Barkli DAN residence, Kazan
Project acknowledgement in the supplied statement: the Barkli team and Leonid Kazinets.

PRODUCTION
Created by Anton Biletskiy-Volokh with Framewright, my project for repeatable, agent-assisted video production:
https://github.com/markoblogo/framewright
More of my work: https://abvx.xyz/

The supplied photos and videos show the actual artwork. Photographs are animated through camera reframing; the original calligraphy is preserved. A separate six-second radial animation is an original visual interlude created for this film with p5.js, rather than part of the mural. English narration uses local Supertonic 3; the original instrumental score was composed with Tone.js. The source-video sound was removed.

Artwork and source media remain the work of their respective creators. Project facts are drawn from the supplied artist statement. This is an independent editorial art film.

items.videoDescription:
Claude can already generate animations and videos. But there's always been one annoying problem.
What happens when you want to actually edit the result?
An AI-generated MP4 isn't an editable Premiere Pro timeline. You can't just open it in After Effects and start adjusting individual layers, animations, or keyframes.
Well, that gap is finally starting to close.
Meet Tesseract by Mirage, a creative toolkit that lets AI agents create, edit, and export projects compatible with Adobe Premiere Pro and After Effects.
And the interesting part? Your AI agent can work directly with editable project files without controlling a graphical interface.

Here's what Tesseract can do:
- Create videos and motion graphics through AI agents
- Export editable Premiere Pro projects (.prproj)
- Export After Effects compositions (.aep)
- Import existing Adobe projects for AI-assisted editing
- Modify supported timelines, layers, and animations
- Render finished videos without an Adobe subscription
- Work through code and structured project files instead of mouse clicks and screenshots

The project converters are also open source under the MIT license.
There are some limitations: format support is still partial, and After Effects export is experimental. Complex effects, fonts, and animations may not transfer perfectly. Mirage
But the bigger picture is fascinating.
Until recently, AI-generated creative work often ended with a finished file you couldn't meaningfully modify.
Now we're moving toward AI agents producing real, editable creative projects that humans can continue working on.

Imagine asking Claude to create a motion graphics sequence, opening the result in After Effects, adjusting a few keyframes, and finishing it yourself.
Or doing the reverse: giving an existing Premiere Pro project to an AI agent and asking it to make changes.
AI handles the production. You keep creative control.
That's a much more interesting future for AI-assisted video production than simply generating another MP4.

items.title: Unreal Engine 5.9: AI Agents, Unreal MCP, Canvas & WebGPU
items.excerpt: Epic Games just released Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview, bringing AI coding agents directly into Unreal Editor, a new generative workspace called Unreal Canvas, and experimental browser exports using WebAssembly and WebGPU. B
items.videoDescription:
Epic Games just released Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview, bringing AI coding agents directly into Unreal Editor, a new generative workspace called Unreal Canvas, and experimental browser exports using WebAssembly and WebGPU.

But here's the wildest part: Epic says this Preview was built primarily using swarms of AI coding agents in approximately ONE WEEK.

Engineers supervised, reviewed, and tested the work while AI agents helped port features and implement the experimental web platform.

Here's what's new in Unreal Engine 5.9:

• Unreal Assistant: work with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode directly inside Unreal Editor.

• Unreal MCP: expanded Model Context Protocol tools give agents access to level creation, Blueprints, rendering, materials, geometry, debugging, profiling, source control, and more.

• Autonomous asset workflows: agents can search the Fab marketplace, browse your asset library, and install compatible 3D assets into projects.

• Unreal Canvas: a generative workspace available inside Unreal Editor and on the web for creating concept art, images, videos, and 3D meshes.

• Scene-aware AI generation: use existing scenes, reference images, camera perspectives, and composition to guide generated content.

• Expanded Python API: automate more engine functionality, including physics, Niagara, materials, audio, PCG, networking, and UI.

• WebAssembly + WebGPU: compile supported Unreal experiences to run directly in compatible browsers without installing the game or using a Pixel Streaming server.

• AI-assisted engine development: Epic used multiple agents working in parallel to port AI tools from its UE6 development branch and prototype the web target.

The bigger story isn't just AI-assisted game development.

It's AI agents becoming part of both the game engine's interface and the engineering process used to build the engine itself.

Imagine describing an environment, having Claude construct the level, configure materials, create Blueprints, download assets from Fab, and prepare a playable build.

That workflow is getting closer.

IMPORTANT: Unreal Engine 5.9 is currently an experimental MegaJam Preview, not a stable production release. Browser exports require a source-built engine and a C++ project, and several features remain incomplete.

Epic recommends testing on copies of your projects rather than migrating production projects.

items.title: XREAL AURA: Gemini AI Glasses That Can See Your Laptop Screen | Google Android XR
items.excerpt: Google is taking another shot at augmented reality. And this time, I think they might actually be onto something. Well, technically, XREAL built the glasses, while Google brought Android XR and Gemini AI to the party. Me
items.videoDescription:
Google is taking another shot at augmented reality.

And this time, I think they might actually be onto something.

Well, technically, XREAL built the glasses, while Google brought Android XR and Gemini AI to the party.

Meet XREAL AURA, a new pair of lightweight mixed reality glasses that can see your surroundings, display virtual screens, and even let Gemini understand what's happening on your laptop.

And for the first time in quite a while, I'm genuinely tempted to try a new XR device.

Here's what makes XREAL AURA interesting:

Under 95 grams: Much lighter than traditional mixed reality headsets.

70° field of view: A wide virtual workspace with transparent lenses.

Snapdragon Reality Elite: Qualcomm's new XR platform handles spatial computing.

External compute puck: The processor and battery live in a separate wired device.

Android XR: Access millions of compatible Google Play apps, including 150+ XR experiences.

Virtual monitors: Connect your laptop via USB-C and place its screen anywhere in your environment.

Gemini AI: An assistant that understands both your physical surroundings and your virtual workspace.

But here's the feature that really caught my attention.

Gemini can actually see what's on your computer screen.

Imagine sitting at your desk with several virtual displays floating around you.

You're working on a project, looking at code, reading a document, or exploring a 3D scene.

And instead of switching to another application to ask AI for help, you simply talk to Gemini.

"What's happening in this window?"

"Help me organize my workspace."

"Explain this diagram."

"Show me where I should click."

Gemini can understand the content you're viewing and even highlight relevant elements in your field of vision.

That's a much more interesting approach to AI interfaces than putting another chatbot in another browser tab.

And there's something else I appreciate.

These actually look like glasses.

Not a ski mask strapped to your face.

Not an enormous headset that makes you look like you're preparing for a mission to Mars.

Just relatively compact, transparent XR glasses connected to a small computing device.

Of course, the separate puck and cable are still compromises.

And we're not talking about completely standalone, everyday AR glasses yet.

Now for the painful part.

The price.

Starting at $1,099 for the 12 GB / 256 GB version

$1,299 for the 16 GB / 512 GB version

Orders open in the US, Canada, South Korea, and Japan

First shipments expected in mid-November 2026

No confirmed European release date yet

Those are promotional launch prices available through the end of 2026.

And yes, $1,099 is still a lot of money for something that might eventually spend more time in a drawer than on your face.

But here's why I find this development genuinely encouraging.

After spending years working in AR and VR, I've been waiting for the industry to move beyond bulky headsets.

Not because the technology isn't fascinating.

Because the hardware has remained one of the biggest obstacles to making spatial computing part of everyday life.

And now we're finally seeing a combination that starts to make sense.

Lightweight glasses. A real operating system. Existing applications. Virtual displays. And an AI assistant that understands what you're seeing.

The individual technologies aren't entirely new.

But bringing them together in a reasonably portable form factor could make a real difference.

I'm not convinced XREAL AURA is the final answer.

Especially at this price.

But for the first time in years, I'm looking at a new XR device and thinking: I actually want to build something for this.

Now, Google and XREAL, could we please have a European release?

And perhaps a slightly less ambitious price tag?

Not through scientific diagrams, but through mesmerizing digital sculptures, flowing particles, and constantly transforming structures.

Meet Magnetic Currents, an extraordinary experimental motion design project by creative studio Media.Work.

And the visuals are absolutely hypnotic.

Created as part of the studio's ongoing series of visual explorations, the project transforms magnetism into a poetic study of movement, attraction, and transformation.

Here's what makes it so fascinating:

Magnetic fields: Invisible forces interpreted through dynamic 3D structures.

Particle systems: Thousands of elements flowing, gathering, and dispersing.

Digital sculptures: Monumental forms that emerge, deform, and dissolve.

Abstract motion: A delicate balance between order and chaos.

Experimental CGI: A combination of sophisticated 3D animation, material exploration, and artistic direction.

But there's something deeper behind these beautiful visuals.

Magnetic Currents explores the tension between structure and dissolution.

Solid forms become fluid. Particles organize themselves into complex patterns, only to fall apart again.

What appears chaotic gradually reveals an underlying order.

And what looks permanent turns out to be temporary.

It's a fascinating artistic interpretation of how invisible forces influence the world around us.

This isn't AI-generated video or a scientific simulation.

It's carefully crafted experimental computer graphics, where physical phenomena become a source of creative inspiration.

And personally, I love projects like this.

No products to sell. No complicated narrative.

Just an idea, an invisible force, and a team of artists exploring how beautiful it can become.

Sometimes the most interesting things in the universe are the ones we can't see.

items.videoDescription:
Google Meet can now translate conversations across 63 languages in near real time, letting people speak their native languages while everyone else hears AI-translated speech.

And the translated voice can even sound like the original speaker.

Powered by Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, Google's latest speech-to-speech AI technology brings us closer to a world where language barriers no longer define who we can communicate with.

Here's how it works:

• 63 supported languages: translate conversations between different languages within the same meeting.

• Real-time voice translation: hear AI-generated speech just a few seconds after someone speaks.

• Voice preservation: translated speech aims to maintain the speaker's original vocal characteristics, intonation, and rhythm.

• Automatic language detection: Google Meet recognizes spoken languages without requiring users to manually switch between them.

• Multilingual meetings: participants can independently choose which language they want to hear.

• Live translated captions: synchronized subtitles accompany the translated speech.

• Web and mobile support: available on supported Google Meet desktop, Android, and iOS clients.

The technology uses Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, an AI model designed to process and translate speech continuously rather than waiting for complete sentences.

It's not perfect. Translation errors and delays still happen, and access requires eligible Google Workspace or Google AI plans.

But the implications are enormous.

International business meetings. Remote teams. Education. Cross-border collaboration. Conversations between people who don't share a common language.

For decades, real-time universal translation belonged to science fiction.

Now it's becoming a standard video conferencing feature.

The digital Tower of Babel is getting closer.

items.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash Is Here! 15-Second AI Videos, 30% Cheaper & Editable by Chat
items.excerpt: Google just made AI video generation longer, cheaper, and considerably more interesting. Meet Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, the latest update to Google's AI video generation model. And honestly, the most exciting feature isn't
items.videoDescription:
Google just made AI video generation longer, cheaper, and considerably more interesting.

Meet Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, the latest update to Google's AI video generation model.

And honestly, the most exciting feature isn't the longer clips or the lower price.

It's the ability to edit your videos through an ongoing conversation.

Imagine generating a cinematic scene and then simply telling the model:

"Change the background to a forest."

"Make the lighting more dramatic."

"Replace the product with this one."

"Now create a vertical version for YouTube Shorts."

And the AI continues working on the same video without requiring you to describe the entire scene from scratch.

That's the real upgrade.

Here's what's new in Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash:

15-second videos: Up from the previous 10-second limit.

30% cheaper generation: Approximately $0.07 per second at 720p.

Conversational editing: Change objects, backgrounds, lighting, weather, and aspect ratios through follow-up prompts.

Better character consistency: Google claims improved preservation of faces, clothing, and product details.

More natural dialogue: Improved lip synchronization and conversations involving multiple characters.

Smoother camera movement: Fewer unwanted cuts during complex camera movements, including FPV flythroughs.

Reference-based generation: Use images and other supported visual references to guide the result.

Multiple resolutions: Generate at 360p or 720p, with higher-resolution output options up to 4K.

And the pricing is getting interesting.

At 720p, Google's new output price is approximately:

10-second video: $0.70

15-second video: $1.05

60 seconds of generated footage: $4.20

Those figures are based on video output pricing. Input tokens, additional edits, and other usage can increase the total cost.

But here's what I find particularly useful.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash supports multi-turn editing through Google's Interactions API.

Instead of treating every generation as a completely separate request, developers can preserve the conversation context and continue refining their video.

That's an important shift.

Because real creative production rarely works like this:

Write one perfect prompt. Generate one perfect video. Done.

It usually looks more like:

Generate. Review. Change the lighting. Fix the character. Adjust the camera. Change the background. Try again.

And that's exactly the kind of workflow AI video tools need to support.

Google also claims that Omni 1.2 Flash is better at maintaining visual consistency across multiple shots and complex motion.

But there are still limitations.

Fast sports movements, complicated physics, and rapid changes in the storyline remain challenging.

And Google's quality improvements are currently based primarily on its own demonstrations, rather than extensive independent comparisons.

Availability:

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is now generally available through the paid Gemini API and Google Cloud's Vertex AI.

The model identifier is:

gemini-omni-1.2-flash

And if you're already using the previous version, there's an important date to remember.

Starting December 3, 2026, API requests to gemini-omni-1.1-flash will automatically route to version 1.2 at the new pricing.

Regional availability and feature restrictions still apply.

And here's the bigger picture.

We've spent years getting better and better at generating short AI videos.

But the next major improvement might not be another jump in visual quality.

It might be the ability to actually direct and revise those videos without starting over every time.

Less prompt lottery.

More creative control.

And at $0.07 per second, experimenting is becoming considerably more affordable.

The future of AI filmmaking might look less like generating clips and more like having an ongoing conversation with your editor.

https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/interactions-overview

items.videoDescription:
What if you could explore the human body like a 3D video game?

Peel away anatomical layers. Isolate individual muscles. Watch the skeleton move. Or zoom straight inside a beating heart.

Google DeepMind just demonstrated exactly that with Gemini 4 Argon.

And here's the interesting part.

Instead of building everything manually, Gemini combined three open-source datasets into a fully interactive 3D anatomy visualization.

Here's what the demonstration shows:

Anatomical layers: Switch between muscles, skeleton, organs, and other structures while the body is moving.

Individual muscles: Isolate specific muscles and examine how they relate to surrounding anatomy.

Beating heart: Zoom inside an animated heart and explore its internal structures.

Interactive biomechanics: See anatomical structures in motion rather than as static textbook illustrations.

Medical information: Explore anatomical details and associated clinical metadata.

This isn't simply an AI-generated picture of the human body.

It's an interactive application assembled from real anatomical data using AI-written code.

And that's what makes this experiment so interesting.

Think about how many hours of research, data preparation, 3D modeling, and software development traditionally go into creating educational tools like this.

Now imagine an AI agent helping turn existing scientific datasets into interactive learning experiences.

Of course, this is a Google demonstration, not an independently validated medical education product. Anatomical accuracy still needs to be verified.

But the possibilities are fascinating.

We're moving from asking AI to explain how the human body works to asking it to build an entire interactive body we can explore.

Anatomy textbooks are about to get some serious competition.

items.videoDescription:
What if you could run a powerful AI video generation model on your own computer, without renting expensive cloud GPUs?

And what if you only needed 8 GB of VRAM?

Meet FreeVideo, an open-source project designed to bring MiniMax H3 video generation to consumer hardware.

Yes, the same family of AI video models usually associated with powerful GPU servers.

Except this time, you can run it locally.

Here's what FreeVideo offers:

8 GB VRAM + 16 GB RAM: The developers' claimed minimum hardware requirements.

MiniMax H3: AI video generation powered by the 8-step VDN-H3 model.

ComfyUI integration: Generate and customize videos through familiar workflows.

LoRA support: Customize generation with community LoRAs.

First and last frame control: Guide how your videos begin and end.

Multimodal references: Use images, videos, and audio as references.

Windows installer: Automatically installs the environment and downloads the necessary models.

Local processing: Generate videos on your own hardware.

But how fast is it really?

The developers published some interesting benchmarks.

For a 10-second video at 1344×768 resolution on Windows:

RTX 5090 (32 GB VRAM): 122 seconds

RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB VRAM): 486 seconds

RTX 4060 Ti (16 GB VRAM): 558 seconds

So yes, we're talking about roughly eight minutes to generate ten seconds of video on an RTX 5060 Ti.

Not exactly real-time generation.

But here's an important detail.

The developers also report 13.8 seconds per sampling step for an 8 GB VRAM and 16 GB RAM configuration.

There's a catch: That measurement was performed on an NVIDIA H200 with artificially restricted memory, not an actual consumer 8 GB graphics card.

A complete end-to-end benchmark for the minimum 8 GB VRAM + 16 GB RAM configuration hasn't been published in the official documentation.

So treat the minimum requirements as a promising technical claim, not a guarantee of practical performance on every home PC.

How does FreeVideo make this possible?

Under the hood, it uses Video DeltaNet's hybrid attention architecture and an adaptive execution engine.

Instead of trying to squeeze the entire model into GPU memory, FreeVideo distributes model weights across VRAM, system RAM, and disk, loading what it needs during generation.

And that's what makes this project interesting.

AI video generation is gradually moving from expensive cloud infrastructure to hardware people already own.

It might take several minutes to generate a short clip today.

But running a sophisticated video model locally on a relatively modest GPU is a significant step toward making AI video production more accessible.

And unlike paying per generation through an API, local inference doesn't come with a per-video cloud bill.

Your GPU does the work.

Your electricity bill gets the invoice.

items.videoDescription:
Remember when AI assistants were just little text boxes on our screens?

Well, apparently, that wasn't human enough.

Meet Echo by Realbotix, a humanoid robot with realistic silicone skin, facial expressions, and AI-powered conversations.

And yes, you can now preorder one.

For approximately $85,000.

Finally, ChatGPT can tell you "I understand how you feel" while looking directly into your eyes.

Here's what Realbotix is offering:

Humanlike appearance: Realistic silicone skin, animated facial expressions, and natural-looking movements.

Four personalities: Choose between Aria, Mila, Dave, and Amar, each with a different appearance, voice, and character.

AI conversations: Advertised compatibility with ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini.

Personalized interactions: Adjust your robot's personality and conversational behavior.

Two sizes: A tabletop companion or a full-size humanoid with articulated fingers.

But here's where things get really interesting.

Meet Vinci Vision, a $24,950 upgrade that gives your robot something resembling social awareness.

According to Realbotix, Vinci can:

Recognize familiar faces.

Maintain eye contact during conversations.

Track behavior and engagement.

Interpret facial expressions and emotional cues.

Adapt its interactions based on what it sees.

So now your chatbot won't just give you a questionable answer.

It can also watch your facial expression change while you're reading it.

Wonderful.

Of course, accurately identifying someone's emotions from facial expressions is a difficult scientific problem. Realbotix hasn't published independent validation of Vinci's emotional recognition accuracy.

But at least we know exactly how much the attempt costs.

Let's talk money.

Tabletop Echo: $11,950

Full-body Echo: $59,950

Vinci Vision upgrade: $24,950

Full-body Echo + Vinci: $84,900

Required Vinci AI subscription: $199 per month

Preorder deposit: $199

Without Vinci, AI subscriptions start at $19.99 per month.

And what exactly does your $85,000 robot do?

Primarily, it talks, listens, makes facial expressions, maintains eye contact, and interacts with people.

Walking around your house and doing the dishes? Not part of the advertised package.

So think less "robot butler" and more "very expensive AI conversation partner."

Realbotix plans to manufacture just 250 Echo robots in 2027:

225 tabletop units and 25 full-body versions.

Deliveries are expected to begin in the second half of 2027, initially in the United States.

And here's what I find fascinating.

We've spent years trying to make chatbots sound more human.

Now we're putting those chatbots inside machines that look increasingly human, too.

But does an AI actually become more understanding just because it has a face?

Or are we simply making it easier for humans to believe that it understands us?

That's a much more interesting question than whether a silicone robot can smile convincingly.

Although I suspect the first customers will come up with some rather creative applications long before the user manual catches up.

The future of AI companionship is here.

It has a face.

It has a personality.

And naturally, it has a monthly subscription.

items.title: Alef Model A: The $300,000 Flying Car That Turns 90° in Midair | FAA Approved for Testing
items.excerpt: We've been promised flying cars for decades. And somehow, we've finally reached the point where someone is actually building one. Meet the Alef Model A, a $300,000 electric flying car designed to drive on ordinary roads,
items.videoDescription:
We've been promised flying cars for decades.

And somehow, we've finally reached the point where someone is actually building one.

Meet the Alef Model A, a $300,000 electric flying car designed to drive on ordinary roads, take off vertically, and transform itself into an aircraft.

And its engineering is wonderfully bizarre.

Here's how it works.

The Model A looks like a futuristic sports car. But underneath its carbon-fiber mesh body are eight hidden propellers.

When it's time to fly, the vehicle takes off vertically, like a giant quadcopter.

And then comes the really interesting part.

The entire body is designed to rotate 90 degrees sideways.

Suddenly, the car's body becomes a set of aerodynamic wings.

Meanwhile, the passenger cabin uses a gimbal mechanism to stay upright.

Yes, the car turns sideways. You don't.

Here are the planned specifications:

Eight electric propellers: Hidden inside the vehicle's body.

Vertical takeoff and landing: No runway required.

200 miles (320 km) of driving range: According to the manufacturer's targets.

110 miles (177 km) of flight range: Also a manufacturer estimate.

Compact dimensions: Designed to fit into ordinary garages and parking spaces.

Emergency parachute: A ballistic recovery system designed for the entire vehicle.

Redundant systems: Multiple propulsion and control components intended to improve safety.

And here's where things get interesting.

Alef has already received an FAA Special Airworthiness Certificate.

But there's an important distinction.

This was experimental flight authorization for its prototype, not full certification for unrestricted commercial passenger flights.

The company has demonstrated actual vertical flights, including footage of its prototype flying over a Tesla Cybertruck and a Roadster.

The full sideways transition and advertised range still need broader public validation.

And there's another rather amusing connection.

Alef is backed by Tim Draper, one of Tesla's early investors.

Apparently, investing in electric cars wasn't ambitious enough. Now he wants them to fly.

So how much does the future cost?

Expected price: $299,999

Regular preorder deposit: $150

Priority reservation: $1,500

Reported reservations: More than 3,600

First limited deliveries: Targeted for late 2026

Production expansion: Planned for 2027

Those first deliveries are expected to involve a small number of hand-built vehicles used under controlled testing conditions, not mass-market flying cars.

And yes, there's still the minor problem of aviation regulations, permitted takeoff locations, and figuring out where thousands of these things would actually fly.

But here's what I love about this project.

For decades, flying cars have existed mainly in science fiction.

The Fifth Element. Blade Runner. The Jetsons.

Now someone is genuinely trying to build a vehicle that drives to your destination until the road gets inconvenient, then takes to the air.

Will it become practical everyday transportation?

That's still very much an open question.

But watching an electric car lift off the ground and fly over another car is already a pretty remarkable sight.

The future is looking interesting.

And apparently, parking is about to become a three-dimensional problem.

items.title: Redshift 2027.0 Is Here! Procedural Fur, ACES 2, Faster GPU Rendering & Archicad
items.excerpt: Maxon just released Redshift 2027.0, and this update brings some genuinely useful improvements for 3D artists. New procedural fur, better GPU memory management, faster rendering, improved real-time previews, and expanded
items.videoDescription:
Maxon just released Redshift 2027.0, and this update brings some genuinely useful improvements for 3D artists.

New procedural fur, better GPU memory management, faster rendering, improved real-time previews, and expanded support for professional 3D applications.

And apparently, rendering fur no longer needs to involve quite so much suffering.

Here's what's new.

1. Procedural Fur Object

Redshift now includes a native procedural system for generating fur, hair-like fibers, grass, and textile surfaces.

Instead of building enormous amounts of geometry manually, you can generate these details at render time.

The system provides controls for density, length, gravity, curl, taper, and randomization.

It also supports motion blur, instancing, UV mapping, and Redshift materials.

Think fuzzy fabrics, carpets, upholstery, grass, and product visualization.

All without turning your scene into a terrifying collection of individual hair meshes.

2. Better GPU Memory Management

This is probably one of the most important improvements under the hood.

Redshift 2027 introduces a redesigned VRAM management system with more efficient memory allocation, improved resource sharing, and better support for unified memory.

It can also load scenes across multiple GPUs in parallel.

And Maxon reports rendering improvements of up to 15% in a tested architectural scene.

That's not a universal 15% speed boost for every project, of course.

Actual results will depend on your scene, hardware, and rendering configuration.

But faster scene loading and improved responsiveness are always welcome.

3. ACES 2 Color Management

Redshift now supports ACES 2, the updated color management standard used in professional film and VFX pipelines.

This provides a more modern foundation for consistent color reproduction and interoperability across applications.

Cinema 4D now uses the ACES 2 OCIO configuration by default, while other supported applications can configure it manually.

4. Redshift Live Gets More Realistic

The real-time rendering engine has received several improvements:

Ray-traced depth of field

Improved refraction through transparent materials

Transparent shadows

Area light spread

Faster shader compilation

The goal is simple: make the interactive preview look closer to the final render.

Which means fewer surprises after you've spent an hour getting the lighting just right.

5. Native tyFlow Inferno Support in 3ds Max

For VFX artists, Redshift now supports tyFlow Inferno volumetric simulations.

That means improved integration for rendering fire, smoke, and other volumetric effects directly within the 3ds Max workflow.

There's also a dedicated Redshift tyFlow modifier to simplify volume shading.

6. Redshift Comes to Archicad

Architectural visualization artists get another interesting addition.

Redshift for Architects now supports Graphisoft Archicad through a native plugin.

Architects can preview materials, adjust lighting, and create photorealistic renderings without constantly exporting their models into another application.

And when a project needs more sophisticated animation or cinematic presentation, it can move into Cinema 4D.

So what's the bigger picture?

Redshift 2027 isn't just about adding another fancy rendering feature.

It's about improving the everyday workflow.

Less geometry management.

More responsive previews.

Better memory utilization.

More consistent colors.

And fewer unnecessary trips between applications.

For motion designers, VFX artists, and architectural visualization studios, those improvements can matter more than another spectacular demo scene.

Because the most valuable renderer isn't necessarily the one that produces the prettiest image.

It's the one that helps you produce that image without spending the rest of your life watching a progress bar.

Redshift 2027.0 was released on October 14, 2026.

items.title: HyperFlow H3 Flash: 14B AI Video Model Generates Video + Audio in Just 6 Steps!
items.excerpt: What if you could shrink a 31-billion-parameter AI video model to just 14B, cut generation to six steps, and keep synchronized stereo audio? Well, VIDEO REBIRTH just did exactly that. Meet HyperFlow H3 Flash, a compresse
items.videoDescription:
What if you could shrink a 31-billion-parameter AI video model to just 14B, cut generation to six steps, and keep synchronized stereo audio?

Well, VIDEO REBIRTH just did exactly that.

Meet HyperFlow H3 Flash, a compressed, few-step version of MiniMax-H3 designed to make high-quality AI video generation faster and more accessible.

And unlike many video models, it generates video and stereo audio together.

No separate audio generation pipeline. No manually synchronizing sound effects afterward.

Here's what makes it interesting.

1. A 54% smaller transformer

The original MiniMax-H3 uses approximately 31 billion parameters.

HyperFlow H3 Flash reduces that to:

13.7B parameters for text-to-video and keyframe-guided generation.

13.9B parameters for reference-to-video.

The developers achieve this through structural pruning and low-rank factorization.

2. Just six generation steps

Instead of the usual dozens of denoising steps, HyperFlow offers three presets:

4 steps: Faster generation.

6 steps: Balanced default.

8 steps: Higher-quality output.

All with CFG set to 1.0.

That's a serious reduction in computational work.

3. Video AND stereo audio

The model produces 1344 × 768 video at 24 FPS, with synchronized 32 kHz stereo audio.

Supported clip lengths range from approximately 5 to 15 seconds.

4. And yes, there's a real-time configuration

According to VIDEO REBIRTH, its NVIDIA SOL-H3 integration supports real-time inference on a cluster of four Blackwell accelerators.

For a 5.2-second clip at six steps, the published benchmarks show:

4 × B200: 8.7 seconds

1 × H200: 36 seconds

RTX 5090: 92 seconds

RTX 4090: 152 seconds

RTX 3090: 315 seconds

So no, your RTX 4090 isn't suddenly generating cinematic video in real time.

But it's getting more practical.

5. Consumer GPU support with GGUF

The model is available in INT8 and GGUF formats.

The Q4_K_M transformer checkpoint is approximately 9.1 GB, making it suitable for optimized local workflows.

The developers provide ComfyUI integrations for 24 GB GPUs, including RTX 3090 and RTX 4090.

Just remember that the 9.1 GB figure is the transformer file size, not the total GPU or system memory requirement. You'll also need the text encoder and video/audio decoders.

6. Four creative workflows

HyperFlow H3 Flash supports:

Text-to-video

Image-to-video

First-and-last-frame animation

Reference-to-video

You can use reference images to guide a scene, or work with video and audio references through the Python implementation.

And here's the bigger picture.

We're watching open-weight video models become smaller, faster, and considerably more flexible.

Instead of relying entirely on enormous cloud models, artists are getting increasingly capable local workflows.

Of course, there's a catch.

The model weights use the MiniMax H3 Community License, not an unrestricted open-source license. Downloading and using them in the EU, UK, US, or South Korea requires prior authorization from MiniMax.

So check the terms before installing.

Still, reducing a model this large to six sampling steps while preserving joint audio-video generation is a significant technical achievement.

The future of AI video might not just be bigger models.

It might be making the existing ones dramatically more efficient.

Model weights and benchmarks:
https://huggingface.co/VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash

GitHub, installation and ComfyUI workflows:

items.title: What If Claude Existed in 1998? Windows 95 Meets Volkov Commander
items.excerpt: What if Claude had been released in 1998? Before cloud computing. Before AI agents. Before everyone decided that every application needed a browser-based interface. Meet Claude '98, an imaginary version of Anthropic's AI
items.videoDescription:
What if Claude had been released in 1998?

Before cloud computing. Before AI agents. Before everyone decided that every application needed a browser-based interface.

Meet Claude '98, an imaginary version of Anthropic's AI assistant, designed in the glorious style of Windows 95 and Volkov Commander.

Blue panels. Gray dialog boxes. Pixel fonts. Keyboard shortcuts.

And absolutely no rounded corners.

The future of artificial intelligence, as imagined by someone who just installed Windows 95 from 13 floppy disks.

Forget fancy dashboards and animated sidebars.

In 1998, we had everything we needed:

A proper two-panel file manager.

Function keys that actually did something.

Dialog boxes with suspiciously serious buttons.

A 56K modem connecting us to the future.

And the comforting possibility of a fatal exception at any moment.

Now imagine running Claude inside that environment.

Claude: How can I help you today?

Me: Build an autonomous AI agent.

Claude: Please insert Disk 2.

Honestly, there's something strangely satisfying about combining modern AI with old-school computer interfaces.

Maybe it's nostalgia.

Maybe it's the simplicity.

Or maybe we just miss the days when software looked like software instead of a collection of floating glass rectangles.

Welcome to 1998. The AI revolution has arrived 28 years early.

And yes, I'd probably use this interface every day.

Retro interface concept inspired by Windows 95 and Volkov Commander. Not an official Anthropic product.
