items.excerpt: Think you know what's running inside your Claude Code sessions? You might be surprised. Meet /stack, a free, open-source Claude Code mod that reveals practically everything installed, configured, and available in your AI
items.videoDescription:
Think you know what's running inside your Claude Code sessions?

You might be surprised.

Meet /stack, a free, open-source Claude Code mod that reveals practically everything installed, configured, and available in your AI coding environment.

And if you're using Claude Code regularly, this is one tool worth checking out.

Here's what /stack shows you:

Skills: Every installed skill and where it comes from

Subagents: Available AI agents and their configurations

Commands: Built-in and custom slash commands

Hooks: Scripts and automation running during your sessions

MCP servers: Connected external tools and integrations

Plugins and mods: Additional features installed in Claude Code

Settings and memory: Configuration and context files affecting behavior

Output styles: Custom instructions controlling how Claude responds

Everything appears in an interactive dashboard, organized by configuration scope: Enterprise, User, Project, Local, Plugin, and CLI flags.

But here's where it gets really useful.

You can see what's actually active, what's disabled, and what's being overridden by another configuration.

Ever wondered why Claude suddenly behaves differently between projects?

Or why your sessions seem to consume so many tokens?

Or which MCP servers, skills, and instructions are actually being loaded?

/stack helps you investigate what's happening under the hood.

And there's another interesting bonus.

You can explore built-in Claude Code commands, skills, and subagents, including components you might never have noticed in the documentation.

Install /stack:

npx claude-code-templates@latest --mod ui/stack-viewer

Then open Claude Code and run:

/stack

The mod scans your environment and displays the results in an interactive side panel.

It's a configuration inspector, not a direct token profiler, but understanding what's loaded is an excellent starting point for troubleshooting bloated or unpredictable sessions.

Because sometimes the problem isn't the AI model. It's the enormous stack of things you've quietly installed around it.

Save this one. You'll probably need it.

Gemini 4 Carbon just turned historical photographs and engineering blueprints into an interactive 3D reconstruction of the Eiffel Tower's construction from 1887 to 1889. All starting from a single prompt.

And it wasn't working alone.

Using Google's new /swarm feature in Antigravity, a team of Gemini 4 Carbon agents collaborated to build an interactive Three.js exhibition.

Here's what makes this experiment interesting:

• One prompt: the entire multi-agent workflow was initiated with a single instruction.

• Historical reconstruction: original photographs and engineering drawings provided the reference material.

• Multi-agent collaboration: Google's /swarm system coordinates specialized AI agents working on different parts of a complex project.

• Interactive 3D: the result is a Three.js experience, not just a collection of AI-generated images or a prerecorded animation.

• 1887–1889: the exhibition recreates the construction period of one of the world's most recognizable engineering landmarks.

The bigger story is agentic development.

Instead of asking AI to generate an image of the Eiffel Tower, Google demonstrated a system where multiple AI agents collaborate to transform historical source material into an interactive software experience.

Could AI agent swarms become the next major tool for 3D reconstruction, interactive museums, digital heritage, and creative coding?

items.excerpt: What if AI could reverse the rendering process? Meet Unrender, a wonderfully strange AI tool that takes a finished video and turns it into something resembling an untextured 3D playblast. No materials. No realistic light
items.videoDescription:
What if AI could reverse the rendering process?

Meet Unrender, a wonderfully strange AI tool that takes a finished video and turns it into something resembling an untextured 3D playblast.

No materials. No realistic lighting. Just that beautiful grey clay-render aesthetic every 3D artist knows.

And you don't even need to open Blender.

Created by JP Costa, Unrender takes an ordinary video and transforms it into a simulated 3D viewport render.

Here's how it works:

• Video to fake playblast: upload a finished shot and get back a grey, untextured version.

• AI-powered transformation: the tool runs on Comfy infrastructure, with Kling reportedly used in the video generation workflow.

• No 3D software required: no Blender, Maya, or Unreal Engine needed.

• Up to 10 seconds: supports MP4, MOV, and WebM files, processing the first 10 seconds of longer clips.

• Still image support: JPG, PNG, and WebP images are also accepted.

• Free test: one complimentary run per email, subject to availability.

• Bring your own API key: connect your Comfy API key for additional generations using your own credits.

But here's the funny part.

Unrender doesn't actually reconstruct your scene in 3D.

There's no editable geometry, no 3D mesh, no camera rig, and no scene file to export.

You simply get another video that LOOKS like a traditional CG playblast.

So what's the practical use?

Maybe creating fake VFX breakdowns, experimenting with reverse-render aesthetics, or producing behind-the-scenes-style visual effects.

Or maybe it's just an entertaining technical experiment.

Either way, it's an interesting reversal of the usual AI video workflow.

Everyone is trying to turn rough 3D scenes into photorealistic videos.

Unrender takes the photorealistic video and turns it back into the rough-looking version.

https://www.unrender.app/

Created by JP Costa:
https://x.com/jp_costa

items.title: Tesseract by Mirage: Claude Can Now Create Photorealistic 3D Videos Without Diffusion!
items.excerpt: What if the future of AI video generation isn't actually video generation? What if, instead of asking a diffusion model to hallucinate thousands of pixels across hundreds of frames, we simply let an AI agent build a real
items.videoDescription:
What if the future of AI video generation isn't actually video generation?
What if, instead of asking a diffusion model to hallucinate thousands of pixels across hundreds of frames, we simply let an AI agent build a real 3D scene and render it?
Well, Mirage just demonstrated exactly that.
Meet Tesseract, a creative engine designed specifically for AI agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and ChatGPT.
And this might be one of the most interesting developments in AI-assisted filmmaking.

Mirage, the company behind Captions, has built something fundamentally different from traditional text-to-video generators.
Tesseract doesn't generate a finished video by predicting what every frame should look like. It gives an AI agent the tools to construct an editable scene, control its components, and render the result using a native graphics engine.
Here's how Tesseract works.
The system combines two main components:
Tesseract Runtime: A native creative engine accessed through a command-line tool called tsrct.
Agent Skills: Specialized instructions that teach AI agents how to create videos, motion graphics, 3D scenes, and visual designs.
The agent doesn't need to click through hundreds of menus in Blender, Unreal Engine, or After Effects.
Instead, you describe what you want in natural language.

For example:
"Create a cinematic nighttime kitchen. Rain is falling outside, the floor is reflective, and the camera slowly moves toward the window."
Your agent translates that brief into a structured Tesseract project.
And here's the critical difference: the project remains editable.

Inside the .tsrct document, the agent can control:
3D geometry: Objects, meshes, shapes, and their spatial relationships.
Materials: Physically based surfaces, roughness, reflections, and transparency.
Lighting: Individual lights, shadows, and atmospheric effects.
Cameras: Position, focal length, movement, and animation.
Timeline: Keyframes, animation curves, layers, and transitions.
Audio: Sound effects, dialogue, music, and synchronization.

Version 0.5.0 introduced editable 3D scenes, polygon modeling, physically based materials, camera animation, and path-traced rendering.

The engine supports both:
Raster rendering: Faster previews for checking composition, camera movement, and animation.
GPU path tracing: Higher-quality offline rendering with realistic reflections, indirect illumination, refraction, and shadows.
And here's where the story gets particularly interesting.

Now we're giving AI agents the ability to understand and manipulate the scenes behind those pixels. The difference between generating an image of a world and actually constructing that world.

items.excerpt: What if physics textbooks weren't just pages of formulas and static diagrams? What if you could actually step inside the illustrations, experiment with physical forces, and discover how the world works? Meet Every Joule,
items.videoDescription:
What if physics textbooks weren't just pages of formulas and static diagrams?

What if you could actually step inside the illustrations, experiment with physical forces, and discover how the world works?

Meet Every Joule, a beautiful interactive 3D physics textbook created by developer @techartist_ using Claude Opus 5.5 and Three.js.

And honestly, this is the kind of educational technology I'd love to see everywhere.

Instead of simply reading about energy, students can interact with animated 3D models, change variables, make predictions, and see what happens.

The project covers 10 physics lessons, including:

Kinetic and potential energy: Explore how objects store and transfer energy.

Springs and elastic energy: Experiment with stretching, compression, and movement.

Bouncing balls: Discover where the energy goes when an object gradually stops bouncing.

Heat and insulation: Explore how energy moves through materials.

Power and efficiency: Understand how different systems convert and transfer energy.

Power stations: Follow energy from electricity generation to everyday devices.

Conservation of energy: See how energy changes form without simply disappearing.

And here's what makes it special.

The illustrations literally rise out of the pages as interactive 3D objects.

Energy flows through glowing visual pathways.

Students can predict an outcome, test their ideas, and reveal the explanation.

It's not just a digital textbook with prettier graphics.

It's an interactive learning environment built around experimentation.

And the entire experience runs in a web browser using Three.js.

No expensive educational hardware. No complicated installation.

Just a browser, a modern graphics engine, and AI-assisted development.

But here's what I find most interesting.

The developer used Claude Opus 5.5 to help transform educational content into interactive software.

Imagine applying this approach to chemistry, biology, astronomy, engineering, or mathematics.

Instead of asking students to memorize how a mechanism works, let them take it apart.

Instead of describing an experiment, let them perform it virtually.

Instead of explaining a physical phenomenon with a static illustration, let them change the conditions and observe the consequences.

Of course, interactive simulations still need scientifically accurate models and thoughtful educational design.

But imagine if every textbook looked like this.

We spend so much time discussing how AI will change education through personalized tutors and chatbots.

Maybe one of its most exciting contributions will be something much simpler.

Making knowledge something you can actually explore.

And personally, I think that's a far more interesting future than another AI assistant summarizing the same textbook.

items.excerpt: What if you could create a fully rigged and animated 3D creature in less than an hour? Not just a pretty 3D model. An actual character with a skeleton, swimming animations, and a convincing bite. This entire shark was cr
items.videoDescription:
What if you could create a fully rigged and animated 3D creature in less than an hour?

Not just a pretty 3D model. An actual character with a skeleton, swimming animations, and a convincing bite.

This entire shark was created using AI tools. And the whole process took just 45 minutes.

Here's how it was made.

Step 1: Generate the shark

Tripo AI created the original 3D mesh and skeletal rig.

Step 2: Bring it to life

Claude Opus 5.5 connected to Blender through MCP and procedurally created the idle and swimming animations.

No manually keyframing every movement.

Step 3: Make it bite

This is where things get really interesting.

Instead of manually animating the attack:

Claude rendered the rigged shark against a green background with tracking markers.

Gemini Omni 1.1 generated a reference video of the shark performing a bite.

Claude analyzed the generated motion and recreated it on the actual 3D rig inside Blender.

The result? An animated 3D shark with reusable, editable movements.

And the numbers are pretty impressive:

45 minutes from start to finish

7% of the weekly AI usage quota

Three AI-powered tools working together

A complete 3D character animation workflow

Of course, it's not perfect yet. Motion reconstruction, rigging, and procedural animation still have limitations.

But the interesting part is what this workflow represents.

AI-generated video is no longer just the final output. It can become a motion reference for creating actual 3D animation.

And unlike a flat generated video, the resulting Blender scene can be further edited, refined, and reused.

Imagine what this means for indie game developers, animators, and small creative studios.

From an idea to an animated 3D creature in 45 minutes.

We're getting remarkably close to a world where creating digital characters becomes more about creative direction than manual production.

items.title: Vercel Agent Desktop: AI Agents Can Control Your Mac Without Screenshots | Claude & Codex
items.excerpt: What if your AI agents could use your entire computer without constantly taking screenshots, analyzing pixels, and moving your mouse around? And what if multiple agents could work while you continued using your computer?
items.videoDescription:
What if your AI agents could use your entire computer without constantly taking screenshots, analyzing pixels, and moving your mouse around?

And what if multiple agents could work while you continued using your computer?

Meet agent-desktop, a new open-source project from Vercel Labs that brings the efficient approach of agent-browser to desktop automation.

And this could be a significant improvement for AI computer use.

Here's the problem.

Traditional computer-use agents often behave like humans.

They take a screenshot, analyze the image, figure out where to click, move the mouse, and repeat.

It works, but the process can be slow, expensive, and surprisingly fragile.

Agent Desktop takes a different approach.

Instead of relying on screenshots, it reads the operating system's native accessibility tree.

That gives AI agents structured information about what's actually on your screen:

Buttons and menus: Identify interactive elements directly.

Text fields: Read and modify supported interface elements.

Windows and applications: Navigate between desktop apps.

Stable element references: Interact with specific controls instead of guessing pixel coordinates.

Structured JSON: Give AI agents compact, machine-readable interface information.

And here's where things get really interesting.

Agent Desktop supports headless interactions.

That means supported actions can run through accessibility APIs without moving your physical mouse pointer or stealing focus.

Your AI agent can work in the background while you keep using your computer.

And there's more.

Multiple agents can share the same desktop environment.

Each agent can have its own visual cursor overlay, making it possible to see where different agents are working.

These are virtual cursor indicators, not independent physical mouse pointers. Operations requiring real mouse input are coordinated to avoid conflicts.

But the possibilities are fascinating.

Imagine one agent inspecting a spreadsheet while another works with your development tools, and a third handles a desktop application.

All coordinated through structured interfaces rather than endless screenshots.

Why does this matter?

Because computer use has been one of the most expensive and unreliable parts of AI automation.

Reading structured interface data instead of repeatedly processing screenshots could significantly reduce the amount of information an agent needs to handle.

And make desktop automation more predictable.

What else is included?

Native Rust implementation

Support for macOS, Windows, and Linux

CLI and C library interfaces

Integration with AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex

Session management, traces, and verification tools

Optional screenshots for visual workflows

Open-source Apache 2.0 license

Install Agent Desktop:

npm install -g agent-desktop

Check the installation:

agent-desktop version

On macOS, enable the required Accessibility permissions:

agent-desktop permissions --guide

You can also install the agent skill:

npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop

Of course, accessibility-based automation has limitations. Some applications don't expose every interface element, and certain actions may still require traditional mouse input or screenshots.

And desktop automation still requires carefully managed permissions, especially when agents can access sensitive applications.

But the direction is extremely interesting.

We're moving from AI agents that watch your computer to AI agents that understand its interface.

And maybe the future of computer use isn't teaching AI to click faster.

It's teaching AI that clicking like a human was never the best approach in the first place.

https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop

Official documentation:
https://agent-browser.dev/desktop

items.title: DeepSeek Creator Mode: Build Your Own AI Agent Interface Just by Prompting
items.excerpt: What if your AI assistant could redesign its own interface whenever you wanted? Not just change the colors. Actually build new tools, install them as plugins, and integrate them directly into the application. Meet Creato
items.videoDescription:
What if your AI assistant could redesign its own interface whenever you wanted?

Not just change the colors.

Actually build new tools, install them as plugins, and integrate them directly into the application.

Meet Creator Mode for DeepSeek Harness, a new feature that lets users customize their AI agent workspace using natural language.

And this is a genuinely interesting direction for agentic software.

Here's the idea.

Back in August, DeepSeek introduced its open-source agent harness, built around one simple philosophy:

Everything is a plugin.

Instead of treating the interface as a fixed product, DeepSeek designed an extensible system where functionality can be added through plugins.

Now Creator Mode takes that idea even further.

You describe what you want. The agent builds it.

It can write the plugin code, integrate the new interface components, and install the functionality directly into your running workspace.

And the demonstrations are pretty wild.

DeepSeek has published seven example prompts showing what Creator Mode can build:

Video editor: Create a video editing workspace with a preview window, timeline, clip editing, and natural-language controls.

Custom interface themes: Redesign the entire application's appearance, including a pixel-art theme.

Conversation analytics: Build a dashboard showing token usage, estimated costs, conversation statistics, and CPU activity.

Interactive 3D visualizations: Create a gallery of famous landmarks or explore how a Transformer processes information.

Poster designer: Generate a custom visual design tool with editable typography and shader backgrounds.

Scientific paper reader: Build a document viewer with highlighting, annotations, and chat integration.

And here's the most fascinating part.

These aren't separate websites your AI creates and then forgets about.

They're plugins designed to become part of the agent's own working environment.

Want a new sidebar? Describe it.

Need a specialized dashboard? Ask for one.

Don't like the interface? Change it.

Your AI harness is no longer just a tool you use. It's a tool you can continuously redesign.

Of course, that doesn't mean every idea will work perfectly from a single prompt.

DeepSeek explicitly notes that several demonstrated plugins required multiple iterations to reach their final state.

And automatically generated plugins still need testing, particularly when they have access to files, tools, or sensitive information.

But the broader concept is compelling.

We're moving from customizable AI assistants to AI assistants that can customize themselves.

And that raises an interesting question.

Why should every user have the same interface when an AI agent could build the workspace that best fits their actual needs?

The next generation of AI software might not have a fixed interface at all.

Just capabilities, plugins, and whatever you decide to create.

items.title: MiniMax H3 + 360 Orbit LoRA Turns AI Video Into 3D Gaussian Splats | Houdini 22
items.excerpt: What if you could turn a single image into a 3D scene without manually modeling anything? Not by directly generating a mesh. By making an AI video model invent the missing camera angles, then reconstructing the scene in
items.videoDescription:
What if you could turn a single image into a 3D scene without manually modeling anything?

Not by directly generating a mesh.

By making an AI video model invent the missing camera angles, then reconstructing the scene in 3D.

And yes, this workflow actually exists.

Meet a fascinating experiment combining MiniMax H3, 360 Orbit LoRA, Gaussian Splatting, and Houdini 22.

The idea is surprisingly elegant.

Step 1: Generate a 360-degree camera orbit

Start with a reference image and use the 360 Orbit LoRA for MiniMax H3 to generate a video of the camera moving around the subject.

Instead of creating arbitrary motion, the LoRA encourages the model to keep the subject in place while the virtual camera changes its viewpoint.

Step 2: Turn the video into multiple views

Extract frames showing the subject from different angles.

These frames become the visual references for reconstructing a three-dimensional representation.

Step 3: Reconstruct the scene using Gaussian Splatting

This is where Houdini comes in.

Using ML Train GSplats in Houdini 22, the workflow trains a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation from a set of images and their corresponding camera positions.

Instead of building a conventional polygon mesh, Gaussian Splatting represents the scene using thousands of small, spatially arranged Gaussian primitives.

The result can be viewed from new angles inside a 3D environment.

And here's my favorite detail.

It's Houdini.

Not Blender.

No disrespect to Blender, but as someone who spent years around professional 3D production, there's something strangely satisfying about seeing modern AI workflows finding their way into Houdini.

Why is this interesting?

Because AI video generation is becoming more than a way to produce finished clips.

It can also become a source of synthetic multi-view data for 3D reconstruction.

One image becomes a camera orbit.

The orbit becomes a collection of views.

Those views become a 3D Gaussian Splat scene.

There is an important limitation, though.

An AI-generated camera orbit isn't the same as photographing a real object from every angle.

The model has to invent surfaces it cannot see, and inconsistencies between frames can affect the reconstruction.

Gaussian Splats also aren't automatically production-ready polygon meshes with clean topology, UVs, and rigging.

But as an experimental creative workflow?

It's a pretty fascinating combination of generative video and procedural 3D production.

From pixels to motion. From motion back into 3D.

And we've only just started exploring what these models can do beyond their original purpose.

items.title: Claude Can Now See Your Bank Account! | Anthropic Personal Finance + Plaid
items.excerpt: Remember when AI assistants were just answering questions, writing emails, and generating code? Well, apparently, now they want to know where all your money went. Meet Claude Personal Finance, a new feature from Anthropi
items.videoDescription:
Remember when AI assistants were just answering questions, writing emails, and generating code?

Well, apparently, now they want to know where all your money went.

Meet Claude Personal Finance, a new feature from Anthropic that lets you connect your actual bank accounts and ask Claude questions about your finances.

And yes, your AI assistant can finally tell you exactly how much money you've wasted this month.

Wonderful.

Here's how it works.

Anthropic has partnered with Plaid, the financial connectivity platform used by thousands of financial applications.

You choose which bank accounts to connect, authenticate directly through Plaid, and grant Claude read-only access to your financial information.

What can Claude actually do?

Track your spending: Find out where your money went this month.

Analyze transactions: Categorize expenses and identify spending patterns.

Monitor subscriptions: Discover recurring payments you may have forgotten about.

Check upcoming bills: See what's due before your next payday.

Plan your budget: Ask whether you can afford a vacation, a major purchase, or another subscription you probably don't need.

Spot unusual charges: Identify duplicate payments, unexpected fees, and suspicious spending patterns.

Create dashboards: Generate spending charts, cash flow summaries, and financial overviews.

And here's the interesting part.

Claude can read up to 24 months of transaction history from your connected accounts.

So you can ask something like:

"Claude, why did I spend so much money last month?"

And instead of receiving generic financial advice, it can actually examine your transactions.

Or:

"Can I afford a two-week trip to Turkey without destroying my family budget?"

Claude can look at your balances, upcoming payments, and spending history to help you estimate the impact.

Now for the obvious question.

Are we really comfortable giving an AI assistant access to our bank accounts?

Anthropic says the integration is strictly read-only.

According to the company:

Claude cannot transfer money between accounts.

It cannot make purchases or initiate payments.

It cannot execute investment trades.

It doesn't receive your banking passwords.

You can disconnect your accounts whenever you want.

And there's another privacy promise.

Anthropic says conversations inside the Personal Finance hub aren't used to train its AI models.

However, financial information shared with Claude outside that dedicated hub is subject to your regular privacy settings.

The connected data is also handled by Plaid and relevant service providers under their respective policies.

So while read-only access is a meaningful safeguard, connecting your finances still involves sharing sensitive information with additional services.

And there's one more catch.

Claude can make mistakes when interpreting financial data. Balances may be outdated, and missing accounts or duplicated transactions can distort the picture.

So don't fire your accountant just yet.

Availability:

Claude Personal Finance launched in beta on November 5, 2026.

It's gradually rolling out to:

Claude Pro

Claude Max

Claude Ultra

United States only, for now.

The feature works on the web, desktop, iOS, and Android, but isn't currently supported in Claude Code, scheduled tasks, or Claude Duet.

And here's what I find particularly interesting.

AI assistants are gradually moving from answering questions about the world to understanding our actual lives.

Our emails.

Our calendars.

Our work.

And now our bank accounts.

In theory, that could make personal financial planning considerably more accessible.

In practice, I'm looking forward to a conversation like this:

Me: "Claude, where's my money?"

Claude: "Well, according to your transactions, you spent $847 on AI subscriptions, $326 on API credits, and another $199 on a tool you opened once."

Me: "I understand. Please disconnect my bank immediately."

The future of personal finance is looking interesting.

And slightly judgmental.

items.title: Why Do Streetlights Look Like Stars? This Eye Simulator Shows You.
items.excerpt: Ever noticed how streetlights, car headlights, and distant stars turn into glowing halos, spikes, and strange patterns at night? Well, someone built a simulator that lets you explore exactly why that happens. Meet Engisc
items.videoDescription:
Ever noticed how streetlights, car headlights, and distant stars turn into glowing halos, spikes, and strange patterns at night?
Well, someone built a simulator that lets you explore exactly why that happens.

Meet Engiscope, an interactive browser-based tool that simulates how light behaves as it passes through the human eye.
And it's surprisingly mesmerizing.

Here's what you can experiment with:
- Pupil size: See how changing the opening of your eye affects light patterns
- Eyeglass prescription: Adjust sphere, cylinder, and astigmatism axis
- Eyelashes and eyelids: Discover how they create distinctive light streaks
- Optical aberrations: Experiment with distortions, halos, and starbursts
- Chromatic aberration: Watch different colors of light separate
- Night scenes: Explore simulated glare from bright lights in darkness

The simulator uses optical calculations, including something called the point spread function (PSF), to model how a tiny point of light spreads into patterns.
It's not a medical diagnostic tool or a perfect reproduction of your individual vision, but it's a fascinating way to explore the physics behind what we see.
And the best part?
You can change the parameters and watch the results evolve.
Turns out, your eyes have been doing procedural light effects long before computer graphics existed.

Try Engiscope yourself:
https://graycrawford.com/engiscope

items.videoDescription:
What if one of the most powerful AI video models could become an incredibly fast image generator?

Not by simply asking it to generate a single frame.

By rebuilding its architecture specifically for image generation.

Meet P-H3-Image, a new open-weight AI image generation and editing model from Pruna AI, built on top of MiniMax H3 Video.

And the engineering behind it is fascinating.

Here's the idea.

When an AI model learns to generate videos, it also learns something about how the visual world works.

Objects from different angles. Changing perspectives. Lighting. Movement. Spatial relationships.

So why not take that knowledge and use it to generate better still images?

That's exactly what Pruna decided to explore.

But they didn't just modify the output format.

They substantially redesigned the original model:

Smaller text encoder: Distilled the original 32B encoder into a 4B version.

Optimized transformer: Reduced the main processing architecture from 33B to 20B parameters.

New image decoder: Retrained the decoder to produce sharp single images instead of video frames.

8-step generation: Reduced the original 50 diffusion steps to just eight.

Smarter prompting: Added an automatic prompt enhancer based on Qwen3.5-9B.

Quantized weights: Reduced the smallest model download from 143 GB to approximately 20 GB.

And the performance numbers are pretty wild.

According to Pruna's benchmarks on an NVIDIA B200:

At 4 megapixels:

Original MiniMax H3: 12.4 seconds

P-H3-Image: 2.6 seconds

At 8 megapixels:

Original MiniMax H3: 30.6 seconds

P-H3-Image: 5.8 seconds

That's roughly 5× faster, with a much smaller memory footprint.

Of course, these are developer-reported measurements, not independent benchmarks.

And here's what P-H3-Image can actually do:

Text-to-image: Generate images from 2 to 16 megapixels.

Image editing: Modify existing images using natural-language instructions.

Multi-reference composition: Combine up to eight source images in a single scene.

Photorealistic visuals: Generate portraits, editorial photography, cinematic scenes, and realistic environments.

Creative styles: Produce illustrations, anime frames, drawings, prints, and graphic designs.

Local inference: Run the quantized model through ComfyUI.

Pruna recommends 8 MP as the sweet spot for image quality, although lower resolutions can be faster.

And yes, you can run it without a B200.

The smallest W4A8 configuration requires approximately 21 GB of VRAM for 8 MP generation.

That's still a substantial hardware requirement, but considerably more accessible than the original video model.

And here's another interesting detail.

P-H3-Image now has native ComfyUI support.

Starting with ComfyUI 0.44.0, released November 4, 2026, you can use the model without installing third-party custom nodes.

Pruna has also published ready-made workflows, quantized weights, and a Diffusers pipeline.

There are limitations, of course. Hands, small background figures, and fine details can still produce artifacts, especially at lower resolutions. Dense text remains unreliable.

And the model is open-weight under the MiniMax H3 Community License, not an unrestricted open-source license.

But here's what I find most interesting.

We're starting to see AI models being repurposed across different creative disciplines.

A video model becomes an image generator.

The knowledge learned from generating motion becomes useful for understanding still images.

And instead of training everything from scratch, developers can build on existing models, specialize them, compress them, and make them dramatically more efficient.

Pruna already explored a similar approach with Wan Image, based on Wan 2.1.

Now they've done it again with MiniMax H3.

Maybe the next big image model won't actually start as an image model at all.

And that's a pretty interesting direction for generative AI.

https://www.pruna.ai/blog/oss-p-h3-image-launch

Model weights and Diffusers:
https://huggingface.co/PrunaAI/P-H3-Image

ComfyUI weights and ready-made workflows:
https://huggingface.co/PrunaAI/P-H3-Image-Comfy

items.title: Do You Believe in Life After Death? This Interactive 3D Visualization Explores 130,000 Answers
items.excerpt: What happens after we die? It's one of humanity's oldest questions. And someone decided to turn 130,000 people's answers into an interactive 3D experience. Meet Life After Death?, a fascinating data visualization created
items.videoDescription:
What happens after we die?

It's one of humanity's oldest questions. And someone decided to turn 130,000 people's answers into an interactive 3D experience.

Meet Life After Death?, a fascinating data visualization created by Alvin Chang for The Pudding.

The project draws on survey responses from nearly 130,000 people across 23 countries, exploring how our beliefs about death, religion, and the afterlife differ across cultures and generations.

But instead of presenting another collection of boring charts, Chang built something much more interesting.

A virtual room filled with 1,500 people.

Each little character represents a real survey respondent, positioned according to their age and beliefs.

And the entire room is interactive.

Here's what you can explore:

Belief in the afterlife: See how people differ in what they believe happens after death.

Age and generations: Explore how beliefs vary across age groups.

Individual responses: Click on a character to learn more about their answers.

Interactive categories: Switch between survey questions and watch the characters change colors or move into new groups.

Global perspectives: Discover patterns across different countries and cultures.

The underlying research comes from the Global Flourishing Study, with additional historical context from international values surveys.

And here's what I find particularly beautiful about this project.

It turns statistics back into people.

Instead of looking at abstract percentages, you're surrounded by hundreds of tiny human figures, each representing someone with their own perspective on one of life's biggest mysteries.

It's part data journalism, part interactive art, and part philosophical exploration.

And a wonderful example of how creative coding and data visualization can make complex research feel surprisingly personal.

130,000 answers. 23 countries. One question nobody can definitively answer.

What do you believe?

Explore the interactive visualization:
https://pudding.cool/2026/10/lifeafter/

Created by Alvin Chang for The Pudding.

#DataVisualization #InteractiveArt #CreativeCoding #LifeAfterDeath #DataJournalism #Shorts

items.excerpt: You spent hours building your project. Now you need a video to show it off. What if Claude Code could handle that part too? Meet Brag, an open-source AI agent skill that turns your project into a polished promotional vid
items.videoDescription:
You spent hours building your project. Now you need a video to show it off.

What if Claude Code could handle that part too?

Meet Brag, an open-source AI agent skill that turns your project into a polished promotional video with a single command.

Here's what it does:

Analyzes your project to understand what you've built

Identifies the most interesting features and selling points

Creates a visual concept and promotional storyline

Produces animated motion graphics and transitions

Adds background music and sound effects

Renders a shareable MP4 video

Generates promotional copy for your product launch

All from one command: /brag

The standard workflow uses Hyperframes for video composition and rendering. There's also a lightweight /brag-slim version optimized for Claude Opus 5.5.

And it isn't limited to Claude Code. The skill also supports Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and other compatible coding agents.

Install it for Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add latent-spaces/brag
/plugin install brag@brag

Then open your project and run:

/brag

That's it. Your AI agent takes care of the creative workflow, from understanding your product to producing a launch-ready video.

Of course, you can still refine the result. But the fascinating part is how much of the production process can now be handled by the same AI agent that helped build the software.

First, AI helped us write the code. Now it wants to handle the marketing too.

At this rate, the only thing left for developers to do is pretend they're running a company.

Brag on GitHub:
https://github.com/latent-spaces/brag

items.title: StableGen: Generate Rigged 3D Characters Locally with AI | Free Blender Add-on
items.excerpt: What if you could describe a 3D character in a single prompt and get a textured, rigged model directly inside Blender? Without relying on expensive cloud-based 3D generation services? Meet StableGen, a free, open-source
items.videoDescription:
What if you could describe a 3D character in a single prompt and get a textured, rigged model directly inside Blender?

Without relying on expensive cloud-based 3D generation services?

Meet StableGen, a free, open-source Blender add-on that brings AI-powered 3D generation, texturing, and character rigging into your existing workflow.

And the best part? It works with AI models running on your own hardware.

Here's what StableGen can do:

Text to 3D: Generate textured 3D models from simple text descriptions.

Image to 3D: Turn reference images into actual 3D geometry.

Automatic rigging: Create character skeletons and skin weights using SkinTokens.

AI texturing: Generate detailed textures using SDXL, Qwen Image, and other supported models.

PBR materials: Create albedo, roughness, metallic, and normal maps.

Texture editing: Modify specific parts of a model without regenerating everything.

Animation support: Retarget existing FBX and BVH animations onto generated characters.

Game engine export: Export assets to Unity, Unreal Engine, Godot, or web-based 3D projects.

And here's how it works.

StableGen combines several specialized AI models through ComfyUI.

TRELLIS.2 generates the 3D mesh.

SkinTokens builds the character rig.

Diffusion models generate and refine the textures.

And Blender brings everything together into an editable 3D asset.

No need to manually switch between multiple AI generation websites.

But there's an important catch.

Running these models locally still requires a capable computer.

The developers recommend an NVIDIA GPU, with around 8GB of VRAM for SDXL texturing and 16GB or more for some advanced image models.

You'll also need Blender, ComfyUI, and enough disk space for the model weights.

And while automatic rigging is impressive, complex characters may still need manual cleanup before they're ready for production.

Still, this is a fascinating development for indie game creators, 3D artists, and anyone experimenting with AI-powered character creation.

We're moving from generating static 3D objects to creating assets that can actually be animated, edited, and used in games.

And increasingly, we can do it on our own machines.

From a text prompt to a rigged 3D character. Right inside Blender.

StableGen on GitHub:
https://github.com/sakalond/StableGen

Free and open source under GPL-3.0.

items.title: NVIDIA Open-H3 IC: AI Video Upscaling to 4K Without Face Drift
items.excerpt: NVIDIA just released Open-H3-Regenerate-2K-IC, an open-weight AI video refinement model that upgrades low-resolution MiniMax H3 videos to 2K and 4K while preserving faces, lip sync, text, and scene composition. And it ca
items.videoDescription:
NVIDIA just released Open-H3-Regenerate-2K-IC, an open-weight AI video refinement model that upgrades low-resolution MiniMax H3 videos to 2K and 4K while preserving faces, lip sync, text, and scene composition.

And it can generate the high-resolution result in just THREE diffusion steps.

This is NVIDIA Research's alternative to MiniMax's proprietary H3-Regenerate-2K API, with a fundamentally different approach to video consistency.

Traditional AI video refinement often adds impressive details but can subtly change faces, mouth movements, eyes, and even text between frames.

Open-H3-IC addresses this problem through In-Context generation.

Instead of repeatedly adding noise to the original video, it keeps a clean version of the source inside MiniMax H3's Ref2VA transformer.

The high-resolution video is then generated alongside that reference, allowing the model to continuously attend to the original footage.

Here's what's new:

• In-Context video refinement: the original video remains accessible to the transformer throughout generation.

• Better facial consistency: aims to preserve facial identity, expressions, eye details, and lip movements.

• Improved text preservation: reduces the risk of signs and lettering turning into unreadable artifacts.

• Native 4K output: supports 1080p, 2K (2560×1440), and 4K (3840×2160) regeneration.

• Three-step diffusion: the default up3 sampler uses only three transformer passes to refine the video.

• Latent-space upscaling: enlarges video representations before generating new high-resolution detail.

• Ref2VA architecture: combines a clean low-resolution reference with high-resolution target generation.

• Audio preservation: keeps the original video's soundtrack unchanged.

• Open implementation: NVIDIA has published inference code and model weights for local deployment.

• Flexible sampling: choose three, four, or eight diffusion steps depending on the workflow.

The real breakthrough isn't simply making AI videos sharper.

It's generating new detail while keeping the original video as a persistent reference.

For AI filmmakers and VFX artists, that could mean fewer unwanted facial changes, more reliable lip sync, and better consistency during high-resolution refinement.

But this isn't magic.

Face drift and other artifacts are reduced, not mathematically eliminated. The workflow also requires substantial GPU resources, and the model weights are subject to the MiniMax H3 Community License.

The frequently cited 5x speed comparison refers to NVIDIA's earlier Open-H3-Regenerate-2K model, not a separately validated benchmark for this new IC version.

https://nvlabs.github.io/Sana/Open-H3-Regenerate-2K/#ic

https://github.com/NVlabs/Sana/tree/sol-engine/models/Open-H3-Regenerate-2K/IC

Model weights:
https://huggingface.co/Efficient-Large-Model/Open-H3-Regenerate-2K-IC

items.videoDescription:
What if you could take a picture of an everyday object and instantly see what's inside?

Not with an X-ray. Not by physically taking it apart.

Just one photo and generative AI.

Meet Liquid Photos, an experimental AI-powered visual interface originally developed at AXL Venture Studio by Sasha Ivanov and his team.

And the demonstration looks absolutely fascinating.

Here's the idea.

Take a photo of a camera, watch, game controller, or another everyday object.

The AI analyzes the image and generates an interactive exploded view, visually separating the object into its individual components.

Imagine being able to:

Explore the apparent internal structure of everyday objects.

Pull components apart through an interactive interface.

Examine how different parts fit together.

Transform ordinary photographs into visual explanations.

Explore products without manually creating detailed 3D models.

And here's what makes it particularly interesting.

The system doesn't simply display a static AI-generated image.

It's part of a broader approach to interactive generative media, where photographs become experiences you can manipulate and explore.

Of course, there's an important limitation.

AI-generated exploded views aren't necessarily accurate engineering reconstructions.

The model can infer what might be inside an object, but the actual components and their arrangement may differ from reality.

Still, imagine the possibilities for education, product design, technical illustrations, e-commerce, and interactive storytelling.

Instead of reading a complicated explanation of how something works, you could explore a visual representation yourself.

We're moving from AI that generates pictures to AI that makes pictures interactive.

And I find that a considerably more interesting direction.

The project has since evolved into Liquid Interactive, with Liquid Photos available for early access.

items.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein vs Krea 3: Two New AI Image Models That Change the Game
items.excerpt: Two new AI image models just dropped. And they're approaching the same problem from completely different directions. Black Forest Labs released FLUX 3 Image Klein. Krea launched Krea 3. One focuses on powerful, affordabl
items.videoDescription:
Two new AI image models just dropped. And they're approaching the same problem from completely different directions.

Black Forest Labs released FLUX 3 Image Klein. Krea launched Krea 3.

One focuses on powerful, affordable image generation that can run on your own GPU.

The other is all about making professional image editing ridiculously fast.

And both are worth a closer look.

1. FLUX 3 Image Klein: Powerful AI That Runs on 8GB VRAM

Black Forest Labs just released a surprisingly capable 5.6-billion-parameter image model with open weights.

Here's what makes it interesting:

5.6B parameters: A relatively compact model for image generation and editing

Up to 4K output: High-resolution image generation, although quality may vary at larger sizes

10 reference images: Combine multiple visual references in one generation

Bounding box controls: Specify exactly where objects should appear

8GB VRAM: The INT8 version can run on consumer NVIDIA GPUs

Under 9 seconds: Generate a 1MP image on an RTX 4070 using the optimized 16-step model

From $0.009 per image: API pricing at 1K resolution

There's also a base model designed for fine-tuning and a distilled version optimized for faster inference.

One important detail: the weights use the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and businesses earning under $5 million annually, subject to its terms.

2. Krea 3: AI Image Editing in Under 8 Seconds

Meanwhile, Krea has introduced a new image model focused on something that matters enormously in actual creative workflows.

Editing existing images without ruining everything else.

Here's what Krea 3 offers:

Under 8 seconds: Most edits complete at native 2K resolution

6 reference images: Combine multiple visual references

Character consistency: Preserve faces and identities across edited scenes

Product preservation: Change backgrounds while keeping logos, labels, and details intact

Fast scene changes: Modify lighting, environments, materials, and composition

$0.03 per image at 1K

$0.06 per image at 2K

Krea 3 looks particularly interesting for advertising, product photography, and creative production.

Although there's a catch.

Its image editing capabilities look considerably more convincing than some of its text-to-image results, where artifacts can still be noticeable.

And despite the speed improvements, we're not quite at real-time editing yet.

So which one is more interesting?

FLUX 3 Image Klein is compelling if you want local generation, model customization, low API costs, and more control over image composition.

Krea 3 looks especially useful if you're editing existing visuals and need fast, consistent results.

But here's the bigger picture.

AI image generation is getting cheaper. AI image editing is getting faster. And the difference between generating an image and actually working with it is finally starting to disappear.

At this rate, spending several minutes waiting for a single AI image edit will soon feel positively prehistoric.

items.videoDescription:
I was watching Claude Code coordinate its army of AI agents. And suddenly, things got a little terrifying.
The task? Working with 60 videos simultaneously.
Claude decided that the most efficient way for me to review the results was to put all 60 videos on a single screen.

At once.
With everyone talking.
The result? A wall of tiny talking heads, a deafening wall of noise, and one very confused human.
It's hilarious. For now.
But imagine explaining to AI agents in a couple of years why humans can barely handle three tasks at once.

"Oh, I see," the AI will say politely. "Interesting. But why is this biological jelly telling me what to do?"
Welcome to the future of human-AI collaboration.
AI agents are getting faster. Humans aren't.

items.title: Google's Elephant-Goldfish Model: Smarter AI Coding With Fresh Agents
items.excerpt: Google just open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM), a new plugin that changes how AI coding agents design, review, and plan software. The philosophy is simple: "Design with an elephant. Review with a goldfish." A
items.videoDescription:
Google just open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM), a new plugin that changes how AI coding agents design, review, and plan software.

The philosophy is simple:

"Design with an elephant. Review with a goldfish."

And it's a surprisingly clever approach to one of the biggest problems in AI-assisted software development: agents becoming biased by their own context.

Here's how it works.

THE ELEPHANT

An AI agent with deep project context remembers your architecture, requirements, previous decisions, and technical constraints.

It helps brainstorm solutions, evaluate trade-offs, and prepare a detailed software specification before implementation.

THE GOLDFISH

Fresh AI subagents review that specification without seeing the original conversation.

They examine the document and relevant source code, challenge assumptions, identify missing requirements, and look for architectural risks.

Because they weren't involved in the original decisions, they can spot problems that a context-heavy agent might overlook.

WHAT'S INCLUDED?

• AI-assisted brainstorming and architecture planning.

• Structured software specification generation.

• Multi-agent reviews with isolated contexts.

• Detection of missing assumptions and design inconsistencies.

• Documentation bootstrapping for existing codebases.

• Drift detection between approved specifications and actual code.

• Integration with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Google Antigravity.

• Free and open source under Apache 2.0.

The important idea is that more context isn't always better.

Long-running AI coding sessions can accumulate assumptions, reinforce earlier mistakes, and become increasingly confident in flawed decisions.

EGM separates the agent that designs the solution from the agents that challenge it.

The developer still makes the final architectural decisions and approves the specification before implementation.

This doesn't replace automated tests, code review, or engineering judgment. It's an additional verification layer designed to catch problems earlier.

The plugin originated inside Google, but the GitHub repository explicitly states that it is not an officially supported Google product.

GitHub:
https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model

Documentation:
https://egm.dev/

Install for Claude Code:

claude plugin marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model
claude plugin install egm@egm

Install for Codex CLI:

codex plugin marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model
codex plugin add egm@egm

Would you trust an AI agent to review its own architecture, or would you rather give the job to an agent with a completely fresh perspective?

items.title: Blender Running on iPhone Duo?! Eevee, Cycles & AI-Generated 3D Worlds | Hyper3D
items.excerpt: Remember when running Blender required a proper desktop workstation? Well, apparently, we're now putting it on foldable phones. Hyper3D by Deemos just demonstrated Blender running on Apple's iPhone Duo, complete with Eev
items.videoDescription:
Remember when running Blender required a proper desktop workstation?

Well, apparently, we're now putting it on foldable phones.

Hyper3D by Deemos just demonstrated Blender running on Apple's iPhone Duo, complete with Eevee and Cycles rendering engines.

And the 3D scene wasn't even modeled manually.

It was generated from a single image using Hyper3D WorldGen.

Yes. One image. An entire 3D environment. Blender running on a foldable iPhone.

Welcome to 2026.

Here's how the demonstrated workflow works.

Step 1: Generate a 3D world from one image

Hyper3D WorldGen analyzes a reference image and reconstructs an editable three-dimensional environment.

Unlike a simple image-to-3D generator, WorldGen attempts to understand an entire scene:

Identifies individual objects and their positions

Generates editable 3D meshes

Reconstructs spatial relationships

Estimates scale, orientation, and physical properties

Combines mesh objects with Gaussian Splatting for environmental detail

Step 2: Bring the scene into Blender

The generated environment can be exported for further editing in professional 3D software.

And here's where Deemos decided to show off.

Instead of opening Blender on a workstation, they demonstrated it running on the iPhone Duo.

Apple's foldable iPhone offers a larger 7.6-inch display when unfolded, giving creators more room to interact with complex interfaces.

Step 3: Edit and render on the phone

The demonstration shows Blender running with support for both rendering engines:

Eevee: Real-time rendering and interactive scene previews

Cycles: Physically based rendering for more advanced lighting and materials

The idea is fascinating.

Generate an entire environment with AI, open it in a professional 3D application, adjust the scene, experiment with lighting, and continue working without sitting at your desktop computer.

But there's an important catch.

This is a technical demonstration, not an announcement of an official, publicly available Blender release for iPhone.

The Blender Foundation's official roadmap still lists native iPad and iOS support as an initiative on hold.

And Deemos hasn't published enough technical details to independently verify how the mobile port works, which Blender features are supported, or how Eevee and Cycles perform under sustained workloads.

So don't expect to replace your RTX workstation with an iPhone just yet.

Still, here's why I find this particularly exciting.

We're seeing two technologies moving toward each other.

AI is making complex 3D content dramatically easier to create.

And powerful mobile hardware is making professional creative tools increasingly portable.

Put those together, and the possibilities become genuinely interesting.

Imagine taking a photograph, generating a complete editable 3D environment, and making changes while sitting in a café or traveling.

No workstation. No complicated manual modeling process.

Just an idea, AI-generated geometry, and a professional 3D editor in your pocket.

We've spent decades making computers powerful enough for 3D creation.

Now we're trying to make 3D creation portable enough to go anywhere.

And apparently, someone at Deemos really wanted to run Cycles on a phone.

items.title: Super Mario 64 in Mixed Reality at 90 FPS! Built with Claude Opus 5.5 + PICO
items.excerpt: Remember playing Super Mario 64 on the Nintendo 64? Now imagine pulling Mario out of the game and watching him run around on your actual desk. Well, someone just made that happen. Developer and XR specialist Lucas Martin
items.videoDescription:
Remember playing Super Mario 64 on the Nintendo 64?

Now imagine pulling Mario out of the game and watching him run around on your actual desk.

Well, someone just made that happen.

Developer and XR specialist Lucas Martinic has recreated Super Mario 64 as a fully interactive mixed reality experience using Claude Opus 5.5 and PICO CLI.

And the result is absolutely magical.

This isn't just a giant virtual screen floating in your room.

It's a genuine 3D experience where the original game world exists inside your physical environment.

Here's what makes this experiment special:

Native 90 FPS: The original Super Mario 64 runs at 90 frames per second in mixed reality.

True 3D rendering: The world has proper spatial depth, rather than simply displaying a flat game window.

Mixed reality gameplay: Explore the Mushroom Kingdom through a floating portal in your room.

Mario in your room: Literally pick Mario up from the game and place him on your real desk.

AI-assisted development: Claude Opus 5.5 and PICO CLI helped bring the experience to life.

Original game mechanics: Experience the classic Nintendo 64 gameplay in an entirely new way.

And here's my favorite part.

This isn't an AI-generated imitation of Super Mario 64.

It's the actual game, adapted from its decompiled code to work in a spatial computing environment.

The developer used Claude Opus 5.5 together with PICO's development tools to create the mixed reality integration.

The demonstration runs on unreleased PICO hardware, and the mod isn't publicly available yet.

It's also an independent fan project, not an official Nintendo or PICO release.

But here's why I find this so exciting.

We've spent decades playing video games inside rectangular screens.

Now we're getting closer to a world where those games can escape the screen and become part of our physical surroundings.

And with AI coding agents dramatically simplifying XR development, experiments like this are becoming increasingly accessible to independent creators.

A 30-year-old video game. Modern mixed reality hardware. One developer. And an AI coding agent.

Sometimes the future of gaming isn't about creating another photorealistic AAA blockbuster.

Sometimes it's about bringing a little piece of your childhood into the real world.

And honestly, watching Mario run around on a desk might be one of the most charming XR experiments I've seen recently.

items.title: Meshy AI Turns Any Photo Into a 3D-Printable Relief | Image to 3D in Seconds
items.excerpt: What if you could turn an ordinary photograph into a physical 3D sculpture? Not just generate a 3D image. Actually create a raised relief that you can print, engrave, or turn into a decorative object. Meet Meshy's new 3D
items.videoDescription:
What if you could turn an ordinary photograph into a physical 3D sculpture?

Not just generate a 3D image.

Actually create a raised relief that you can print, engrave, or turn into a decorative object.

Meet Meshy's new 3D Relief tool, which transforms a single photograph into a printable 3D relief model.

And the process is surprisingly simple.

Here's how it works:

Upload a photo: Choose a portrait, illustration, artwork, or another image.

Choose the relief type: Select Low Relief or High Relief depending on how much depth you want.

Generate the geometry: AI interprets the image and creates a raised 3D surface with a flat back.

Adjust the depth: Fine-tune the size, thickness, and carving depth in an interactive preview.

Export the result: Download a 3D model for printing or a depth map for engraving.

And here's where things get interesting.

Meshy offers two different approaches.

Low Relief (Bas-Relief)

Creates a relatively shallow raised surface, with details extending only slightly above the background.

Perfect for coins, badges, plaques, decorative signs, and engraved-style artwork.

High Relief

Creates stronger depth separation, making foreground objects stand out much more dramatically.

Better suited for decorative wall panels, portraits, sculptures, and more expressive designs.

But the really useful part is the export.

Meshy supports:

STL and 3MF: For 3D printing.

16-bit depth maps: For laser engraving and other height-map workflows.

Adjustable carving depth: Control how far details extend from the surface.

Flat-backed geometry: Makes the resulting object easier to print and mount.

Live preview: Experiment with dimensions and depth without regenerating the model.

According to Meshy's documentation, generating a relief takes approximately 50 seconds and costs 20 credits.

Adjusting the depth and other settings afterward doesn't consume additional generation credits.

And here's why I find this particularly useful.

We've spent years generating beautiful AI images.

But turning those images into actual physical objects has usually required additional modeling, sculpting, or specialized software.

Now you can take a photograph, convert it into a relief, export an STL, and send it to a 3D printer.

Imagine creating personalized wall art, decorative panels, custom badges, souvenirs, or even physical versions of your favorite AI-generated illustrations.

Of course, there's an important limitation.

This isn't full 3D reconstruction.

Meshy generates a relief based on what it can infer from one image. It doesn't recover the true geometry of the entire object.

Lighting, shadows, perspective, and background separation can all influence the result.

And multi-color printing and texture mapping aren't supported in the current Relief workflow.

Still, it's a fascinating connection between generative AI and physical manufacturing.

Because the future of AI-generated visuals isn't necessarily limited to screens.

Sometimes you might actually want to hold the result in your hands.

One photo. One AI-generated relief. One 3D printer.

And suddenly, your image becomes a physical object.

Try Meshy 3D Relief:
https://www.meshy.ai/

Official step-by-step tutorial:
https://www.meshy.ai/tutorials/how-to-make-a-3d-relief

Documentation and technical details:
https://help.meshy.ai/en/articles/900000043-how-to-use-meshy-to-design-relief-models

items.title: Claude Code & Codex: Understand AI-Generated Code Before You Merge | diff-tour
items.excerpt: Your AI coding agent just modified 15 files, added 800 lines of code, and proudly announced: "All done. Everything works." Great. But do you actually understand what it changed? Meet diff-tour, a free, open-source tool t
items.videoDescription:
Your AI coding agent just modified 15 files, added 800 lines of code, and proudly announced:

"All done. Everything works."

Great.

But do you actually understand what it changed?

Meet diff-tour, a free, open-source tool that walks you through code changes the way an experienced software engineer would review them.

It works with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other AI coding assistants.

And instead of dumping a giant Git diff in front of you, it creates an interactive, step-by-step explanation.

Here's what diff-tour does:

Explains the big picture: Why the changes were made and how they fit into your existing codebase.

Shows what matters: Highlights the files you should examine, including related files that weren't modified.

Asks the right questions: What happens if something fails? Can this safely run twice? Will existing functionality still work?

Identifies real problems: Separates must-fix issues from optional improvements and explains why suspicious-looking code might actually be safe.

Teaches you to think like a senior engineer: Sometimes it asks you to predict what could go wrong before revealing the explanation.

Uses actual Git data: Every displayed line of repository code comes directly from Git, not from something the AI invented.

And here's the interesting part.

The entire review runs in read-only mode.

Your AI agent can inspect and explain the code, but it cannot modify your repository during the tour.

The tool uses your existing Claude Code or Codex account, and generating a review typically takes around 2–5 minutes, according to the developers.

How to install diff-tour on macOS or Linux:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/init-co-jp/diff-tour/main/install.sh | sh

Then navigate to your Git project and run:

tour

Choose the changes you want to review and let the walkthrough begin.

You can navigate between explanations, explore code, answer questions, and investigate potential problems before merging anything.

My suggestion: add this to your AI coding workflow.

Let Claude Code or Codex implement a feature.

Run tour to understand the changes.

Identify the issues that actually need fixing.

Give those findings to Claude Opus 5.5.

Ask it to explain its proposed fixes before touching any code.

Approve the changes, run the tests, and review the final diff.

Here's a prompt you can use with Opus 5.5 after the review:

"diff-tour reviewed my latest code changes and identified these must-fix issues:

[PASTE FINDINGS HERE]

For each issue, explain how you plan to fix it and which files you'll modify. Wait for my approval before making any changes.

Once approved, implement the fixes, run the relevant tests, and report which issues are resolved and which remain."

Of course, an AI-generated review doesn't replace proper testing or human judgment.

But it gives you something increasingly valuable in the age of agentic coding.

Understanding.

Because generating code is getting ridiculously easy.

Understanding, maintaining, and safely shipping that code is still your responsibility.

And frankly, having a patient senior-engineer-style walkthrough every time your AI agent finishes a task sounds pretty useful.

diff-tour on GitHub:
https://github.com/init-co-jp/diff-tour

Free, open source, MIT licensed.

#ClaudeCode #OpenAICodex #DiffTour #CodeReview #AICoding #VibeCoding #Shorts

items.title: Microsoft TokenEconomizer: Cut Claude Code & Codex Costs by Up to 30.9%
items.excerpt: What if your AI coding agents could do the same work while spending significantly less money? Without switching to a cheaper model. Without rewriting your prompts. And without sacrificing much, if any, performance? Micro
items.videoDescription:
What if your AI coding agents could do the same work while spending significantly less money?

Without switching to a cheaper model. Without rewriting your prompts. And without sacrificing much, if any, performance?

Microsoft Research just released TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin designed to make AI coding agents more efficient.

And the benchmark results are pretty impressive.

According to Microsoft's research:

18.4–30.9% lower average costs across five agent and model combinations.

30 out of 30 tests across repositories and model configurations showed cost reductions.

4 out of 5 configurations improved their task success rates.

277 SWE-Bench tasks were used to evaluate the system across six repositories.

And here's the interesting part.

TokenEconomizer doesn't modify the AI model itself.

Instead, it learns how your agents work and helps them stop wasting resources on the same problems over and over again.

Here's how it works:

1. Micro-Skills: Stop Rediscovering Your Codebase

Your agent keeps forgetting which commands work, where files are located, and how your project is configured.

TokenEconomizer can learn these details from previous sessions and reuse them.

Less repetitive research. Fewer unnecessary tool calls.

2. Tool Pruning: Stop Loading Tools Nobody Uses

Every available tool consumes context.

TokenEconomizer identifies tools that repeatedly go unused and removes them from subsequent sessions.

Your agent gets a leaner working environment without losing access to the tools it actually needs.

3. Failure-Loop Detection: Stop Repeating the Same Mistakes

Ever watched Claude Code or Codex try the same broken solution five times?

TokenEconomizer detects suspicious failure loops and can prompt the agent to change its approach.

It doesn't automatically terminate your session. It helps the agent recognize when it's getting nowhere.

And it works with:

Claude Code

OpenAI Codex

GitHub Copilot CLI

Pi

OpenCode (experimental support)

Want to try it?

Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer.git

For Claude Code:

claude plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer"
claude plugin install tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer

For Codex:

codex plugin marketplace add "$PWD/TokenEconomizer"
codex plugin add tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer

Run the installation commands from the directory containing the cloned repository. Keep that directory in place because the plugin runs from it.

One important detail: tool pruning and failure-loop detection are enabled by default, while Micro-Skills must be enabled separately.

And here's why I find this particularly interesting.

We've spent the last few years making AI coding agents smarter, giving them larger context windows, more tools, and increasingly sophisticated reasoning capabilities.

But we've paid much less attention to making them economical.

An AI agent that solves a $2 problem for $20 isn't particularly intelligent from a business perspective.

TokenEconomizer takes a different approach.

Instead of asking the model to think harder, it helps the agent remember what already worked, ignore what it doesn't need, and recognize when it's stuck.

Of course, the reported savings come from controlled benchmarks. They're not guaranteed for every project, and one tested configuration showed a small decline in task success.

Still, this is exactly the kind of optimization that could make autonomous coding agents more practical for everyday development.

The future of AI coding isn't just smarter models. It's smarter use of the models we already have.

And saving 20–30% on agent costs sounds like a pretty good start.

TokenEconomizer on GitHub:
https://github.com/microsoft/TokenEconomizer

Research paper and interactive benchmarks:
https://tokeneconomizer.github.io/

Free and open source under Apache 2.0.

items.videoDescription:
n8n just launched Nod, a free, open-source desktop AI agent that can browse websites, use your apps, and complete real-world tasks on your computer.

Think Claude Cowork, OpenAI Codex, or other autonomous AI assistants, but with n8n's automation DNA.

Nod is a standalone application from n8n Labs, currently available as a research preview.

What's inside?

• Local sandbox: Nod operates in an isolated environment with its own browser and workspace.

• MCP integration: connect external tools and services through the Model Context Protocol.

• Browser automation: navigate websites, fill out forms, download files, and complete multi-step tasks.

• App integrations: work with Gmail, Google Calendar, Slack, Notion, and other connected services.

• Bring your own AI model: support for multiple AI providers, including OpenAI and Anthropic.

• Scheduled tasks: automate recurring activities like monitoring prices, preparing reports, and checking invoices.

• Permission controls: Nod checks actions against your instructions and asks for approval when necessary.

• Open source: the code is available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license.

Unlike traditional n8n workflows, Nod is designed for individual users who want to delegate tasks directly to an AI agent.

It's an interesting entry into an increasingly crowded desktop agent market.

The real question is whether n8n's automation experience can make Nod more reliable and useful than the alternatives.

Nod is still experimental, and its security checks and task execution aren't guaranteed to be error-free.

items.excerpt: What if you could generate a 3D character, give it a skeleton, and make it walk, run, or jump using nothing but text prompts? Tripo just upgraded its Rigging & Animation tools in Tripo Studio. And it's another step towar
items.videoDescription:
What if you could generate a 3D character, give it a skeleton, and make it walk, run, or jump using nothing but text prompts?

Tripo just upgraded its Rigging & Animation tools in Tripo Studio.

And it's another step toward turning AI-generated 3D models into actual animated game assets.

Here's what's new:

Full-body auto-rigging: Automatically creates skeletons, including hand and finger bones.

5 skeleton presets: UE5 Mannequin, Mixamo, VRM 1.0, Unity Humanoid, and ActorCore.

Text to Motion: Describe an action and generate a 1–10 second animation.

Multi-stage Motion: Combine up to five actions into one sequence.

Animated export: Export rigged characters with skeletal animations for use in external software.

Want your character to walk, turn around, sprint, jump, and land?

Just describe the sequence.

And the interesting part is that you can choose the target skeleton before generating the animation.

That could save developers a considerable amount of manual bone mapping when moving characters into Unreal Engine, Unity, Blender, or other 3D software.

But there's a catch.

AI-generated doesn't automatically mean production-ready.

Tripo itself acknowledges that automatic skinning can produce deformation problems, particularly around shoulders, hips, and fingers.

And you can't manually fix the skeleton or skin weights inside Tripo Studio.

For that, you'll still need Blender, Maya, or another professional 3D application.

A few technical details:

Humanoid rigging supports up to 100,000 triangles.

Characters should start in T-pose or A-pose.

Auto-rigging costs 20 credits.

Text-to-Motion generation costs another 20 credits.

Preset animations from the library are free.

And yes, A-pose is officially supported.

Some traditional riggers are probably already preparing their angry comments.

But here's my bigger question.

Why are so many AI startups trying to reinvent entire creative software packages?

We've already got Blender, Maya, Cinema 4D, Unreal Engine, Premiere Pro, After Effects, DaVinci Resolve, and Nuke.

Mature tools with enormous communities and decades of development behind them.

Do we really need another miniature animation studio inside every AI startup?

I'd much rather see brilliant AI plugins and integrations for the software professionals already use.

Let AI handle the repetitive work.

Let experienced artists keep their familiar tools, workflows, and creative control.

Tripo already offers DCC integrations, and that's precisely the direction I'd love to see expanded.

Because the future of AI-assisted 3D production shouldn't require rebuilding the entire creative industry from scratch.

Better AI tools. Inside better existing software.

That sounds like a much more useful revolution.
