items.title: Plasticity 2026.2 Is Here! Asset Libraries, Curvature Analysis & New NURBS Modeling Tools
items.excerpt: Plastic Software just released Plasticity 2026.2, bringing some very welcome improvements to one of the most interesting hard-surface modeling tools around. New asset libraries, better surface analysis, improved snapping
items.videoDescription:
Plastic Software just released Plasticity 2026.2, bringing some very welcome improvements to one of the most interesting hard-surface modeling tools around.

New asset libraries, better surface analysis, improved snapping, and a completely new constraint system.

And if you're tired of modeling the same bolts, hinges, and mechanical components for the hundredth time, there's some particularly good news.

Here's what's new.

1. Assets: Your own reusable 3D library

This is probably the biggest workflow improvement in the update.

Plasticity now lets you organize your models into reusable asset libraries.

Create a component once, save it, and drag it into another project whenever you need it.

Build collections of mechanical parts.

Organize reusable components into folders.

Drag assets directly into your viewport.

Export and share asset libraries with other artists.

Reuse existing geometry instead of rebuilding everything.

Basically, LEGO for industrial designers.

Except the pieces can have considerably more complicated surfaces.

2. Curvature Analysis Shader

Plasticity now includes a dedicated shader for analyzing surface curvature.

And this is particularly useful when you're trying to achieve smooth, high-quality NURBS surfaces.

There are three visualization modes:

Gaussian: Reveals abrupt changes in surface curvature.

Mean: Helps evaluate overall surface smoothness.

Max: Highlights areas that could cause problems during thickening or offset operations.

So instead of discovering that your beautifully modeled surface has problems at the very end, you can catch them while you're still working.

3. Project Align

A new modeling tool for aligning surface control vertices to a reference surface.

You can align geometry along a vector direction or the surface normal, using Constrained or xNURBS solving methods.

This gives artists more control when connecting complex curved surfaces.

One important detail: Project Align is available in Plasticity Studio.

4. Surface Constraints: G0, G1, and G2

The Studio edition also introduces a new constraint system designed to maintain continuity between connected surfaces.

For anyone unfamiliar with NURBS terminology:

G0: Surfaces meet at the same position.

G1: Surfaces meet with matching tangent directions.

G2: Surfaces maintain curvature continuity for smoother transitions.

The interesting part is that these constraints can remain active while you transform the geometry.

So when you adjust one surface, Plasticity can help preserve the relationship with its neighbors.

That's a significant improvement for detailed product design and complex hard-surface modeling.

There is one limitation, though.

Constraints are not yet saved with the project file.

They currently work within the active modeling session.

5. Better Snapping and Modeling Tools

Plasticity 2026.2 also improves 15 existing modeling commands.

Highlights include:

Improved Edge Align and Vertex Align.

New Collinear alignment options for Class A-style modeling.

Better control over partial surface alignment.

Improved Move, Rotate, Slide, and Bridge Curve tools.

Visual highlighting when Boolean, Hollow, or Thicken operations fail.

Better snapping to construction planes and instanced objects.

Faster PolySpline viewport rendering.

And there are plenty of smaller interface improvements.

The Outliner has been refined, the viewport is more customizable, and there's now a Home View command to return to a standard isometric perspective.

But here's what I find interesting about this release.

Plasticity has always occupied a rather unusual position between traditional CAD software and artistic 3D modeling.

It offers precise NURBS geometry without forcing artists into a complicated engineering workflow.

And with reusable Assets, surface constraints, and better analysis tools, it's becoming increasingly practical for larger projects.

Instead of constantly rebuilding geometry, you can start developing your own library of components and spend more time actually designing.

That's particularly appealing for product visualization, sci-fi hard-surface modeling, industrial design, and concept art.

And it's a reminder that not every meaningful software update needs a giant AI button.

Sometimes, better modeling tools are exactly what artists need.

Plasticity 2026.2 was released on October 19, 2026.

Official release notes:
https://doc.plasticity.xyz/release-notes/whats-new-2026.2

Plasticity website:
https://www.plasticity.xyz/

items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: The New King of Open-Weight Speech Recognition?
items.excerpt: What if AI could transcribe an entire meeting, distinguish every speaker, translate conversations, and tell you exactly when each word was spoken? Even when several people are talking over each other? Meet NVIDIA Nemotro
items.videoDescription:
What if AI could transcribe an entire meeting, distinguish every speaker, translate conversations, and tell you exactly when each word was spoken?

Even when several people are talking over each other?

Meet NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, a new open-weight speech recognition model designed to handle some of the most difficult problems in audio transcription.

And according to NVIDIA's benchmarks, it's setting new standards for open-weight speech AI.

Here's what Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe can do:

40 languages: Transcribe and process multilingual conversations.

Speaker diarization: Identify who's speaking, even when voices overlap.

Word-level timestamps: Assign precise start and end times to individual words.

Speech translation: Translate spoken content into other languages.

Smart transcription: Remove filler words, clean up grammar and punctuation, or preserve every spoken word.

Audio understanding: Answer questions about the contents of a recording.

Long recordings: Process up to 60 minutes of audio in a single request.

Context-aware recognition: Improve transcription of names, technical terminology, and specialized vocabulary.

And here's where things get interesting.

Most transcription tools struggle when several people speak simultaneously.

Think podcasts, business meetings, interviews, or chaotic group conversations.

NVIDIA designed Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe specifically to handle these situations.

The benchmark results are impressive.

According to NVIDIA's published evaluations:

4.71% word error rate on the English Open ASR Leaderboard.

4.62% word error rate on the multilingual Open ASR Leaderboard.

15.80% speaker-attributed word error rate across several challenging multi-speaker datasets.

These results place Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ahead of the other open-weight systems NVIDIA compared against.

And there's another interesting technical detail.

Despite its 34 billion total parameters, the model activates only approximately 4.3 billion parameters during inference.

That's thanks to its hybrid Mixture-of-Experts architecture, which combines speech encoding, speaker identification, and language processing.

The model is available in several formats:

BF16 for maximum accuracy

FP8 for reduced memory requirements

NVFP4 for optimized deployment on NVIDIA Blackwell hardware

But there's a catch.

This isn't a tiny speech model you can casually run on any laptop.

The standard BF16 deployment is documented for an NVIDIA H100 with 80 GB of memory, while optimized variants require other high-end GPUs.

And although NVIDIA reports extremely high transcription throughput with its optimized inference stack, those particular performance improvements aren't all included in the public release yet.

Still, this is a significant development for open-weight AI.

Imagine processing hours of interviews, podcasts, meetings, and video footage without manually identifying speakers or synchronizing subtitles.

Or building AI agents that can analyze entire conversations, extract important details, translate speech, and generate searchable transcripts.

For creators, researchers, developers, and businesses working with audio, that's a pretty powerful toolkit.

We're moving from AI that simply converts speech into text to AI that actually understands the structure and context of a conversation.

And increasingly, you can run that technology on infrastructure you control.

Try NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe:
https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B

Official research and benchmarks:
https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe/

items.title: H3 Dials: Control MiniMax H3 AI Videos With 14 KB Files (No Training)
items.excerpt: What if you could control AI-generated video with sliders instead of training LoRAs or endlessly rewriting prompts? Meet H3 Dials by MatlowAI, a new training-free steering system for MiniMax H3 that turns simple text pro
items.videoDescription:
What if you could control AI-generated video with sliders instead of training LoRAs or endlessly rewriting prompts?

Meet H3 Dials by MatlowAI, a new training-free steering system for MiniMax H3 that turns simple text prompt pairs into tiny 14 KB control files.

And these controls can change dynamically throughout a video.

Instead of training a new model, H3 Dials extracts directions from MiniMax H3's processed text embedding space.

Give it two contrasting prompts, like "completely frozen scene" versus "explosive dynamic movement," and it creates a reusable steering dial.

Negative values push generation toward one concept. Positive values push it toward the other.

Here's what makes H3 Dials interesting:

• 14 KB steering files: tiny .safetensors files instead of large trained LoRA adapters.

• No model training: generate custom controls from contrasting text prompts in approximately one minute.

• Interactive sliders: control motion, atmosphere, lighting, visual style, and other learned directions directly in ComfyUI.

• Dial stacking: combine multiple steering vectors to influence several visual characteristics simultaneously.

• Time curves: animate the strength of each dial throughout a video instead of applying one constant setting.

• Precise visual effects: trigger a half-second anime-style impact frame during a punch, then return to the original cinematic style.

• LoRA compatibility: combine steering dials with existing LoRA adapters.

• Pika H3 Flex support: demonstrated with faster distilled MiniMax H3 workflows.

• ComfyUI integration: use ComfyUI-MAINodes and ComfyUI-Dials to create, load, combine, and animate steering controls.

The biggest innovation is temporal control.

Imagine a fight scene that stays photorealistic until the moment of impact, briefly transforms into a dramatic ink-drawn anime frame, and then returns to realism.

H3 Dials can modulate that effect through a time curve without training a dedicated video LoRA.

But there are limitations.

Dials steer concepts the underlying model already understands. They cannot teach it entirely new characters or visual concepts, and extreme strengths can introduce unwanted changes to motion, identity, or audio.

The steering files are released under the MiniMax H3 Community License, while the ComfyUI-Dials code uses AGPL-3.0.

items.title: Openjutsu: Free Open-Source Higgsfield Genjutsu Alternative | MiniMax H3 + ComfyUI
items.excerpt: Remember when ComfyUI challenged the AI community to rebuild Higgsfield's popular creative tools? Well, the joke is turning into actual software. Meet Openjutsu, a free, open-source alternative to Higgsfield Genjutsu tha
items.videoDescription:
Remember when ComfyUI challenged the AI community to rebuild Higgsfield's popular creative tools?

Well, the joke is turning into actual software.

Meet Openjutsu, a free, open-source alternative to Higgsfield Genjutsu that lets you replace people, outfits, objects, and backgrounds in existing videos.

And the best part?

It runs locally on your own GPU.

This project is part of the broader #OpenSourceHiggsfield movement launched by ComfyUI with a rather cheeky message:

"Higgsfield said they'd open source their platform. Let's help."

And apparently, developers took that seriously.

So what can Openjutsu actually do?

1. Replace people in videos

Upload a video, provide a reference photo, and replace the original character with someone else.

The system attempts to preserve the original movements, gestures, camera angles, edits, and soundtrack.

And we're not talking about a simple face swap.

Openjutsu can replace an entire character, including their hairstyle, clothing, and body appearance.

2. Replace multiple characters

Advanced mode supports up to four characters, each with their own reference image.

Imagine taking a music video and replacing the entire band with completely different characters.

3. Edit objects and environments

Change clothing, hairstyles, props, or backgrounds.

Remove unwanted objects or introduce new visual elements.

4. Fix the results

Dedicated post-processing tools help improve facial details, correct colors, and reduce some of the artifacts introduced by video generation.

And here's how it works under the hood.

Openjutsu combines several existing AI models into one coordinated workflow:

MiniMax H3: Regenerates the video while following the original motion.

SAM 3.1: Tracks people and objects throughout the footage.

Qwen3-VL: Analyzes scenes and helps identify the correct characters.

ComfyUI: Orchestrates the entire generation pipeline.

FLUX.3 Klein: Provides additional image preparation and relighting capabilities.

The application itself is built with Next.js and uses ComfyUI as its generation backend.

But here's the really interesting part.

You don't necessarily need an expensive cloud GPU.

The developer tested Openjutsu on an RTX 4060 Ti with 16 GB VRAM and 64 GB system RAM.

It's not exactly fast.

A six-second video at 480p takes approximately 6–13 minutes on that configuration.

But it works.

And you don't have to upload your footage to a commercial video-generation service.

Of course, there are limitations.

Mirrors and reflections can confuse the system. Complex scenes may require manual corrections. Faces sometimes need additional processing.

And using reference photos of real people requires appropriate permission, especially when publishing synthetic footage.

But here's what I find fascinating about this entire movement.

We're discovering that many impressive AI applications are essentially sophisticated workflows built around existing foundation models.

The models themselves are enormously expensive to train.

But the applications built around them?

Those can often be recreated, customized, and improved by independent developers.

And with modern AI coding agents, building those applications is becoming considerably easier.

This is a pretty interesting shift in the economics of AI creative software.

A company builds a polished product around powerful models.

The community studies the workflow.

Someone rebuilds it using open tools.

And suddenly there's a free alternative you can run on your own machine.

The Openjutsu application is available under the MIT license, although the underlying AI models retain their own licenses and usage restrictions.

Maybe the future of creative AI won't belong exclusively to companies with the prettiest interfaces.

Maybe it'll also belong to developers who can reconstruct the entire experience over a weekend.

And judging by the #OpenSourceHiggsfield movement, they're already having quite a lot of fun doing it.

items.videoDescription:
Apparently, Unitree decided that the best way to introduce its new humanoid robot was to make an action movie.

And honestly, I'm not complaining.

Meet Unitree H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian, a humanoid robot that looks like it walked straight out of a sci-fi blockbuster.

In the official demonstration, it:

Punches and kicks car doors, leaving visible damage

Performs backflips and martial arts moves

Jumps from a 4-meter-high platform

Confronts an armed attacker in a staged security scenario

Pushes a mannequin away from an approaching car

Lifts the front of a vehicle in a simulated rescue operation

Yes, apparently, robot bodyguards now come with their own stunt choreography.

And Unitree claims up to 8 hours of endurance.

There's a catch, though.

That figure refers to standing endurance, not eight hours of continuous kung fu.

The company also hasn't explained whether these impressive moves were performed autonomously, remotely controlled, or through preprogrammed sequences.

So while the hardware looks extraordinary, we're not quite at the point where you can hire a robot to independently handle your personal security.

And I have to admit, the rescue scene raised a few questions.

I'm not entirely sure the mannequin survived the robot's rescue attempt any better than the approaching car.

But my favorite part?

After showing us a humanoid machine smashing cars, jumping four meters, and fighting attackers, Unitree ends with a friendly reminder:

Please use the robot safely and in a friendly manner.

Of course. What could possibly go wrong?

items.videoDescription:
What if a language model could check several possible continuations at once? UBTree combines a parallel unigram proposer, a parallel bigram selector and a verification tree to speed up speculative decoding.

If you've ever opened a complicated ComfyUI workflow and wondered whether you're looking at an AI pipeline or a bowl of spaghetti, this one's for you.

Meet ComfyUI Zip Ties, a free, open-source extension that brings actual cable management to your node graphs.

And it's ridiculously satisfying.

Here's how it works.

Hold Z, drag your mouse across a bunch of tangled connections, and watch them snap together into a neat ribbon.

That's it.

Your ComfyUI workflow just went from an electrical engineering nightmare to something resembling a professionally managed server rack.

And the developer didn't stop there.

Version 0.3 includes:

Colorful zip ties: Organize your cables with different colors.

90-degree bends: Because apparently even virtual cables need proper routing.

Wire highlighting: See exactly which connections you're bundling before making a mess.

Reroute support: Tidy even the most complicated workflows.

Adjustable ties: Move, rotate, recolor, or remove them whenever you want.

Copy and paste: Zip ties follow your nodes when copying connected sections.

Persistent layouts: Your carefully organized cables are saved with the workflow.

And here's the best part.

The extension doesn't modify how your AI workflow actually runs.

It simply makes the connections easier to read and manage.

No extra AI models. No GPU requirements. No unnecessary Python dependencies.

Just one small JavaScript extension making everyone's life a little less miserable.

How to install:

Open ComfyUI-Manager, search for Zip Ties, and click Install.

Or use the Comfy CLI:

comfy node install comfyui-zip-ties

Then hold Z and start organizing your cables.

The project is free, open source, and MIT licensed.

The developer has also submitted a feature request to integrate similar functionality directly into ComfyUI.

And honestly, after seeing this, I don't know how we've survived without it.

We've built AI models capable of generating entire cinematic worlds.

But apparently, one of the most satisfying innovations of 2026 is a virtual cable tie.

Sometimes the smallest improvements are the best.

items.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Real-Time AI Game Rendering at 67 FPS on RTX 5080!
items.excerpt: What if your GPU could turn a simple low-poly game into a photorealistic world in real time? Not by replacing the game engine with a hallucinating AI model. By letting the game engine handle the actual game while AI hand
items.videoDescription:
What if your GPU could turn a simple low-poly game into a photorealistic world in real time?

Not by replacing the game engine with a hallucinating AI model.

By letting the game engine handle the actual game while AI handles the graphics.

Meet Matrix-Game 4.0 by Skywork AI, an open-source hybrid system combining a playable 3D game engine with real-time neural rendering.

And the performance numbers are getting seriously interesting.

67 FPS on an RTX 5080.
58 FPS on an RTX 5070 Ti.
Up to 83 FPS on an RTX 5090.

All at 864 × 480 resolution.

But there's an important detail: those figures measure steady-state neural-rendering throughput under specific benchmark conditions, not guaranteed end-to-end gameplay FPS.

So how does it work?

Matrix-Game 4.0 separates gameplay from visual generation.

1. The game engine handles reality.

A native C++20 engine manages physics, collision detection, character movement, player controls, and game rules.

It renders a lightweight, low-poly version of the scene.

Nothing particularly beautiful. Just enough geometry to establish what actually exists and where everything belongs.

2. AI handles the appearance.

A causal diffusion transformer takes that simple RGB stream and transforms it into detailed video frames.

In real-time mode, it uses the lightweight TAEHV video codec and just one denoising step.

Four output frames are generated per latent chunk.

3. The HUD stays outside the neural network.

Health bars, crosshairs, interface text, and audio are handled separately.

Which is clever.

Because asking diffusion models to generate readable numbers and consistent UI elements is an excellent way to discover entirely new forms of mathematics.

4. The GPU does the heavy lifting.

The optimized implementation uses:

FP8 linear layers

Fused CUDA kernels

CUDA Graphs

Optional SageAttention

Streaming video generation

The researchers also report 60 FPS interactive gameplay on an RTX 5090, with approximately 112 ms from a keypress to the corresponding displayed frame.

That's a different measurement from the 83 FPS rendering-throughput benchmark.

And you can actually play it.

The release includes three environments:

Medieval Castle: Third-person combat in a medieval setting.

Ancient Egypt: A shooter with pyramids and ancient architecture.

City Racing: Urban driving with racing and police-chase modes.

There's also a browser-streaming workflow, so the game can run on a remote machine while players interact through WebRTC.

But here's what I find most interesting.

The game doesn't rely on the AI remembering where every wall, object, or enemy should be.

The engine knows.

The neural network's job is primarily to make the scene look convincing.

This is a much more practical division of responsibilities than asking a video model to invent the graphics, physics, and gameplay simultaneously.

Of course, we're not suddenly replacing Unreal Engine.

The released models are specialized for their supplied environments, the resolution is still modest, and visual consistency can degrade with unfamiliar geometry or rapid camera movement.

And the GPU requirements are hardly modest either.

But the direction is fascinating.

Traditional game engines calculate the world and render it.

Pure generative world models try to predict everything.

Matrix-Game combines the two.

A deterministic game engine for rules.

A generative model for visual appearance.

And potentially, AI coding agents to modify the game itself.

Maybe the future of game graphics isn't entirely traditional rendering or entirely neural generation.

Maybe it's a hybrid where each technology does what it's actually good at.

And getting this approach running at real-time speeds on consumer GPUs is a meaningful step.

items.excerpt: Claude Fable 5.2 is creating CGI animations from scratch by writing Python code to control Blender. No traditional text-to-video generation. Real 3D scenes, procedural geometry, animation, lighting, and rendering driven
items.videoDescription:
Claude Fable 5.2 is creating CGI animations from scratch by writing Python code to control Blender.

No traditional text-to-video generation. Real 3D scenes, procedural geometry, animation, lighting, and rendering driven by code.

In this demonstration shared by Jeremy Berman, Claude Fable 5.2 generates Python scripts that construct a 3D world inside Blender.

Instead of manually building every object and adjusting settings through the interface, an AI coding agent can program the scene directly.

Why does this matter?

• AI-driven 3D creation: Claude writes Python code to construct and manipulate Blender scenes.

• Procedural modeling: geometry, materials, and scene elements can be defined programmatically.

• Animation through code: camera movements and object animations can be controlled using Python.

• Traditional CGI rendering: Blender generates the final frames using its rendering pipeline rather than a diffusion-based video generator.

• Editable results: scripted scenes can be modified, re-rendered, and integrated into existing 3D workflows.

• AI-assisted filmmaking: coding agents could eventually automate increasingly large parts of CGI production.

The interesting part isn't simply that AI can produce an impressive animation.

It's that the animation comes from a programmable 3D environment rather than an opaque sequence of generated video frames.

The camera, lighting, geometry, and animation can remain accessible for further editing.

And that raises a much bigger question.

Could independent filmmakers eventually create full CGI movies for just a few thousand dollars?

We're not there yet. Feature-length production still requires consistent characters, coherent storytelling, art direction, rendering infrastructure, editing, sound, and extensive quality control.

But experiments like this suggest that AI coding agents could significantly reduce the technical effort and cost of producing computer-generated animation.
